As industries rapidly integrate AI technologies, the demand for professionals proficient in AI skills has surged. Job postings with generative AI increased by 15,625% from 2021 to 2024, according to the Lightcast “Speed of Skill Change” report, underscoring significant market demand. Additionally, Lightcast found that AI skills command a 28% salary premium in the Beyond the Buzz: Developing the AI Skills Employers Actually Need report. Who is the ideal candidate for this program? This course is ideal for business professionals, business owners, and consultants seeking practical solutions to turn automation ideas into reality without relying on a development or engineering team. Learners taking this course should be regular users of ChatGPT, Claude, or other generative AI tools and be ready to advance their skills beyond prompting to build automated workflows. How is AI Automation different from AI Essentials? The AI Essentials course covers foundational generative AI skills, like AI prompting, which involves entering specific instructions or queries into AI systems like ChatGPT to generate desired outputs, such as text, images, or code. It involves crafting text prompts to achieve the user's goals. AI Automation goes a step further. It focuses on automating tasks by integrating AI tools into structured workflows. This course teaches you how to connect AI with no-code automation tools like Make.com, Zapier, and n8n to streamline processes, reduce manual work, and enhance efficiency. To learn more about the different AI courses, email us at support@ziplines.com , and someone from our team will get back to you. Are there any prerequisites for the course? Yes. Learners taking this course should be regular users of ChatGPT, Claude, or other generative AI tools and be ready to advance their skills beyond prompting to build automated workflows. Will I have a completed portfolio at the end of the course? The course and the Playbook projects will provide you with content to create a portfolio, but you are responsible for creating a portfolio on the platform of your choice. How many hours a week should I expect to spend on the program? Expect to dedicate approximately 6-8 hours weekly to engaging with online, on-demand content crafted by expert AI practitioners. This includes immersive hands-on activities and assignments within our online learning management system (LMS). You can also attend optional live sessions each week. These two-hour online sessions are a great place to engage with expert AI practitioners who will help you fine-tune your workflows and stay current on the latest AI news. Sessions are recorded and available to watch on demand if you are unable to join live. Will I earn a certificate? Yes, upon successful completion of the course, you will earn a university-issued certificate of completion that verifies your knowledge and hands-on experience in AI Automation. This prestigious credential will help you feel more confident–and help you stand out to your current team or potential employers. What do I need to do to pass the course? In order to receive a certificate of completion, learners must complete 100% of online coursework, achieve 70% or better on each module assessment, and submit all course playbooks. Will I receive credit for this course? No, this is a noncredit course. As such, it is not eligible for financial aid. However, many employers offer reimbursement for continuing education, so check with your human resources department to determine your eligibility. What payment options are offered? There are multiple payment options for this course. The first way is to pay upfront, online. This option also provides the largest savings. We offer both installment and financing options. To find out if you qualify for either of these payment options, fill out the enrollment form to be directed to the payment page. From there, you can click on the "Get Qualified" link to see what options are available. Many employers also offer tuition reimbursement. Our guide gives you suggestions and templates for how to ask your employer to cover the cost of the course. View our reimbursement guide. What is your cancellation and refund policy? We are confident in the quality of our learning experience, having supported thousands of learners and received hundreds of 5-star reviews. Because we believe so strongly in the value and impact of our course, we offer a 7-day money-back guarantee from the start date. If the course isn't the right fit for you, you can withdraw within the first week of your course and receive a full refund, no questions asked. Where does the program take place? Everything is online. You’ll access on-demand content and assignments through our online learning platform and join the optional instructor-led live sessions once a week through a video conference platform. The live sessions are recorded and available for playback on demand. The online Learner Dashboard can be accessed from anywhere with an internet connection on a computer. Who is Ziplines Education? Ziplines Education is a market-driven education company based in Silicon Valley, CA. Kennesaw State University Community and Professional Education collaborates with Ziplines Education to offer innovative and highly rated certificate courses that help adult learners and working professionals build work-ready digital skills and earn industry-recognized credentials. However, many employers offer reimbursement for continuing education, so check with your human resources department to determine your eligibility. What payment options are offered? There are multiple payment options for this course. The first way is to pay upfront, online. This option also provides the largest savings. We offer both installment and financing options. To find out if you qualify for either of these payment options, fill out the enrollment form to be directed to the payment page. From there, you can click on the "Get Qualified" link to see what options are available. Many employers also offer tuition reimbursement. Our guide gives you suggestions and templates for how to ask your employer to cover the cost of the course. View our reimbursement guide. What is your cancellation and refund policy? We are confident in the quality of our learning experience, having supported thousands of learners and received hundreds of 5-star reviews. Because we believe so strongly in the value and impact of our course, we offer a 7-day money-back guarantee from the start date. If the course isn't the right fit for you, you can withdraw within the first week of your course and receive a full refund, no questions asked. Where does the program take place? Everything is online. You’ll access on-demand content and assignments through our online learning platform and join the optional instructor-led live sessions once a week through a video conference platform. The live sessions are recorded and available for playback on demand. The online Learner Dashboard can be accessed from anywhere with an internet connection on a computer. Who is Ziplines Education? Ziplines Education is a market-driven education company based in Silicon Valley, CA. Kennesaw State University Community and Professional Education collaborates with Ziplines Education to offer innovative and highly rated certificate courses that help adult learners and working professionals build work-ready digital skills and earn industry-recognized credentials. Search The Archives Search The Archives Operator And Or Not Enter your search terms Limit by record type Search all record types Limit to collections Limit to digital materials Search field Keyword Title Creator Subject Notes Identifier From year To year Add row About This Catalog: The Kennesaw State University (KSU) Archives catalog contains descriptive information about the content and context of collections preserved within the KSU Archives and Williams Rare Book Museum. These descriptive resources, also known as finding aids, are searchable and allow researchers to discover information about archival materials that may be of interest to them. The archival records described in these finding aids are accessible in our reading room, and links to relevant digital archives are included when available. Using the Catalog: The KSU Archives catalog supports a variety of search techniques. Researchers can conduct keyword searches using the ''Search the Archives'' field above. This field allows researchers to filter searches by collections, digital materials, keywords, titles, subjects, and notes. Researchers can also use the top ribbon to limit searches by Repository, Collection, Digital Material, Subjects, Names, and Record Groups. Filter by Repository: conduct searches within the KSU Archives collection or the Williams Rare Book Museum collection. Filter by Collection: access finding aids for all collections in the KSU Archives and the Williams Rare Book Museum. Filter by Digital Material: access born-digital and digitized materials in the KSU Archives and the Williams Rare Book Museum. Please note that many items in the KSU Archives and Williams Rare Book Museum exist only as physical items and may not have digital surrogates. Filter by Subjects, Names, and Record Groups: access topical themes and names, as well as the record groupings found in the KSU Archives and Williams Rare Book Museum. For additional help, check out our guide to searching and browsing the KSU Archives and Special Collections or watch a video tutorial . Navigating a Finding Aid: Researchers can use finding aids to discover information about a collection’s context, structure, and content. Collection Overview tab: provides contextual information about the collection, including provenance, subjects represented, biographical information, access policies, etc. Collection Organization tab: describes the collection's hierarchical organization. Hierarchies generally include a combination of series, subseries, boxes, files, and items. The right side bar outlines this same information. Container Inventory tab: allows researchers to search for content within the top-level containers of a collection. To search for specific subjects or items represented in a collection, select the ''Collection Overview'' tab and enter a search term into the ''Search Collection'' field on the right. Click the ''Search'' button and view your results. To learn more about the Kennesaw State University Archives and Special Collections, visit our homepage . Looking for digital collections? Here, at Kennesaw State University’s Geer College of the Arts, our highly accomplished faculty and professional staff prepare students for success in a complex global society. We bring together bold thinkers, passionate creators and boundary-pushing performers from the School of Art and Design, Department of Dance, Bailey School of Music, and Department of Theatre and Performance Studies. Our artistic community embraces experimentation, critical thinking and creative risk-taking. Whether on stage, in the studio, or within the community, our students gain hands-on experiences in cutting-edge facilities that shape their creative practice and broaden their worldviews. Geer Family College of the Arts Facilities at Kennesaw State University The facilities of the ever-expanding ArtsKSU district are devoted exclusively to the teaching and presenting of music, theatre and performance studies, dance performance and visual arts. Dr. Bobbie Bailey & Family Performance Center Howard Logan Stillwell Theater Dance Theater Zuckerman Museum Dr. Bobbie Bailey & Family Performance Center The Dr. Bobbie Bailey & Family Performance Center boasts an acoustically superb 624-seat performance hall with variable acoustics that may be optimally configured for musical theater performance, superior live audio reproduction, digital multi-track recording and live video streaming. Learn more and take a virtual tour here . Home to the Bailey School of Music, the Center hosts over 70 performances each year in addition to rehearsals, seminars, recording sessions, and master classes for KSU music students and faculty. The facility also houses the 3,600-square-foot Katherine Scott Rehearsal Hall, acoustically isolated from the performance hall but integrated in the facility’s audio recording and communications infrastructure. The Music Building houses music classrooms, a music technology classroom, studios, practice rooms and the intimate Music Recital Hall. The Joe Mack Wilson Building is home to numerous classrooms, music studios, a theatre technology classroom, the offices of the Dean of the Geer College of the Arts, the Department of Music, and the Department of Theatre and Performance Studies. The Wilson Building is also home to the Zuckerman Museum of Art’s Fine Arts Gallery; it regularly features student exhibitions. Address: 488 Prillaman Way, Kennesaw, GA 30144 KSU Arts District Map Rental Application Howard Logan Stillwell Theater The Department of Theatre and Performance Studies boasts the 320-seat Howard Logan Stillwell Theater, a contemporary proscenium theatre with the option of an orchestra pit or an extended apron. It features a computer controlled lighting system along with a state-of-the-art sound system and is home to many large performances by the Department of Theatre and Performance Studies. The Studio Theater, located next to the Stillwell, is an intimate laboratory theatre used for classes and experimental or contemporary productions. The Onyx Theater, a black box theater used for smaller productions, is in The Wilson Annex. Other theatre facilities include the Scene Shop at Chastain Point and the Costume Shop at KSU Center. Address: 471 Bartow Ave NW, Kennesaw, GA 30144 Directions Call Dance Theater The Department of Dance boasts a state-of-the-art dance facility at Chastain Pointe. The 16,000-square-foot facility houses three large dance studios, faculty offices, student lounge, shower and restroom facilities, a classroom, a costume shop and a scene shop—bringing profound opportunity for the Kennesaw State University Dance Program. Along with being one of the largest studios in metro Atlanta, the main studio is fully equipped with a state-of-the-art A/V system, Harlequin Cascade flooring and a new Steinway piano. Take a virtual tour here ! Address: 1200 Chastain Road, Suite 300, Kennesaw, GA 30144 Opened in March of 2017, the Dance Theater on the Marietta campus (pictured) is the only one of its kind in the Atlanta area built specifically to serve the technical and performance needs of Kennesaw State Dance. This 450-seat facility serves as a home for dance in the region, providing professional standards of dance flooring, lighting, and A/V technology. A unique contemporary aesthetic makes the interior design of this facility unlike any other in the region. The grand drape, for instance, is distinctively unique in its visual appeal and technical functionality. The KSU Dance Theater is located just 15 miles north from downtown Atlanta. Address: 860 Rossbacher Wy, Marietta, GA 30060 Directions Call Zuckerman Museum A unit within the School of Art and Design, the Bernard A. Zuckerman Museum of Art serves as a vital academic resource and cultural focus for students, faculty and members of the community. This KSU Art Museum presents significant works from the University’s permanent art collection and regularly exhibits contemporary works of various media by local and nationally-recognized artists. The Museum's Fine Arts Satellite Gallery in the Wilson Building features faculty, student and alumni projects. At the Geer College of the Arts, we believe every student deserves the support they need to thrive — both creatively and personally. Success in the arts is built not only through talent and hard work, but through a community that cares for one another. Whether you're facing an unexpected financial hardship, looking for academic guidance, or seeking health and wellness resources, we're here to help. Explore the resources below, including the Gary Martin Hays Helping Hands Fund, your amazing academic advising team, and campus support services, to find the assistance you need throughout your journey at Kennesaw State. Don't see what you need? Never hesitate to reach out to the dean's office (Wilson 201 | 470-578-6742). We're here to support your journey. The Gary Martin Hays Helping Hands Fund Purpose The Fund is a flexible financial assistance program for students in the Geer College of the Arts (GCA) at Kennesaw State University. It will provide $1,000 awards for up to 10 students per academic year in need of emergency financial assistance. Selection Criteria Applicants must be enrolled and majoring in a degree within the Geer College of the Arts and demonstrate a personal need due to an unexpected circumstance, crisis, or emergency where financial assistance would make a difference, in the student’s ability to cover the cost of tuition, books, class materials unique to the Arts, and living expenses (rent, food, gas) where the inability to pay would result in a life-altering situation. Our focus is on the development of music education, performance, and scholarship within our community. Our school takes pride in being an all-Steinway institution. Together, we inspire passionate musicians, scholars, and educators, who will continue to enhance our community. We invite you to join us on this incredible journey! Friends of the Bailey School of Music brings together patrons and advocates who believe in the transformative power of music. Amber Solana: Choreographic Copyrights: The Case of Fuller v. Bemis Loïe Fuller’s “Serpentine Dance,"... “a show of swirling silk and rainbow lights”, became an international phenomenon and it forever impacted how dancers can get copyrighted in today’s society. Join me in exploring this research topic I chose for my Dance History Research Project! Amber Solana is a second-year double majoring in dance with a modern concentration and marketing. She’s danced for 16 years and competitively danced for 9 of those years with Studio 4 the Arts in Powder Springs, Ga. She has been a member of the KSU Dance Company and she represented the KSU Dance Department at the 2023 KSU College of the Arts Gala as a performer. Amber has also been a part of a dance film with 4Sight Productions and performed at the 2023 Fall for Fall Dance Festival in Atlanta under choreographer McKaylah Bristow. She is forever grateful for the experiences she has gained from the KSU Dance Department and she is looking forward to the rest of her college career here at KSU! James Doster: Stephen Sondheim's "Assassins," An All-American Review Stephen Sondheim is one of the most famous composers in Broadway history. His masterfully evocative scores such as Sweeney Todd , Into The Woods , and West Side Story are famous, even with people that are not theatre artists. Assassins is one of Sondheim’s most under-appreciated works, as it cleverly holds the mirror up to American society through it’s most notorious brand of criminal: the Presidential assassin. Assassins criticizes the American dream, by exploring the pressures that are put upon Americans to achieve it, and when they fail to do so, their anger turns to the figurehead who promised the dream to them. Assasins weaves together these themes of betrayal, opportunity, rage, and sadness to form a beautiful piece that should be considered one of Sondheim’s finest works. James Doster is an aspiring actor and singer. He is a sophomore student at KSU, majoring in Theatre and Performance Studies with a concentration in Musical Theatre. He has performed in productions such as Chicago , Curtains , and Rosencrantz & Guildenstern are Dead . He loves learning guitar, writing, singing and his orange cat, Little Man. Issa Solís: “Why is the Collision Model a Holistically Effective Strategy to Rehabilitate Incarcerated Youth?” Theatre and Performance Studies senior Issa Solís has been involved with the New Connections Collision Project as a peer mentor and most recently a student assistant. In this presentation, she offers a case for theatre-based rehabilitation for incarcerated youth. Issa is a senior at Kennesaw State University with a major in Theatre and Performance Studies and a minor in Latin American Studies. Issa's biggest passion lies in the intersection between art and community engagement. She is blessed to be involved in local art activism with the New Connections Collision Project, a collaboration between Kennesaw State University, the Georgia Department of Juvenile Justice, and the Alliance Theatre. When Issa graduates, she hopes to attend graduate school to receive a master's degree and continue to work in art and community engagement. Carly Walters: “Twyla Tharp: Deuce Coupe” “Deuce Coupe is noted to be one of the most influential ballets of the 1970’s because of Twyla Tharp’s commitment to push boundaries and change what is traditionally accepted as ballet repertoire.” Carly Walters is a junior double majoring in dance with a ballet concentration and business management. She previously trained in the pre-professional academy at the Atlanta Academy of Ballet and Dance. She is certified in level one of the Revolutionary Principles of Movement curriculum and is also continuing her dance education by being an instructor. She has attended summer intensives with Texas Ballet Theater, American Ballet Theatre, and the Orlando Ballet School. Alexis Young, "Exploring the Intersection of Dance and AI: A Dancer's Perspective" Join me as I discuss my perspective as a dance major and research assistant in the field of Generative AI. Discover how this technology can serve as a tool for creative expression and feedback in the world of dance, offering new possibilities for both artists and audiences alike. Alexis Young is a senior dance major at Kennesaw State University, specializing in modern dance. As a research assistant to esteemed Professor Andrea Knowlton during the spring 2023 semester, Alexis is delving into the fascinating realm of dance and Generative AI. With 12 years of extensive dance experience under her belt, Alexis plans to combine her passion for dance with her upcoming pursuit of a Doctorate in Physical Therapy. Her ultimate goal is to aid dancers by preventing injuries and offering rehabilitation through a unique and innovative approach. With our nationally recognized faculty of artists, designers, art educators and scholars, we are committed to exploring the convergence of art, design, and creative inquiry. Whether you are an undergraduate or a graduate student, the Kennesaw State University School of Art and Design provides a rigorous education, no matter which degree you choose. Banner Artwork: Matthew Hedeen Undergraduate Students Areas of Study Bachelor of Fine Arts in Art Choose a concentration in Art Education, Art History, Ceramics, Comics & Sequential Art, Graphic Communications, Illustration, Painting and Drawing, Photography & Video, Printmaking, Sculpture, or Textile & Surface Design. Bachelor of Fine Arts in Digital Animation Choose between either the 2D Animation or 3D Animation concentrations. Admissions Information Students must apply to KSU before they apply to the School of Art and Design. Students who apply to KSU and select an Arts major will automatically have their major classified as Art Interest. Art Interest students cannot begin their major coursework until they are admitted to an Art major. The Art Interest program designation is only applicable for one semester of enrollment at Kennesaw State University, after which students must submit an entrance portfolio for entrance to the School of Art and Design and declare a degree. If a student is accepted to the School of Art and Design, their major will be changed from Arts Interest to the concentration they applied to. If a student has not been admitted, advising will prompt them to choose a major outside of the School of Art and Design. We encourage students to plan ahead so that they can be admitted and start coursework in their desired major. Start your application to the School of Art and Design on site with staff to assist should you have any questions. In First-year Foundations and other courses, students will switch between traditional materials and digital platforms. The laptop will serve as a creative tool and portable studio, allowing students to work smoothly across classrooms and other campus workspaces. Therefore, students admitted to the Kennesaw State University School of Art and Design should have a laptop and a high-speed external hard drive. Students interested in the 3D Animation concentration are encouraged to purchase Dell or HP Windows/PC laptops. Students interested in the 2D Animation concentration and Graphic Communications are encouraged to buy MacBook Pro laptops. Students pursuing other programs, such as Studio Art, Art History, or Art Education, can succeed with either Windows/PC or Mac laptops. Students will solve problems at an advanced level through collaborative inquiry with disciplinary experts. This interdisciplinary/integrated degree mirrors our desire to break free of the limits of discipline-specific constraints. This fully online program offers concentrations in Art Education, Digital Animation and Museum Studies. These sessions will provide a comprehensive overview of the program, helping you determine how it aligns with your academic and creative goals. This process requires approval and can take up to two weeks to appear on DegreeWorks. Course substitutions are used in situations such as: Transfer credit that satisfies a degree requirement but needs to be moved on your DegreeWorks A course (with prior approval) was taken to satisfy a degree requirement Internship credit that has been approved to satisfy a specific course requirement Please submit your request in a timely fashion especially if the substitution affects your financial aid. Course Override Course override is the process of receiving prior approval from the department to register for a specific course. Please note: you will need to register for the course through your Owl Express once the override is approved. Course overrides are used in situations such as: A registration error was received and you met the course prerequisite or received prior approval Transfer students please note: you may need to submit an override request form each semester if your transfer course is counting as a prerequisite A closed course requires prior department approval Please submit your request in a timely fashion especially during registration as classes fill up quickly. Requests will be handled in the order in which they are received. Transfer to the School of Art & Design? If you are transferring into the School of Art and Design from another school, please email artsadmissions@kennesaw.edu for important information on our portfolio requirements. How Academic Advisors Help You Define and clarify academic goals Apply to programs Monitor the progress you are making towards your degree Ensure the correct course sequencing Register for courses Learn about academic policies and procedures Acquire information about support services on campus such as: Counseling and psychological services First year and major advising Financial aid University admissions University housing CARE center Health clinic Tutoring/writing centers Declare a Major Art & Design Major The School of Art & Design offers three degree programs, and two minor programs for aspiring artists, historians, and teachers: The Bachelor of Fine Arts in Art, with concentrations in ceramics, drawing and painting, graphic communications, photography, printmaking, sculpture, textile and surface design, and sequential art, Illustration, art education, and art history. BFA in Digital Animation Master of Arts in Art and Design Minor in Art History Minor in Classical Studies If you are interested in pursuing the B.F.A., you must apply directly to the School of Art & Design and submit a portfolio of your work. Please note that as these are professional degree programs, the earlier you begin your course of study, the better. Do not wait to complete your General Education coursework before applying, as it is unusual that students can complete these degrees in less than three years from the time of acceptance to the major. There are specific deadlines by which you must submit your portfolio, and it is important that you submit your portfolio as early in your college career as possible. At the same time that you submit your portfolio, you can also request credit for studio art courses based on courses taken at another college or university. Carefully review the information on the School of Art & Design website before you submit your portfolio: Art Admission Information Dance Major Dance offers a Bachelor of Arts in Dance with concentrations in ballet and modern/contemporary, as well as a 15-hour dance minor. If you are interested in pursuing the B.A. in Dance, you must apply directly to the Department of Dance and complete an audition for the faculty. Auditions are held on specific dates each year, and you must submit your application at least one week in advance of your selected date. Our dance minor may be an option for you if you wish to continue your dance training while pursuing another major at KSU. An audition is not required for the dance minor; contact the Department of Dance directly for more information. Dance Academic and Audition Requirements Music Major Accredited by the National Association of Schools of Music, the Bailey School of Music offers two degrees as well as a music minor: Bachelor of Music in Music Education : The Bachelor of Music (B.M.) in Music Education degree is offered with concentrations in General Music Education, Choral Music Education, Band Music Education, and Orchestra Music Education. Bachelor of Music in Music: The Bachelor of Music (B.M.) degree is offered with concentrations in Composition, Instrumental Performance, Jazz Performance, Music Theory, Piano Performance, and Voice Performance. Minor in Music : The KSU Bailey School of Music offers an 18-credit Music Minor for students. The Bailey School of Music approves all music minors and advises students as to all specific requirements of the minor. All programs in music, including the minor, require a separate application to the Bailey School of Music, and an audition on a principal applied instrument or voice. If you are interested in music education or in the B.M. concentrations in Composition or Music Theory, you will also be asked to complete an interview with the faculty. If you are interested in composition, you will submit a portfolio of work in addition to your audition and interview. Please note: You must be in good academic standing with the university (minimum 2.0 adjusted GPA) in order to become a major or minor in the Bailey School of Music. Auditions are held on specific dates each year (in November for January acceptance, and November, February or March for August acceptance). It is important that you apply and audition as early in your college career as possible, as it is unusual that you would be able to complete a degree in music in less than three years from the time you are accepted as a major. Carefully review the information about auditions on the website below before applying: Music Admissions Information Our music minor may be an option for you if you wish to continue your music training while pursuing another major at KSU. Contact the Bailey School of Music directly for more information. All ensembles are open to any student, and, while some do require an audition for placement, others are open to any student who wishes to participate. The ensemble auditions are separate from admission auditions. Music Ensemble Information Theatre & Performance Studies Major The Department of Theatre & Performance Studies is a distinctive undergraduate program that includes theatrical production, musical theatre, storytelling, performance of literature, performance art, and the performance of self in everyday life. The Department of Theatre & Performance Studies offers a Bachelor of Arts in Theatre & Performance Studies with concentrations in acting, performance studies, design/technology, and musical theatre. Please note: While no audition is required to become a major, you must have a minimum 3.0 adjusted GPA to become a major. Auditions are held separately each semester for theatre and musical theatre productions, the KSU Tellers storytelling ensemble, the Kennesaw Improv Society (K.I.S.S.), the Music Theatre Ensemble, and the Music Theatre Practicum. Typically, these fall within the first full week of classes each semester, and often in late April or May for early productions the following fall. It is a free Email service enabling awareness of opportunities and events to students and friends of the KSU community. In order to gain acceptance into a major in the College of the Arts as either a freshmen or transfer freshmen, follow the steps detailed below: 1. Submit your application to KSU a. On the day of your event, the Box Office at your performance location will open one hour before show time. Please note: the Box Office closes 20 minutes after the performance begins. No tickets may be purchased after this time. If you intend to purchase your ticket(s) at the door, please allow plenty of time to do so before the performance begins. Please note, as of January 2026, KSU ticketed events are cashless. Additional Box Office locations are located outside the Stillwell Theater, the Onyx Theater, both on the Kennesaw campus and the Marietta Dance Theater on the Marietta Campus. These Box Offices are also open one hour prior to show time, and will remain open until the show begins. Questions? Please call 470-578-6650 or email boxoffice@kennesaw.edu . Want to volunteer? Box Office Location Dr. Bobbie Bailey & Family Performance Center Kennesaw campus Monday - Friday 11:00 a.m. - 7:00 p.m. Russ Clayton, a founding member of ArtsKSU, with Lindsay Walker, Director of Patron Services. Become an ArtsKSU Member! Support ArtsKSU by becoming an ArtsKSU Member, starting at $25. Enjoy a variety of benefits, including ticket discounts and free exchanges. You’ll also score invitations to the Season Preview event, plus exclusive events throughout the year! Join Today! FAQs How do I order Tickets? Tickets for in-person may be purchased in person, by phone, or online. In person: Visit the Box Office in the Bailey Performance Center from 11 a.m. to 7 p.m. Monday through Friday. Please note: The Box Office is closed for summer break until August 18, 2025. By phone: please call 470-578-6650 from 11 a.m. to 7 p.m. Monday through Friday. Order online . What forms of payment do you accept? Beginning in January 2026, the Box Office will be cashless. We accept Visa, MasterCard, American Express, and Discover. We do not accept tap-to-pay What is the difference between general admission and reserved seating? For general admission events, seat availability is based on arrival. We recommend arriving early to ensure a preferred seat. For reserved seating, your seat is already selected and guaranteed, though we still recommend arriving early. What is the difference between free events and ticketed events? Free events are general admission, meaning seats are available on a first-come, first-serve basis. We recommend arriving early to ensure admittance. Seating in ticketed events is predetermined, though we still recommend arriving early. Do you offer refunds or exchanges? We do not offer refunds, as all sales are final. Exchanges are made at the discretion of Management and there is a 3$ exchange fee. ArtsKSU Members receive free, unlimited exchanges. Is there a waitlist when a show is sold out? Yes, a waitlist is maintained for each performance when a show is sold out. The waitlist will open when the Box Office opens (typically one hour before performance time). Patrons must join the waitlist in person at the Box Office. Names will be added in the order received and cannot be accepted via phone, email or online. Tickets will be offered to patrons on the waitlist as they become available. Patrons should remain nearby and ready to purchase tickets if their name is called. If a patron is not present when their name is called, the staff will move to the next name on the list. All waitlist tickets must be paid at the time of purchase. Eligible passes (e.g., subscription or pass programs) may be used, if applicable. Complimentary tickets are not valid for waitlist distribution. Not all waitlisted patrons may be accommodated and there are cases where no waitlist tickets are released. Are discounts available? Discounted tickets are available for KSU students, alumni ArtsKSU Members, Seniors, Military, and KSU Faculty/ Staff. When purchasing your tickets, please let the Box Office know that you qualify. Group sale tickets are available at a 20% discount for groups of ten or more. Please call the Box Office at 470-578-6650. Should I order my ticket(s) in advance? We always recommend ordering ahead of time, rather than purchasing a ticket at the door. Many shows sell out and ordering ahead of time ensures you get a ticket. The Box Office closes 20 minutes after the performance begins. No tickets may be purchased after this time. If you intend to purchase your ticket(s) at the door, please allow plenty of time to do so before the performance begins. How may I receive updates? You will receive a "Know-Before-You-Go" email detailing information about your ticketed event. If you do not receive it, please check your junk or spam inbox. Subscribe to the Geer College of the Arts email list! This is the best way to receive updates about upcoming events taking place. To sign up for the Geer College of the Arts email, please visit the website and scroll down to enter your email address. What options do you offer for ticket delivery? We offer several options for purchasing tickets: Physical printed tickets are available in person from the Geer College of the Arts Box Office Mobile tickets are available for tickets purchased online or by phone Will Call for picking up tickets on the night of the performance (If you select this option, please bring your ID and arrive early to allow enough time to pick up your ticket; there may be a line for the Box Office.) Do I need a ticket for my child? Yes, every person attending an event needs a ticket. How may I receive a complimentary ticket? If you are eligible to receive a complimentary ticket, complimentary tickets may be requested through the complimentary ticket request form. These tickets must be requested no later than 24 hours before the event. When does the venue (house) open before my event? The venue (house) opens approximately thirty minutes prior to all events for early seating. What are my accessibility seating options? Each venue features accessible seating. Seat maps may be viewed when purchasing tickets. For more details, please call the Box Office at 470-578-6650. Where can I view a seat map? Seat maps may be viewed when purchasing tickets. For more details, please call the Box Office at 470-578-6650. Do you offer assisted listening devices? We offer assisted listening devices in Morgan Concert Hall, Scott Rehearsal Hall, Stillwell Theater, and Onyx Theater. I lost/found something. What should I do? Please stop by, email, or call the Box Office for information about lost and found. Please email boxoffice@kennesaw.edu or call 470-578-6650. Across the Arts District at KSU, students and faculty are already shaping the season of exhibitions, performances and public events ahead, crafting work that reaches new levels of technical rigor and emotional connection. Explore Upcoming Events Visit Museum & Galleries For more information, please visit our Box Office page . Behind every performance, exhibition and creative breakthrough is a community that believes in the power of the arts. ArtsKSU Members play an essential role in supporting student artists, expanding access to transformative educational experiences and bringing exceptional artistic programming to our campus and community. Become an ArtsKSU Member The Robert S. Geer Family College of the Arts 2026-2027 Season is presented through the generous support of Dr. Jerry and Linda Richman. School of Art and Design The School of Art and Design and Bernard A. Zuckerman Museum of Art bring innovative artistry to the greater Atlanta community. Coming this fall: Collective Geometries at the Zuckerman Museum of Art. Featuring works by nationally and internationally recognized artists, including Dyani White Hawk, Marc Mitchell, Dan Walsh, David Novoros and Jonathan VanDyke, whose site-responsive installation will be created specifically for the exhibition, Collective Geometries transforms the gallery into a dynamic conversation that invites audiences to look more closely, question familiar frameworks and discover the unexpected complexity hidden within even the most fundamental forms. All of our exhibitions and events are free and open to the public. We are excited to be opening two new galleries this year in the Arts District of KSU as well. Join us in 2026-2027! Department of Dance This season, we begin with Double Exposure, featuring world premier choreography from the internationally acclaimed Gabrielle Lamb and Phoebe Jewitt. Our fall dance concert is Viewpoints, an evening of contemporary dance that explores how we perceive time, space, memory and one another through movement, featuring original works by KSU Dance faculty, and performed by the award-winning KSU Dance Company. Registration Opens Nov. 1 Spaces fill up fast! Questions? Please email arts@kennesaw.edu or call 470-578-6742. Department of Dance REGISTRATION OPENS 11/1 The KSU Summer Dance Intensive is a dynamic, weeklong program designed for intermediate to advanced high school and incoming college dancers. Participants engage in daily classes in Modern, Ballet, African, Jazz, Tap, Improvisation and repertory with KSU Dance faculty. Through personalized feedback, creative exploration and high-level instruction, students are challenged to grow both technically and artistically. The week culminates in a performance at the KSU Dance Theater, showcasing the work developed throughout the intensive. Department of Theatre and Performance REGISTRATION OPENS 11/1 We are excited to give you the opportunity to experience technical and artistic growth in an environment that fosters creativity and learning. Our three concentrations (Acting, Musical Theatre or Theatre Design and Technology) are separate, but will come together at several points each day, culminating in a spectacular performance showcase at the end of the week, featuring the integration of all the concentrations. School of Art and Design REGISTRATION OPENS 11/1 The KSU Summer Arts & Design Intensive gives high school students and rising college freshmen experience with what being a university student studying art is like. Participants work with professional artists, not only experienced professors, but also active in their fields with connections and creative applications to share. Bailey School of Music REGISTRATION OPENS 11/1 Our music camps are designed for high school students who want to grow as performers and experience college‑level music study. Participants will build confidence, strengthen technique, and explore new musical opportunities through rehearsals, sectionals and masterclasses. Jazz Band Camp June 13-18 Concert Band Camp June 20-25 Piano Camp June 28-30 Choir Camp July 5-10 Orchestra Camp July 11-16 Key Questions and Answers What do I pack for ArtsKSU Summer Intensives? All personal items, toiletries, and personal medications. Bath towels. Bed sheets, blanket, and pillow for a single bed or sleeping bag (Sheet size for dorm beds is Twin Extra-Long). Alarm clock as needed! Clothes for the week. Dress for ArtsKSU Summer Intensive is casual. Athletic shoes are a better choice than flip-flops or sandals for the week as some walking will be involved. Spending money for snacks and vending machines. When / Where do I go for Registration? For Overnight Participants: Dr. Bobbie Bailey Performance & Family Center 488 Prillaman Way, Kennesaw, GA 30144 Student Registration will be held in the lobby of Dr. Bobbie Bailey Family & Performance Center. Parking for registration can be found in lot E, adjacent to the Bailey Center 5:00 pm Registration/Check-in 5:15 pm - 5:45 pm Orientation Overnight Participants are required to attend the orientation session with at least one parent/guardian present. For Day-Only Participants: Arrive early for general instructions. School of Art and Design students should report to the Marietta Campus, Theatre students should report to the Kennesaw Campus, Dance students should report to the Dance Studios at Chastain Pointe. What happens at Registration? At registration, you will receive your schedule for the week, meal plan wristband, and room assignment with access card. Parent(s) and Participants for overnight are required to attend the welcome session/orientation. After the orientation session, the overnight students will move into the Village Suite housing. Students will receive their door key access to rooms in the Village Suites. Each Geer College of the Arts unit will send specific details for their evening (late afternoon) events in early spring! After Registration and Orientation now what? Move into Village Suites Housing! Students will place their belongings in their rooms (might want to at least make your bed!) and proceed to the appropriate units for activities. Each unit will send specifics for this later this Spring (ex. Musical Theatre will host an audition). What is campus housing like? AWESOME! KSU does not have dorms we have SUITES! Summer Intensive students will be housed in the Village Suites which are conveniently located near the Bailey Center and Wilson Building. Dance students will be shuttled to Chastain Pointe via Mini-Vans after breakfast every day and returned by 5:00 p.m. Lunch will be served at Chastain Pointe for Dance students. Village Suites: All suite rooms are air-conditioned with private bedrooms (1 or 2 bedrooms) and private restrooms per suite. ADA-compliant rooms and private rooms are available under special circumstances. Please let us know if special accommodations are needed! What will the daily schedule be like? All students will be in classes, rehearsals, or other activities from 8:30 am – 9:15 pm each day. Lunch is served at noon with dinner around 5:30 pm. There will be some free time for most campers in the afternoons. You may use this time to socialize with other campers in approved areas or rest. Each evening students will participate in a special activity planned. Participants will receive a more detailed schedule later in the spring from each College of the Arts Unit (Dance/Theatre/Music/Art). How do we get around? It will be necessary to walk to your classes and meals each day. The walk takes only a few minutes. Participants are advised to wear athletic shoes to daily activities and bring an umbrella in case of rain. Dance students who are overnight will be shuttled via minivan to Chastain Pointe after breakfast each morning and back to the main campus at dinner. What if I become ill? If a student becomes ill while at the Summer Intensive with an infectious virus, quarantine housing is available to the student until a parent can arrive. Event and Venue Management personnel are on-site 24/7, and always available is KSU PD and 911 as needed. Please complete the health form thoroughly, paying special attention to any specific allergies or conditions that may apply to you. If there is a medical condition the Summer Intensive staff should know of, please tell us about this before the start of this week. Of course, if you get sick or hurt, we expect you to let us know so can help you immediately. Is there a cell phone policy? Cell phones are allowed at the intensive but are expected to be off during all sessions, classes, and rehearsals. Can I park my car on campus? Students for overnight will not be allowed to bring a car onto campus. What about the last day? Performances will be held on Friday afternoon at the Bailey School of Music Building, Stillwell Performing Arts Center, and the Marietta Dance Theatre on the Marietta Campus. Additional information will be sent from each unit this spring. What are the rules? We expect our participants to always behave appropriately, with respect for other students and for the facilities of Kennesaw State University. Naturally, we do not allow harmful or unhealthy behavior (smoking, drinking) under any circumstances. We expect all students to participate in all camp activities and to follow the directions of camp staff and faculty. We rarely encounter any discipline problems at our Summer Intensive. We believe our participants are among the best and brightest students in high schools. In those cases when a student commits gross misconduct or consistently demonstrates an inability to follow the rules, we usually send the individual home. This is rarely necessary, but not out of the question. We want you to have a wonderful experience at the KSU Summer Arts Intensive. General Rules and Policies General Discipline: Students' social and moral behavior is of paramount importance to the success of the total program of the intensive. You are young adults and will be treated as such. Class and Program Attendance: Students are to attend and be punctual to all classes and evening programs except when excused by your counselor, the University Health Center, or the appropriate unit office. Contact your head counselor (RA) or call the office should you become ill. Personal Appearance: While this intensive does not define personal dress, it asks that all participants be neat and dressed in good taste. Always wear appropriate shoes. Smoking: KSU is a smoke-free campus. There is to be NO SMOKING by any student at any time. Alcoholic Beverages: Possession and/or use of alcoholic beverages by anyone will result in expulsion. Drugs: All personnel are advised that federal and state laws prohibit the possession or use of certain drugs. The intensive will immediately expel any person involved with drugs and will turn such cases over to proper civil authorities. Prescribed drugs / medications must be noted on your medical form at check-in. Vehicles: We cannot accept responsibility for automobile accidents. Students are not allowed to ride in or have access to cars while enrolled in the intensive. Day participants are to drive only to reach campus and return home. No overnight campers will be allowed to drive themselves to campus. Illness: In case of illness or emergency, campers may be transported to the University Health Center by staff members. Under no other circumstances will any student ride in any vehicle other than university buses or vans. Use and/or Abuse of Property: Any student defacing property will be liable for damages and considered for expulsion. Campus Curfew: If you stay on campus, you are to be in the Village Suite each night by the scheduled time, be on your floor at 9:45 pm, and be in your room and quiet by 10:30 pm. Room Visitation and Dating: Students must stay on their assigned floor. We do not allow boys in girls’ rooms or halls, and vice versa. For your own protection, keep your door locked even when walking down the hall for a moment. Summer Intensive participants are not to associate with non-intensive personnel. The Summer Intensive Staff reserves the right to enter any Village Suite to ensure the safety or compliance of participating students, protecting university or private property. What if I have more questions? Call us at 470-578-6742 or email arts@kennesaw.edu . If we don't answer right away, leave a message or email and we'll contact you with the answer as soon as possible. Please don't hesitate to let us know, as we want your experience to be as enjoyable and trouble-free as possible. We are looking forward to a great summer intensive and hope you are too. title: KSU Alumnus Michael Kalish Returns to Atlanta After 35 Years to Unveil “Reel Portraits” Exhibition - Geer College of the Arts

Radow College of Humanities & Social Sciences College of Science & Mathematics Graduate College KSU Journey Honors College Southern Polytechnic College of Engineering & Engineering Technology Wellstar College of Health & Human Services Offices & Services Offices & Services University Registrar Parking & Transportation Student Affairs Housing & Residence Life Event & Venue Management University Information Technology Services Fiscal Services University Libraries Academic Advising Campus Operations Strategic Communications & Marketing Policies & Governance Policy Resources University Handbooks Institutional Policies Complaints & Appeals Conflict of Interest General Data Protection Regulation Protecting Minors Public Forum FERPA Governance University Council Administrators Council Staff Senate Faculty Senate Student Government A-Z Index KSU Home Geer College of the Arts News KSU Alumnus Michael Kalish Returns to Atlanta After 35 Years to Unveil “Reel Portraits” Exhibition KSU Alumnus Michael Kalish Returns to Atlanta After 35 Years to Unveil “Reel Portraits” Exhibition KENNESAW, Ga. | Oct 1, 2026 For LA-based artist and Kennesaw State University Alumnus Michael Kalish, returning to Atlanta for the unveiling of his new exhibition, Reel Portraits, feels like a coming home story. “I haven’t been back to Atlanta and shown in over thirty-five years,” he says. Kalish graduated from KSU in 1996, studying art and majoring in psychology while playing outfield for the Owls baseball team. “Launching this collection in Atlanta is really a dream for me. To be able to unveil this collection in a city that holds so many memories for me, to be surrounded by my family, old friends, people I went to school with, guys I played baseball with, and my early collectors, is really a dream.” Kalish’s exhibition for Atlanta Art Fair is a series of original sculptures made from vintage film reels from classic films dating back to 1913. Kalish spent many years searching for classic films and the icons associated with them, James Dean, Marilyn Monroe, Elvis, Judy Garland, and matching those icons with the films that they became known for. “I was able to acquire films like Rebel Without a Cause and Breakfast at Tiffany's, and from there the collection began to expand and overlap with some of my other passions,” Kalish explains. “As an athlete, I've always had a tremendous amount of respect for and interest in athletes, so I was able to acquire some incredible historical footage, including the 1947 Yankees-Dodgers film documenting the season in which Jackie Robinson broke the color barrier. That became one of the sculptures in this series.” Kalish feels that his experience developing his academic, athletic, and artistic skills at KSU all guided his career as an artist. More than anything, baseball taught him how to fail, which he cites as one of the greatest lessons he learned from college. “In baseball, you can fail seven out of ten times and still end up in the Hall of Fame. Choosing a career as an artist is also filled with ups and downs and a long journey toward success. Being an athlete and learning how to struggle, striking out, failing, and then getting back up again, gave me a perspective that I think ultimately set me up for success in this alternative field as a professional artist.” His first exhibitions were collections of sculptures and images repurposed from junkyard objects such as license plates and American truck parts. From there, he began creating large-scale public installations in cities around the country. Two of his most notable projects include reALIze, an interactive, 40-foot outdoor cube made from 1,300 boxing bags and the world's largest monument of Muhammad Ali, and 24M, a massive interactive sculpture that formed a contiguous map of the United States when viewed from above. Kalish would go on to tour 24M with racecar driver Danica Patrick to raise awareness for COPD. Since 2020, Kalish’s newest venture has been acquiring vintage film reels through collectors, libraries, and auction houses and transforming them into one-of-a-kind original portraits. This acquisition journey would culminate into Reel Portraits. Kalish describes the common thread through his work as invention; taking something that already exists, seeing it differently, inventing a new way to tell a story through it, and building community around it. “Ultimately, that's what continues to excite me about being an artist after more than 30 years: seeing the work connect with people in unexpected ways. I'm incredibly grateful for the collectors, galleries, designers, fabricators, and communities that have supported me throughout that journey.” Reel Portraits will be exhibited at Pullman Yards’ Porter Hall at Booth E05 through October 4. ~Story by Cai Burks, Geer College of the Arts ~Photography by Rob Hampton Related Posts A Vision Realized: The Enduring Legacy of Emily Bourne Grigsby and Athos Menaboni Where Reality Gives Way to Imagination: "Branches Etched Across the Sky" Comes to KSU $500,000 Gift from Dr. Audrey Morgan honors KSU Provost - Dr. Ivan Pulinkala Woven Reflections: Reimagining the Karastan Archive to Open New Emily Bourne Grigsby Galleries at KSU Contact Information Kennesaw Campus 1000 Chastain Road Kennesaw, GA 30144 Marietta Campus 1100 South Marietta Pkwy Marietta, GA 30060 Phone 470-KSU-INFO (470-578-4636) Campus Maps Parking Media Resources Campus A-Z Index Academic Calendar Campus News D2L Brightspace University Information Technology Services Related Links Libraries Housing Financial Aid Degrees, Majors & Programs Registrar Job Opportunities Campus Security Global Education Sustainability Accessibility © 2026 Kennesaw State University. That question lives at the heart of Branches Etched Across the Sky, a magical, deeply theatrical work by playwright Addae Moon presented by the Department of Theatre and Performance Studies at Kennesaw State University next month. Directed by Assistant Professor of Theatre Marlon Andrew Burnley, the production invites audiences into a world somewhere between the one we recognize and the one we create in our minds — a liminal space where memory, grief, imagination and reality begin to blur. It is, Burnley says, exactly the kind of material he loves to tackle. The production also represents something of a full-circle moment for the director. Burnley first encountered the play years ago, when it was being developed by a former faculty member at KSU. He later participated in a stage reading of the work after moving to Atlanta in 2018. Since then, the play has remained with him. Now, at KSU, he has the opportunity to bring it to life with a student cast and creative team. And bringing it to life means entering a world that doesn't always play by the rules of the real one. Somewhere between the real and the imagined Moon's characters exist, as Burnley describes it, somewhere between “the consensus realm” of everyday life and an imagined realm shaped by the characters themselves. At the center are Melba, Travis and Delmar, siblings whose lives have been profoundly affected by the death of their mother. Each is artistic -- writers, drawers, creators -- and the play allows their inner worlds to become part of the world onstage. When the characters enter those imaginative spaces, Burnley sees them as something like the mind fabricating itself in real time. “Are we real or are we imaginary?” becomes part of the theatrical game. That makes Branches Etched Across the Sky playful and strange, even as it explores weighty subjects. Moon's story moves through trauma, grief, mental health and complicated family relationships, but it doesn't present those ideas in strictly realistic terms. Instead, it turns inward, transforming the characters' psychological experiences into something the audience can see, hear and inhabit. For Melba, trauma manifests through spells of typing; trances in which words and images pour out of her. What might appear on the surface as an unusual creative impulse becomes something much more complicated: a manifestation of what she is carrying inside. As Burnley puts it, “the sickness is the art.” The play's mystical elements give Moon a way to explore experiences that can be difficult to articulate directly, including generational trauma and the ways family histories can shape the people who come after us. The dramaturgy team for the KSU production describes the play as particularly attentive to the experiences of Black families in the South, while also recognizing the universality of its questions about family, relationships, mental health and the weight of the past. The result is a production that asks audiences to follow the characters somewhere unfamiliar, and to trust the theater to take them there. Making the impossible visible That imaginative quality extends into the production's design. Set designer Alexander Whittenberg, with whom Burnley has collaborated on previous productions, is helping translate the director's vision into a physical environment. Projection designer Arash Baqipur is adding another layer, creating what Burnley describes as a cinematic quality that can lift the play's language into the space. Words won't simply be spoken. They may appear to exist in the air. Burnley's visual prompt was to imagine “words thick in the air;” something that could evoke smoke, memory and the past all at once. It is precisely the kind of theatrical possibility that makes a work like Branches Etched Across the Sky so exciting in a university setting. Because this is not simply about presenting students with a familiar story and asking them to reproduce it. It is about asking them to imagine what theater can do. A place to experiment For Burnley, that spirit of experimentation is inseparable from the rehearsal process. He begins with the expectation that the work should be approached with maturity, bravery and a willingness to go beyond what is comfortable. He also asks his cast to consider a simple question throughout the process: What are you going to do today to surprise yourself? It is a question that reflects something larger about the educational mission behind a production like this. Theater students aren't simply learning lines and blocking scenes. They are learning how to take creative risks, respond to unfamiliar material and discover possibilities they may not have encountered before. Burnley has seen that willingness from this cast. After only eight rehearsals, the actors arrived having memorized the material and were already able to move beyond simply learning the script toward building the world of the production. For Burnley, that is where the real work begins. “We're always building forward,” he says. More than the weight of the past Although Branches Etched Across the Sky deals with grief, trauma and the ways our past can shape us, Burnley doesn't see the play as ultimately being about those things. At its heart, he sees it as a story about imagination, vulnerability and the human capacity to play — to create, to change and to imagine something beyond the circumstances in which we find ourselves. The characters make different choices about whether to move forward, remain where they are or return to the past. The play doesn't necessarily prescribe one answer. Instead, it recognizes something deeply human: that we are all imperfect, all shaped by what has happened to us, and all capable of choosing what happens next. That may be the most fitting reason for KSU students to take on a work like this. Because sometimes the most valuable thing an artist can learn is not how to make something familiar look good. It is how to step into the unfamiliar. How to play. How to be vulnerable. How to make the impossible visible. And, perhaps most importantly, how to surprise yourself. Branches Etched Across the Sky will be presented in the Onyx Theater on October 6-11 . More information and ticketing can be found on the Geer College of the Arts website or by calling the Box Office at 470-578-6650. It stands as the culmination of a deep personal friendship, a lifelong passion for artistic mastery and extraordinary philanthropic vision. The creation of the Emily Bourne Grigsby Gallery and the Athos Menaboni Gallery brings to fruition a transformative legacy bequest from the late Emily Bourne Grigsby, finalized through the dedicated stewardship of her estate’s executor, Alice Kuzniak. Together with $1 million in contributions from the Emily Bourne Grigsby estate and foundational support for the Athos Menaboni Art Fund from donors including June Boykin Tindall, this gift ensures that both historical mastery and future artistic generation will flourish under one roof. Emily Bourne Grigsby: A Renaissance Woman of Vision and Action To understand the spirit behind these new spaces, it helps to know the remarkable woman who made them possible. Emily Bourne Grigsby (1922–2020) was an artist, lawyer, city planner, opera singer and pilot — a life defined as much by curiosity as by accomplishment. Born in Owenton, Kentucky, to an artist mother and a publisher and lawyer father, Grigsby pursued interests that rarely fit within a single discipline. She earned a Bachelor of Arts from Mills College, a Master of Science in City Planning from the Georgia Institute of Technology, and a Juris Doctor from the Woodrow Wilson College of Law, alongside formal studies at the Atlanta College of the Arts. Professionally, she broke barriers as the first woman president of the Fulton County Grand Jury Association and served as an arbitrator for the New York Stock Exchange. Her personal pursuits were no less remarkable: she was an accomplished opera singer who performed with the San Francisco Opera Company, a licensed multi-engine pilot, an interior decorator, a model, and an accomplished painter whose works garnered acclaim across Georgia. Named a “Gracious Lady of Georgia” in 2004, Grigsby devoted her later years to extensive philanthropy supporting wildlife, education and the visual arts. Central to her artistic life was her deep admiration for her close friend, the legendary Georgia artist Athos Menaboni. Driven by a desire to preserve his genius and foster future artists, Grigsby donated two of Menaboni’s original paintings to KSU’s Zuckerman Museum of Art, helped establish the Athos Menaboni Art Fund, and endowed the Athos Menaboni Art Research Scholarship. Her historic final bequest now solidifies that legacy forever. Athos Menaboni, Whooping Crane V, 1961. Oil on African walnut veneer on wood. Gift of Alice Lennie Glover. Bernard A. Zuckerman Museum of Art Permanent Collection. Athos Menaboni, California Quail, c. 1965. Oil on gessoed paper. Gift of William and Joyce Taaffe in loving memory of their son Jaron. Bernard A. Zuckerman Museum of Art Permanent Collection. Athos Menaboni: Capturing the Spirit of Nature Born in Livorno, Italy, in 1895, Athos Rodolfo Giorgio Alessandro Menaboni (1895 – 1990) received formal art training at the Academy of Fine Arts in Florence before immigrating to the United States in 1921. Moving to Atlanta in 1927, he initially earned renown for architectural decorative painting, contributing to iconic landmarks such as the Swan House, the Rhodes-Haverty Building and the Atlanta Cyclorama restoration. However, Menaboni’s true calling emerged in the late 1930s when he began painting naturalistic studies of birds. Developing a signature “undercoat method” using thin layers of oil paint on paper, he achieved a translucent, intricate depth that captivated viewers and led Time magazine in 1950 to declare him the true heir to John James Audubon. His art caught the attention of prominent patrons, leading to a decade-long collaboration with Robert W. Woodruff and The Coca-Cola Company, national museum exhibitions, and the publication of the celebrated 1950 volume Menaboni's Birds. Athos Menaboni, Mallard, c.1962. Oil on illustration board. Gift of Emily Bourne Grigsby. Bernard A. Zuckerman Museum of Art Permanent Collection. Menaboni's connection to Kennesaw State University runs deep. Through the generosity of alumnus D. Russell Clayton and the Robert W. Woodruff Foundation, KSU became a primary home for Menaboni’s work. Now, Grigsby’s legacy gift elevates that sanctuary to new heights. Two Spaces, One Continuum: The Impact on KSU That legacy now takes physical form in two new galleries at the heart of Kennesaw State’s growing Arts District. Though they share a home, each tells a different part of the story. The Emily Bourne Grigsby Gallery looks to nurture current and future generations. Conceived as a flexible and evolving space, it will come alive through the work of students, faculty, and resident artist from the School of Art and Design. Just steps away, the Athos Menaboni Gallery looks to an enduring artistic legacy, creating a permanent place to encounter the life and work of one of Georgia’s most celebrated artists. Rotating exhibitions drawn from KSU’s permanent collection and private loans will continually bring new perspectives to Menaboni’s work. That conversation between past and future begins this fall with Woven Reflections . Its opening marks more than the arrival of a new exhibition. The College honors the supporters and university leaders, whose vision and generosity have created a lasting place for art to be created and treasured. The endowment celebrates the leadership and legacy of Pulinkala, who served as Dean of the Geer College of the Arts, prior to becoming KSU’s Provost and Executive Vice President for Academic Affairs. The gift comes at a moment of growing philanthropic momentum for KSU Dance. In August, the Geer College of the Arts announced the Ivan Pulinkala Dance Scholarship, established by Arts Ambassador LaSona Turk and her husband, former Chairman of the KSU Foundation Board Trent Turk, in partnership with Don Vellek, Robin and Doug Shore, and Maureen and John Patton. Together, these philanthropic commitments demonstrate strong community support for Georgia’s largest collegiate dance program built by Pulinkala. Through these two endowed scholarships, generations of future dance students will receive financial support to pursue their collegiate education in KSU’s nationally acclaimed Department of Dance. The Morgan-Pulinkala Dance Scholarship will help attract and support talented dance majors, providing them with financial resources to grow as artists, educators and performers. The gift extends Morgan’s longstanding legacy of supporting KSU students through scholarships and philanthropy in athletics, nursing, engineering, computing and music. For Morgan, the scholarship is an opportunity to bring that commitment to a dance program she has followed closely over the years. "I have always believed that education is one of the most meaningful investments we can make in the lives of young people,” said Morgan. “The arts have a unique ability to enrich lives, foster creativity and give students the confidence to imagine what is possible. I have been fortunate to watch Kennesaw State University’s dance program grow and flourish under Ivan’s leadership. I am pleased to celebrate his legacy and support the talented young dancers who are helping shape the future of dance.” The KSU Department of Dance was founded by Pulinkala in 2005 and received acclaim for Pulinkala’s choreographic scholarship that was invited to the Kennedy Center and commissioned nationally and internationally. Pulinkala developed KSU’s state-of-the-art studio facilities at Chastain Pointe and the Dance Theatre on the Marietta Campus. He envisioned and raised funds for the creation of the KSU Arts District that will eventually house all four disciplines in the Robert S. Geer Family College of the Arts. Today, the KSU Department of Dance continues to evolve under the leadership of Marsha Barsky into a distinctive epicenter for dance education, performance and creative exploration. “I am deeply grateful to Audrey Morgan, LaSona and Trent Turk, Robin and Doug Shore, Maureen and John Patton, and Don Vellek for their support of KSU Dance,” said Ivan Pulinkala. “These visionary benefactors are leaving a legacy that will transform lives for generations to come through the power of dance education. I am humbled and know that the students who benefit from these scholarships will honor our benefactors through distinguished careers in dance.” These two scholarships will strengthen KSU’s ability to recruit and retain exceptionally talented students while helping recipients pursue the rigorous physical training and intellectual exploration that is foundational to successful careers in dance. These gifts reflect the Geer College of the Arts’ commitment to cultivating an environment where students can develop their artistic voices, expand their intellectual perspectives and prepare for leadership in creative careers. “Dr. Audrey Morgan’s remarkable generosity brings such transformative momentum to KSU Dance,” said Jawshing Arthur Liou, Dean of the Robert S. Geer Family College of the Arts. “Her $500,000 commitment, together with the recently established Ivan Pulinkala Dance Scholarship, represents an unprecedented level of investment in our dance students and the future of the program. They will open doors for talented students, strengthen our ability to attract exceptional dancers, and ensure that Ivan’s legacy continues through the lives and careers of the students.” The two dance scholarships join a growing portfolio of philanthropic investments supporting students, faculty, programs and creative experiences across the Geer College of the Arts. As Kennesaw State University continues to expand its impact as one of the Southeast’s largest comprehensive arts programs within a public research university, these investments play an essential role in positioning the college for its next chapter of growth, innovation and national distinction.
