Chubb, who earned her Executive MBA from KSU’s Michael J. Coles College of Business in 2020, will be recognized by ABC at a ceremony on Oct. 8 at the Stave Room in Atlanta. The Women of Influence awards honor women who have made significant strides in their careers and are making a difference in their organizations and communities. Having experienced housing insecurity as a child, Chubb has made it her life’s mission to help people find affordable homes. “Making sure families have housing they can afford is important to me because my parents divorced when I was young, and my family was housing insecure,” Chubb said. “We had a home, but it was a struggle to afford it, and we lived with the stress of that insecurity for many years.” Chubb learned the ins and outs of the housing industry by working for a bank’s mortgage department before taking a job with the Georgia Housing and Finance Authority (later renamed the Georgia Department of Community Affairs), where she spent 23 years administering federal and state affordable housing programs. She left the GDCA in 2019 to become Chief of Staff to Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms, where she oversaw critical city operations and served as the mayor’s top advisor. In 2022, Chubb joined Columbia Residential as president. Columbia Residential is a real estate developer that partners with governments and community organizations to build affordable housing in Georgia, Louisiana, Texas, Tennessee, and Florida. As her career continued to evolve, Chubb joined the KSU Executive MBA program in 2018 to enhance her leadership skills and to prepare for the next challenge. She graduated while still working for the Mayor’s Office. Designed for experienced working professionals, Kennesaw State's Executive MBA program combines once-a-month weekend residencies, collaborative team experiences, international study, and individualized executive coaching throughout the program to help students sharpen their business acumen and grow into strategic leaders. “My EMBA honed my business and finance skills and positioned me to transition from the public sector to the private sector,” she said. “The finance and economics coursework – not to mention the leadership focus and team setting – challenged me and prepared me for the role I have now as president of Columbia Residential.” Richard James, KSU’s Executive Director of MBA Programs, said Chubb’s recognition as an Atlanta Business Chronicle Woman of Influence reflects the leadership qualities she demonstrated as a student in the program. “Carmen embodies all the qualities that we hope to see from the alumni of our EMBA program,” James said. “She is a powerful leader with a keen understanding of business and a genuine desire to serve others. She has become a role model for our EMBA students.” In addition to her professional achievements, Chubb has also made building up others a part of her personal mission. She regularly mentors young colleagues at Columbia Residential; she sits on the boards of the KSU Foundation, Open Doors Atlanta, and Community ImPACT; and volunteers with Back On My Feet Atlanta, an organization that uses running to promote accountability, social engagement, resilience, and physical fitness. As Chubb prepares to accept the Woman of Influence Award, she is grateful that her career has provided her with countless opportunities to relate to and learn from people of all walks of life. “These connections have made me a better human,” she said, “and that better human shows up in all spaces that I enter: my home, my work, and in my service.” -Patrick Harbin Related Posts Kennesaw State and Ingenico create hub for fintech innovation and learning The Science Behind Being Ignored Online Two KSU students trade the Gold Dome for Capitol Hill KSU, Technovative AI sign pilot agreement with Moultrie Police Department for AI-powered behavioral health detection tool Contact Information Kennesaw Campus 1000 Chastain Road Kennesaw, GA 30144 Marietta Campus 1100 South Marietta Pkwy Marietta, GA 30060 Phone 470-KSU-INFO (470-578-4636) Campus Maps Parking Media Resources Campus A-Z Index Academic Calendar Campus News D2L Brightspace University Information Technology Services Related Links Libraries Housing Financial Aid Degrees, Majors & Programs Registrar Job Opportunities Campus Security Global Education Sustainability Accessibility © 2026 Kennesaw State University. Ours is a community for inclusive excellence in learning and research that respects all our students' needs, responsibilities, and aspirations with personalized support from faculty mentors and professional advisors. As we leverage the strengths of our 3,015 students and the unique perspectives they bring, we continuously innovate to find the best ways to help students learn and prepare for a world of global opportunities. Undergraduate degrees in biology, chemistry, mathematics, physics, and environmental sciences provide opportunities for students to concentrate on human health, forensic chemistry, computational mathematics, engineering physics, or other areas that lead to exciting careers. Our students also engage in contemporary experiential learning opportunities in undergraduate research, service learning, study abroad, and internships that use science and mathematics to make a difference for people and communities. Our college offers graduate programs in chemical sciences and integrative biology, including special Double-Owl pathways designed to expedite attaining a master's degree for undergraduate students. We have an impressive research portfolio of federally funded grants from prestigious institutions such as the National Institutes of Health, National Science Foundation, Department of Defense, and Department of Education, providing over 8 million dollars in research support over the next 5 years. Additionally, we are developing a Ph.D. program in Medical Science, further expanding our academic offerings. Our faculty members excel across a broad spectrum of research areas, with strengths in developmental and organismal biology, microbiology, neuroscience, infectious diseases and drug discovery, theoretical particle physics, mathematical biology, as well as adaptation and change in the environment. These extensive research capabilities provide numerous opportunities for both undergraduate and graduate students to actively contribute to groundbreaking research and make new discoveries. Join us on our journey of unbridled curiosity in exploring nature, humanity, and the technology we invent and use. Heather Koopman Dean, College of Science and Mathematics and Professor of Biology Academic Distinction Statement The College of Science and Mathematics at Kennesaw State University provides a hands-on, research-driven learning environment where students have direct access to cutting-edge facilities and interdisciplinary collaboration. Our unique focus on real-world problem-solving, combined with strong partnerships with local communities and across industry and environmental sectors, positions graduates at the forefront of scientific curiosity, innovation, and sustainability efforts in Georgia and beyond Our Mission and Vision Kennesaw State University transforms lives through academic excellence, innovative research, strong community partnerships, and economic opportunity. We empower our students to become thought leaders, lifelong learners, and informed global citizens by cultivating an inclusive environment that encourages free expression and civil discourse. Kennesaw State will achieve national prominence as a public university known for education, research, and community programs that foster inquiry and advance society. Discover our faculty Discover our faculty, whose scholarship programs are leading to new discoveries in biomedical sciences, forensic science, biotechnology, developmental biology, graph theory; and to innovations in how teachers teach and how students learn science and mathematics. Research in the college is supported by the National Science Foundation, the National Institute of Health, the Department of Defense, the Department of Education, and private foundations. Discover through research Kennesaw State University is a student-centered, research-driven R2 institution. Research is a large part of a student’s studies. CSM departments provide both undergraduate and graduate students increasing research opportunities to collaborate with our faculty in current research providing cutting-edge instrumentation and spacious labs. Often these type of research opportunities are not available to students until the post-doc level. Poster presentation showcases and symposiums throughout the year allow students to share findings about their research. Learn more about Research in the College of Science and Mathematics . Discover your future Our students prepare for graduate schools and the job market through degree programs with customized outcomes that help differentiate themselves from others. There are many career markets for students of CSM to enter upon graduation. Unlimited career opportunities in areas related to biofuel/bioenergy, medical devices and equipment, nuclear medicine, research, pharmaceuticals, climate study, national parks, analytics, education, banking, toxicology, laboratory management, regulatory affairs, and much more! Companies such as Cryolife, Cox Communications, Momar, Aegis Labs, BBDO, Centers for Disease Control, Beecher Carlson, Lexis Nexis, CarMax, Cardlytics, and many more are hiring students in these areas in internship and co-op roles, as well as full time positions after graduation. These dedicated spaces house classrooms, offices, laboratories, collaborative work areas, and research facilities that enhance the educational experience for students and faculty alike. CSM buildings play a vital role in fostering a dynamic, interdisciplinary environment across both locations. Visit the KSU Maps website for more information. CSM Buildings on the Kennesaw Campus Science Building (SC) The Science Building, opened in 1996, is a five-story facility located just south of the Student Center, adjacent to the Science Laboratory Building. Encompassing over 104,000 square feet, it houses laboratories, faculty offices, and research spaces that support multiple departments within the College of Science and Mathematics. The building serves as a central hub for instruction, experimentation, and collaboration in the sciences. Science Laboratory Building (SL) The Science Laboratory is located in between Clendenin and the Science Building on the Kennesaw Campus. Dedicated to scientific teaching and research, the Science Laboratory opened in 2012 featuring 5 floors and over 74,000 square feet. Providing highly effective collaboration and research opportunities for all science and interdisciplinary undergraduate and graduate students and faculty members alike. Clendenin Building (CL) Opening in 2002, the Clendenin Building features over 37,000 square feet and 3 floors of study spaces, state-of-the-art computer classrooms, and faculty offices. Located across from the Siegel Student Recreation & Activities Center, Clendenin houses departments from the College of Science and Mathematics and the College of Computing and Software Engineering. Mathematics and Statistics Building (MS) The Mathematics and Statistics building was built in 1967 and is next to the Sturgis Library and the Technology Annex on the Kennesaw Campus. With over 31,000 square feet, this building is Kennesaw campus home for the Department of Mathematics. There are several instructional spaces, study areas and faculty offices. The department also maintains an office on the Marietta campus, supporting its presence across both locations. Classes for the College of Science and Mathematics also take place throughout the Kennesaw Campus, including, but not limited to, the Prillaman Health Sciences (HS) and Academic Learning Center (ALC) buildings. CSM Buildings on the Marietta Campus Academic Building (H) Established in 1986 and located adjacent to the Lawrence V. Johnson Library, the Academic Building is a three-story facility encompassing over 50,000 square feet. The second floor serves as the primary home for the Department of Physics, including the department’s administrative and faculty offices, classrooms, and laboratories. This building plays a central role in supporting instruction and research in the physical sciences. Crawford Lab Building (E) Established in 1962 and recently renovated in 2024, the Crawford Lab Building is a two-story, 31,000-square-foot facility that houses classrooms, laboratories, and faculty offices for both chemistry and biology. It supports a wide range of teaching and research activities across the life and physical sciences. Mathematics Building (D) The Mathematics Building, constructed in 1962 and spanning 28,595 square feet, serves as the primary location for the Department of Mathematics. There are several instructional spaces, study areas and faculty offices. The department also maintains an office on the Kennesaw campus, supporting its presence across both locations. Science Lab Annex (GAX) The Science Lab Annex is a two-story building that opened in 2020. The Science Lab Annex is almost 10,500 square feet and is located across from the Crawford Lab Building. From its early foundations to its current role as a leading institution in the sciences, our college has continually evolved to meet the needs of students, faculty, and the local/international community. Explore the key milestones throughout the decades that highlight our journey and the lasting contributions we've made in shaping the future of science and mathematics. 2020s 2025 July 1 - Dr. Melanie Griffin appointed Interim Associate Dean of Faculty Affairs and Operations. 2024 July 1 - Dr. Heather Koopman named Dean of the College of Science and Mathematics. 2023 September 1 - Dr. Martin Hudson appointed Interim Associate Dean for Research and Graduate Studies. July 1 - Dr. Vishnu Suppiramaniam appointed Interim Dean of the College of Science and Mathematics. 2021 February 15 - The Department of Statistics and Analytical Sciences moves to the College of Computing and Software Engineering at Kennesaw State University and is established as the School of Data Science and Analytics. 2020 August 1 - Dr. Kojo Mensa-Wilmot named Dean of the College of Science and Mathematics. January 1 - Dr. Marla Bell appointed Interim Dean of the College of Science and Mathematics. 2010s 2019 March 22 - Dr. Don McGarey appointed Interim Dean of the College of Science and Mathematics. Groundbreaking of the Science Lab Annex (Marietta Campus). 2018 $1 million grant received from Howard Hughes Medical Institute (HHMI). December 31 - KSU was upgraded to a doctoral research institution with R2 status by the Carnegie Classification of Institutions of Higher Learning. Link to KSU News article » 2017 July 1 - Dr. Don McGarey was selected to serve as the interim Vice President for Research. Ph.D. in Analytics and Data Science program moves to KSU's Graduate College. Build-out of the 5th floor of the Science Laboratory building is completed. 2016 February 8 - KSU was upgraded to a doctoral research institution with R3 status by the Carnegie Classification of Institutions of Higher Learning. 2015 The former Department of Biology and Physics has officially split into three departments: Department of Ecology, Evolution, and Organismal Biology, Department of Molecular and Cellular Biology, & Department of Physics. Ph.D. in Analytics and Data Science program was approved. Computer Science moves to College of Computing and Software Engineering (CCSE). 2014 The former Department of Mathematics and Statistics has officially split into two departments: Department of Mathematics & Department of Statistics and Analytical Sciences. July 28 - Construction starts on The Oasis, outdoor classroom. November 14 - The Oasis - Outdoor Classroom opens. Birla Carbon Scholars Program launched. Thanks to a generous contribution from Birla Carbon. 2013 August 14 - Bachelor of Applied Computer Science program was approved. 2012 Master of Science in Integrative Biology (MSIB) program was approved. Dr. Mark R. Anderson named Dean of CSM. KSU to offer Master of Science in Computer Science (MSCS), housed in the CSM's Department of Computer Science. Master of Science in Chemical Sciences (MSCB) program was approved. October 25 - The Science Laboratory Building opened, featuring 73,000 square feet, five-stories, six teaching labs and 17 research labs. 2011 Groundbreaking of New Science Lab Addition. Department of Computer Science and Information Systems becomes the Department of Computer Science; Information Systems moves to Coles College of Business. 2010 Dr. Ronald H. Matson appointed Interim Dean of CSM. Former Nursing Building occupied by Department of Mathematics and Statistics and renamed Mathematics and Statistics building. CSM labs open in Prillaman Hall. Advancing the Teaching of Mathematics and Science (A.T.O.M.S.) center jointly opened with Bagwell College of Education in House 59. 2000s 2007 Master of Arts in Teaching (M.A.T. - Science) first offered in collaboration with Bagwell College of Education. Department of Biological and Physical Sciences renamed Department of Biology and Physics. 2006 Master of Arts in Teaching (M.A.T. - Mathematics) offered in collaboration with Bagwell College of Education. Masters of Science in Applied Statistics (MSAS) program added to the curriculum. Department of Mathematics renamed Department of Mathematics and Statistics. 2005 Proposed a new Science Laboratory Building. 2004 CSM acquires much needed van for field trips, research, etc. Thanks to a generous contribution from Dr. Kathleen Fleiszar. 2003 BS in Biotechnology offered (Spring 2003). 2002 The Ann and John Clendenin Building (37,000 sq. ft.) opened. Complex for Applied Science Activities (CASA) and Center for Elections opens in House 57. 2001 Masters of Science in Applied Computer Science degree offered by Department of Computer Science and Information Systems (CSIS). John Clendenin, education advocate and donor for whom the Ann and John Clendenin Computer Science Building is named, received Kennesaw State University's (KSU's) annual honorary doctorate. Arboretum Co-Founders, Dr. Mary Lance and Ed Bostick, honored on 25th anniversary of Arboretum’s dedication. Department of Chemistry renamed Department of Chemistry and Biochemistry. 2000 Dedication of the Joyce H. Pegues Memorial Greenhouse. 1990s 1999 First CSM masters program offered: Master of Science in Information Systems. 1997 Dr. Laurence Peterson becomes the second CSM Dean. 1996 New $15M (104,336 sq ft.) Science Building opens. Original Science Building becomes Nursing Building. Kennesaw State College becomes Kennesaw State University. School of Science and Mathematics renamed College of Science and Mathematics (CSM). Dr. Herbert Davis becomes first Dean for CSM. 1994 School of Science and Allied Health becomes School of Science and Mathematics. Department of Nursing becomes the School of Nursing. 1993 Department of Chemistry and Physics becomes Department of Chemistry. Department of Biology becomes Department of Biological and Physical Sciences. 1980s Science Lab in the 1980's at Kennesaw State University. 1988 Kennesaw College becomes Kennesaw State College. 1987 Department of Computer Science and Information Systems created. 1983 Division of Natural Science and Mathematics name changes to School of Natural Science and Mathematics. Dr. Herbert Davis becomes the first Dean of the School of Science and Allied Health. Four Departments created: Department of Biology Department of Chemistry and Physics Department of Mathematics and Computer Science Department of Nursing 1970s 1976 Kennesaw State University Arboretum dedication 1977 Kennesaw Junior College becomes Kennesaw College. 1976 Dedication of the campus Arboretum by Science and Mathematics faculty as part of the U.S. Bicentennial celebration. 1970 Dr. Herbert Davis becomes Chair of the Division of Natural Sciences and Mathematics. 1960s 1967 Science Building (original) opens (31,615 sq. ft.). 1966 Kennesaw Junior College opens. Division of Natural Science and Mathematics created. Dr. Wesley Walraven is the first Division Chair. 1965 Officially named Kennesaw Junior College (August). 1963 The Georgia Board of Regents approved the creation of a new institution, tentatively named Cobb County Junior College on October 9, 1963. Our community engagement and outreach initiatives are designed to engage, inspire, and empower individuals from all walks of life. Whether you're looking to lend a helping hand, learn something new, or simply connect with others who share your passions, you've come to the right place. Please see different programs and initiatives listed below that CSM is involved in. CSM Blood Drives In the past, the College of Science and Mathematics (CSM) has hosted blood drives in collaboration with the American Red Cross. Atlanta Science Festival CSM/KSU is a proud partner and silver level sponsor of The Atlanta Science Festival (ASF). ASF is an annual public celebration of local science and technology. Curious people of all ages will explore the science and technology in our region and see how science is connected to all parts of our lives. For more information about the Atlanta Science Festival, please visit the website . March 8-22, 2025 Science Olympiad at KSU Science Olympiad is an annual Kennesaw State University (KSU) event co-hosted by the College of Science and Mathematics and the College of Architecture and Construction Management. It is a national competition for middle school and high school students. For more information about Science Olympiad at KSU, please visit website . KSU Mathematics Competition Since 2006, KSU Mathematics Competition is an annual competition for Georgia high school students, both public and private, sponsored by the Department of Mathematics, College of Science and Mathematics (CSM), and Kennesaw State University (KSU). For more information about the KSU Mathematics Competition, please visit the website . Cobb Future Fest In February 2024, The College of Science and Mathematics was proud to be a platinum level sponsor for the Cobb Innovation & Technology Academy (CITA) "Future Fest" Career Festival. For more information about this event, please visit the website . GYSTC SPSU was instrumental in the development of Georgia Youth Science and Technology Center ( GYSTC ) in 1989, which is located on the Kennesaw campus, and holds workshops to expose 4th & 5th grade students to biology in rural Georgia. A representative from the College of Science and Mathematics (CSM) has served in an advisory role for this organization for many years. The state GYSTC, Inc. Board of Directors is a cooperating partner with Kennesaw State University and shares the responsibility of the overall direction of the organization and for helping to secure and provide resources to support the programs. Student Participation Southeastern Trust for Parks and Land SCM 2000 students are partnering with the Southeastern Trust for Parks and Land to use science and mathematics to enhance soil and water quality in a community garden and studying park usage patterns. This relationship was established in 2022 and is ongoing. Faculty participation Anato-bee (February 2024) - High School Anatomy Competition. CPR Training - Since 2023, Department of Ecology, Evolution, and Organismal Biology (EEOB) faculty have been periodically holding sessions to teach Hands only CPR to the broader KSU community so that people are trained to try to save lives in emergency cardiac arrest situations. Woodstock High School STEMposium - The College of Science and Mathematics (CSM) Faculty have participated in the 2023-2024 Woodstock High School STEMposium, a lecture series for high school science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) students. Regional High School and Middle School Science Bowl - Hosted by The College of Science and Mathematics (CSM) and sponsored by the US Department of Energy ( NSB Georgia Regional High School... | U.S. DOE Office of Science (SC) (osti.gov) ). CSM has been involved with this for 20 years. Boy Scouts of America - The Department of Physics hosts the following events in collaboration with Atlanta Area Council, Boy Scouts of America (Atlanta Area Council | Boy Scouts of America (atlantabsa.org)): Boy Scouts Nuclear Merit Badge Workshop (fall) and Boy Scouts Spring STEM Summit (spring) Georgia Academic Decathlon (Georgia Academic Decathlon (pageinc.org)). CSM is involved in the PAGE (Professional Association of Georgia Educators) Georgia Academic Decathlon. It is primarily hosted by the Bagwell College of Education at KSU. Click on the departments listed below for more information. Chemistry and Biochemistry Ecology, Evolution, and Organismal Biology Mathematics Molecular and Cellular Biology Physics Chemistry and Biochemistry The professional guidance and student-focused instruction in the Department of Chemistry and Biochemistry utilizes hands-on training with state-of-the-art instrumentation in synthesis and analytical techniques. All students, starting in their first year, are encouraged to participate in innovative interdisciplinary research experiences to enhance their occupationally relevant degree. Our future-ready graduates are prepared for successful careers in industry, academia, and health sciences. Department website Ecology, Evolution, and Organismal Biology The Department of Ecology, Evolution, and Organismal Biology (EEOB) fosters a dynamic and collaborative academic community where pioneering research and student success converge. With access to an array of ecosystems, from urban to rural, our singular location provides faculty and students with exceptional opportunities for unique research and field experiences. By integrating cutting-edge research with immersive, hands-on learning, students are equipped with the critical skills needed to excel in their current and future careers and are empowered to thrive and to make significant contributions to society. Department website Mathematics Our students experience world-class instruction in the Department of Mathematics from faculty who are deeply invested in student success. Nearly all courses offered by the department are designed and taught entirely by full-time faculty. Our small classes allow instructors to develop close individualized relationships with students that sets them on a path for success whether majoring in mathematics or many other related disciplines. Our department has a vibrant research culture and actively engages in mentoring students in original research projects. Our graduates are fully prepared to enter the workforce in industry or academia where deep analytic and quantitative skills are in high demand. Department website Molecular and Cellular Biology The Department of Molecular and Cellular Biology (MCB) offers a comprehensive and innovative education in core domains of the life sciences including molecular biology, microbiology, developmental biology, and genetics. Our curriculum is enhanced through real world skills-building, inquiry-based courses, experiential learning, and training opportunities in state-of-the-art research and teaching facilities. Our world class faculty are dedicated to understanding biological phenomena and to developing applications that advance society, while also training our students to be the next generation of scientists, health professionals, educators, and enlightened citizens. Department website Physics The Department of Physics engages students through a student-centered, research-driven curriculum, where students are actively involved in high-impact research addressing significant global issues. With a personalized approach, our program fosters the creation of new knowledge and the development of critical thinking and scientific problem-solving skills for our graduates to excel in top-tier graduate programs and the STEM workforce. The department has been continuously accredited by the American Chemical Society (ACS) since 1987 and students completing a baccalaureate degree that meets the ACS Guidelines will receive an ACS-certified degree. All of the degree concentrations could include the course work and experience necessary to satisfy requirements for ACS certification with proper choice of supporting discipline elective credits. We have a bright and energetic faculty and a dedicated, helpful professional staff who are all available to assist our students as they grow and mature as scientists. The faculty members have research interests that span all of the traditional sub-disciplines of chemistry (analytical, biochemistry, inorganic, organic, and physical chemistry) as well as interdisciplinary and translational research projects. Undergraduate research is a critical component of our students' preparation and training, and all of our tenure track faculty members engage in undergraduate research. This provides students with the opportunity to pursue a major field of concentration in physics with the necessary specialization to succeed in a wide array of post-baccalaureate opportunities. The study of physics is a good choice for students desiring positions in industry that are on the cutting edge of engineering and science, as well as for students who wish to continue with Master and PhD programs. For example, physics researchers are investigating the fundamental nature of the proton, top quark and Higgs boson production, laser interactions with semiconductors, light on the 10-15 second time scale, quantum-enabled technologies, bioactive glasses, quantum materials, light-driven topological states of matter, novel magnetic excitations, and black holes. The department research areas include Astrophysics , Atomic, Molecular, and Optical Physics (AMO) , Condensed Matter and Materials Physics , Experimental Particle Physics , and Theoretical Particle Physics . These are keystones of technological and fundamental science progress. They also underlie all of engineering and are a useful second major for those pursuing degrees in mathematics, electrical or mechanical engineering technology. All of our physics students receive job offers that put them in the front lines of fascinating careers and maximize their earnings potential. The program integrates rigorous scientific training with real-world experience to develop highly skilled, workforce-ready leaders who will translate biomedical discovery into meaningful societal impact and healthier communities. The Ph.D. in Biomedical Sciences program will launch in Fall 2027 at Kennesaw State University, an R2 university in northwest metro-Atlanta, Georgia. Application Deadlines Applications for the program are now open for Fall 2027. Priority Deadline: January 15 Final Deadline: April 1 Apply Now More Information Have Questions? View Frequently Asked Questions . Ph.D. in Biomedical Sciences Virtual Information Sessions The KSU College of Science and Mathematics is excited to prepare the next generation of workforce-ready biomedical innovators with our new Ph.D. in Biomedical Sciences program launching in Fall 2027. In these virtual information sessions, program director Melanie Griffin covers topics that include: Admission Requirements Program Research & Curriculum What to Expect as a Student Open Q&A Portion Monday, October 19, 2026, from 12:00 pm to 1:00 pm Questions? Reach out to phdbiomedsciences@kennesaw.edu. Key Program Features Prepares graduates for careers in industry, academia, government, and regulatory science. Opportunity to conduct research with and be mentored by established faculty investigators engaged in cutting-edge biomedical and health research. Participate in immersive internships with leading biomedical and health industry partners to develop real-world, hands-on experience and skill sets. Access to state-of-the-art laboratories, core facilities, and research infrastructure. Comprehensive mentorship, individualized development planning, and strong career placement support. Featured College Research Department of Chemistry and Biochemistry Research Areas Department of Ecology, Evolution, and Organismal Biology Department of Mathematics Research Areas Department of Molecular and Cellular Biology Research Areas Department of Physics Research Areas Frequently Asked Questions How long does the program take? The Ph.D. in Biomedical Sciences is a four-year, 60-credit degree program. When is the application deadline? The early priority deadline is January 15th and the final deadline is April 1st . Visit the Graduate Admissions website to learn how to apply. Is the program in-person or online? The Ph.D. in Biomedical Sciences is a fully in-person program. The program will primarily take place on the Kennesaw campus. However, depending on the home department of the mentoring faculty, research may take place on the Marietta campus. What does program coursework include? The program includes coursework and research in: Drug discovery and development Disease modeling and molecular diagnostics Pharmacology, neuroscience, microbiology, and immunology Regulatory science and clinical trial design Coursework aligns with the job functions of medical scientists in healthcare and therapeutic practices that may include leading translational and preclinical studies, evaluating biomedical interventions, and managing laboratory-based investigations. How many positions are available? The program admits 6-8 students each Fall semester. Do students receive financial support throughout the program? A limited number of graduate research assistantship (GRA) positions with a $32,000 stipend and tuition waiver will be available for each cohort. Do prospective students have to identify a mentor prior to applying? No, prospective students do not have to identify a mentor before applying. However, we strongly encourage applicants to describe their research interests and how they align with potential KSU faculty mentors in their statement of purpose. Applicants should also include any background information relevant to succeeding in the program. Who is eligible to apply? Motivated applicants interested in research-intensive biomedical science careers are encouraged to apply for this program. Eligible applicants include: Recent bachelor’s degree holders with substantial research experience and a strong foundation in biology, chemistry, neuroscience, or pharmacology. Master-level graduates from biomedical, chemical, or life sciences programs seeking doctoral-level training as a biomedical scientist. Non-traditional students, including: Working professionals in biotechnology, pharmaceutical, or diagnostic companies seeking career advancement through advanced training. Veterans with backgrounds in military medicine, clinical research, or bioengineering who hold at least a bachelor’s degree in the fields above. International applicants are also eligible to apply. They should apply by the early deadline to allow sufficient time to secure any required travel and immigration documents. Are there additional requirements for international applicants? International applicants should consult the following Graduate Admissions webpages for the most up-to-date application requirements. Graduate Application Process International Requirements What are the prospective career outcomes after graduation? Career outcomes include a broad range of interdisciplinary biomedical research roles, such as: Medical scientist Translational scientists Regulatory research scientists Clinical laboratory directors Government and industry research advisors Biomedical researcher Any further questions about the program can be directed to phdbiomedsciences@kennesaw.edu Read the Press Release Contact Information Kennesaw Campus 1000 Chastain Road Kennesaw, GA 30144 Marietta Campus 1100 South Marietta Pkwy Marietta, GA 30060 Phone 470-KSU-INFO (470-578-4636) Campus Maps Parking Media Resources Campus A-Z Index Academic Calendar Campus News D2L Brightspace University Information Technology Services Related Links Libraries Housing Financial Aid Degrees, Majors & Programs Registrar Job Opportunities Campus Security Global Education Sustainability Accessibility © 2026 Kennesaw State University. MS in Chemical Sciences Thesis Defense 2:30pm at Clendenin Building, CL 2010 Speaker: Blaise Williams, MSCB student Title: From BN-Doping to Multifunctional Sensing: Engineering Electron-Deficient BN-Heteroarenes with Tunable Photophysical Responses Abstract: Boron-nitrogen-doped polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (BN-PAHs) have emerged as a versatile platform for designing fluorescent materials with highly tunable optical properties. Incorporation of nitro (–NO 2 ) groups into BN-heteroaromatic frameworks produces electron-deficient fluorophores with desirable red-shifted absorption and emission; however, strong intermolecular π···π stacking due to strong dipole-dipole interactions often lead to aggregation-caused quenching (ACQ), severely limiting fluorescence performance. Building on our previous work, we utilized molecular twisting to suppress these detrimental interactions and promote aggregation-induced emission (AIE). Although twisted NO 2 -substituted BN-heteroaromatics successfully alleviate ACQ, poor solubility has remained a significant barrier to comprehensive photophysical characterization. Herein, we incorporated benzoxadiazole- and benzothiadiazole-based electron-withdrawing heterocycles into the BN-heteroaromatic scaffold to overcome this limitation. These structural modifications expand π-conjugation, reduce the HOMO-LUMO energy gap, preserve the twisted molecular geometry, and dramatically improve solubility while maintaining red-shifted optical properties. The enhanced solubility enables detailed investigations of solvent-, temperature-, halide-, and ion-responsive fluorescence behavior. This work establishes a powerful molecular design strategy for developing highly soluble, electron-deficient BN-based fluorophores that combine red-shifted emission, reduced aggregation effects, and exceptional responsiveness to external stimuli. Mathematics Colloquium Series 2:00pm at Mathematics Building, D 218 Speaker : Dr. Krystal Taylor, The Ohio State University Title : “Fractals and the Buffon Circle Problem” Abstract : Fractal sets arise naturally when classical notions of length, area, and smoothness are no longer adequate. A central theme in geometric measure theory is to understand how the dimension and geometry of a fractal set are reflected in its projections. Even some of the simplest questions of this type lead to surprisingly difficult problems connecting geometric measure theory with harmonic analysis, combinatorics, and number theory. One classical example is the Favard length problem, also known as Buffon's needle problem. Given a planar set, its Favard length is the average length of its orthogonal projections. A theorem of Besicovitch implies that a purely unrectifiable set of finite length has Favard length zero. For self-similar sets obtained as limits of finite Cantor constructions, however, a much more quantitative question remains: how quickly does the Favard length of the finite approximations tend to zero? Despite the simple formulation, determining the correct decay rate remains a major open problem. I will describe the geometry behind the classical problem, some of the main ideas that have led to progress, and what happens when linear projections are replaced by nonlinear families. This leads naturally to a nonlinear analogue of Buffon's needle problem—a Buffon circle problem —and to new questions about unions of circles, nonlinear projections, and the geometry of fractal sets. I will discuss recent results in this direction and the new phenomena that appear when lines are replaced by curves. By selecting a fixed point on the sphere, known as pole, one can project all other points onto plane through this fixed point. The plane onto which all the points are projected is perpendicular to the diameter passing through the fixed point. Excluding the pole, this projection is a smooth conformal (angle-preserving) function that maps circle on the sphere to circles or lines on the plane. It is believed that ancient Greek used this projection to map the celestial sphere onto the plane so that motions of the stars could be analyzed using the plane geometry. This presentation explores the process of calculating Cartesian coordinates on the plane from the coordinates of a sphere, and vice versa. The discussion begins with the derivation of the Stereographic Projection of the unit circle (S¹) onto the real line using a parametric line equation. Building on this, the formula for the Stereographic Projection of the unit sphere (S²) onto the complex plane is derived. Stereographic Projection finds applications in Cartography, particularly creating maps in navigating Earth due to its angle preserving property. Moreover, it is utilized in Crystallography, Geology, even in the Photography. References: Rozenfel’d, B. A., & Sergeeva, N. D. (1986). Stereographic Projection. AMS :: Feature Column :: Stereographic Projection. (2020). American Mathematical Society. CSM is pleased to offer a number of significant internal research funding opportunities for faculty, support creative activity and scholarship of faculty, and provide undergraduate students with research and creative experiences to enhance their learning. Department Research Areas Research Opportunities Research Interest Groups Support Facilities Equipment Department Research Areas The research areas at the College of Science and Mathematics allows students to expand their skills beyond their major in various interdisciplinary fields that span across the departments. Students will have the exciting opportunity to engage with dedicated and knowledgeable faculty members to conduct research that helps grow and support our surrounding communities. Each department offers subcategories that fit into the interests within each field for every student to excel in research that matters most to them. Select a department below to learn more about the research possibilities and subcatergories available: Chemistry and Biochemistry Ecology, Evolution, and Organismal Biology (EEOB) Mathematics Molecular and Cellular Biology (MCB) Physics Student Research Opportunities The College of Science and Mathematics (CSM) fosters a dynamic research environment where faculty and students can explore innovative ideas, address real-world challenges, and contribute to meaningful discoveries. From faculty-led projects to one-on-one mentorship, CSM provides our undergraduate and graduate students with opportunities to engage in research across a wide range of scientific and mathematical disciplines. Our research programs empower students to develop critical skills, expand their expertise, and make meaningful contributions to their communities through hands-on experiences and collaborative opportunities. CSM Undergraduate Research Programs Birla Carbon Scholars Program Selected undergrad CSM scholars will work one-on-one with a faculty mentor on their proposed undergraduate research project during the Birla Carbon Scholars Program. Birla Carbon International Scholars Program Undergrad CSM students will conduct research during the spring semester with a faculty mentor and continue their research in India during a six-week summer study abroad experience. Inspire Summer Scholars Research Program The goal of this summer program is to provide experiential learning to undergraduate science and mathematics majors. Students will develop skills to enhance their interest in undergraduate research, service learning, and internships. Mentor Protégé Research Program Gain hands-on research experience through the CSM Mentor Protégé Research Program. Working alongside faculty mentors, students develop critical thinking, problem-solving, and communication skills while contributing to meaningful undergraduate research projects. CSM Graduate Research Programs Peach State Bridges to the Doctorate This National Institutes of Health (NIH) T32 training grant is part of a federal program that aims to develop an enriched pool of well-trained biomedical scientists who will transition from master’s degree programs and complete rigorous biomedical, research-focused doctoral degree programs in biomedical fields. Bridges to the Doctorate program Additional KSU Undergraduate Research Programs First-Year Scholars Program Summer Undergraduate Research Program The Vertically Integrated Projects (VIP) Program Undergraduate Research Projects - Office of Research Research Interest Groups Research Interest Groups (RIGs) help connect PIs across campus to build interdisciplinary teams that span multiple colleges, schools, or units, but for which there is not an established unit on campus. Topics, research questions, and goals are all driven by members of the RIGs. RIGs are a great way to mobilize a team with shared or complementary expertise and goals. The College of Science and Mathematics (CSM) offers collaborative research opportunities in the following interest areas. Click on the research interest groups for more information, as well as the faculty associated. Adaptation and Change in the Environment Biomolecule Structure and Functions Chemical Biology and Drug Discovery in Microorganisms Cell, Developmental and Organismal Physiology Diseases in humans and model systems Materials Science Modeling of Physical and Biological Systems Microorganisms Biology and Infection Photonics and Applications Undergraduate Science and Mathematics Education Theoretical Particle Physics CSM Research Support CSM is committed to supporting success at every stage of the research journey through college-wide and university resources that strengthen the research process and foster continued professional development. From navigating research procedures to accessing laboratory guidelines and compliance resources, our goal is to help researchers turn ideas into impact. Faculty and students are encouraged to take advantage of these tools and resources to support their research goals. The Kennesaw Journal of Undergraduate Research - Peer-reviewed scholarly journal dedicated to promoting academic study and achievement among undergraduate students at KSU. Recruit Undergraduate Researchers - Connects faculty with undergraduate students for research opportunities. Research News - Showcases and promotes KSU faculty research achievements and impact. Learn more about the facilities listed below . Microscopy Core Facility Nuclear Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy Facility Histology Core Facility Scanning Electron Microscopy Facility Joyce and Ira Pegues Memorial Greenhouse Mountains-to-Metro Specimen Collection The Oasis KSU Field Station Microscopy Core Facility The College of Science and Mathematics (CSM) Microscopy Core (MC) provides access to confocal, deconvolution, super-resolution, and other optical microscope systems that are useful for multi-color imaging of live and fixed cells and tissue samples, and high-content screening. This state-of-the-art microscopy facility serves Kennesaw State University (KSU) and external researchers by providing microscopy-related expertise, training, and assistance for advancing their projects on various model organisms. Additionally, MC offers software packages on high-end workstations for image processing and analysis. More information Nuclear Magnetic Resonance The Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) Core Facility at Kennesaw State University (KSU) is part of the College of Science and Mathematics (CSM). It is the only high-resolution NMR facility at KSU; researchers are welcomed from throughout the University. We also provide services to other local universities and external clients. More information Spectroscopy Facility Listed below are the various spectroscopy instruments housed within CSM: Electron Paramagnetic Resonance Spectrometer: The Electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectrometer is a Bruker EMX running at X band (9.2GHz), equipped with an ER 083 electromagnet capable of reaching fields of 13 kG. Available cryogenics allow studies down to a few degrees above the boiling point of liquid helium, 4.2K. This allows studies of rapidly relaxing metal centers. EPR is a spectroscopic technique that provides information by detecting transitions between electron spin states. It is useful for studying molecules with unpaired electrons, including free radicals and metal centers. Paramagnetic probes (spin labels) and spin trapping reagents have greatly extended its usefulness. Jasco 1500 Spectropolarimeter: The Jasco 1500 spectropolarimeter is capable of measuring circular dichroism spectra on proteins, nucleic acids, and peptides. This CD signature is diagnostic of secondary structure formation and can be used to identify folding properties of biomolecules. The instrument is equipped with both fluorescence and absorption optics/light paths and has temperature stabilization via a circulating chiller. Back to top ↑ Histology Core Facility KSU’s Histology Core Facility houses the latest specialized equipment needed to prepare high-quality histological sections for molecular, cellular, and anatomical based research projects. The facility is housed in the 300-square foot research Science laboratory and includes aLeica CM180 Cryostat, a Microm 650V Vibratome, and a Microm 360 Rotary microtome. This suite of equipment allows for the preparation of sections from frozen, paraffin, and agarose-embedded specimens, as well as both fixed and unfixed specimens. In addition, the facility houses paraffin incubators, slide warmers, wet bench workspace, ample storage space, a fume hood, and a dedicated workstation. Scanning Electron Microscopy Facility The Tescan VEGA3 Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM) is fully PC-controlled and equipped with a tungsten heated filament. It has back-scattered electron (BSE) detection capability. In addition, the Tescan VEGA3 is fitted with a Thermo Scientific UltraDry x-ray detector to carry out Energy-Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy (EDX) for elemental analysis. Joyce and Ira Pegues Memorial Greenhouse The greenhouse is 600 square feet and has 8 wire-top benches that are 8 ft x 4 ft (256 square feet of bench space total). The greenhouse can be environmentally control; it has a full wall of negative pressure evaporative cooling and external shade cloth. This allows temperature in the greenhouse to stay below 30.5 degrees C maximum on the hottest summer days. There are two gas heaters in the greenhouse to keep it at desired temperature during the winter. The greenhouse has concrete floor. The greenhouse is located on the Kennesaw campus adjacent to the Science Laboratory building. Mountains-to-Metro Specimen Collection Kennesaw State University (KSU) is located at the intersection of an ecological hotspot in the southern Appalachians and one of the fastest-growing urban areas in the southeastern United States — the Atlanta metro area. The core of the Mountains-to-Metro Specimen Collection includes plants, insects, fish, mammals, amphibians, reptiles, and birds collected across this region. The collection supports active research on local species as well as educational initiatives focused on living organisms and urban ecology. The Oasis - Outdoor classroom The Oasis, a hands-on outdoor classroom, is one of most unique and innovative laboratory spaces on campus, that will enable biology students to study native Georgia plant life. The Oasis was built in the unused courtyard space between the Science building, the Science Laboratory building and the Clendenin building. This initiative, which includes a water basin containing and surrounded by a variety of plant species, was funded by a generous donor, Dr. Joseph Cook, and named "The Oasis" by the College of Science and Mathematics students in the CSM Courtyard naming contest. Construction for Phase I was completed in the Summer of 2014. KSU Field Station The Kennesaw State University (KSU) Field Station, managed by the Office of Research, is a 25-acre property located along a tree-lined road parallel to Interstate 75 approximately two miles from the Kennesaw Campus. Field Station projects span multiple colleges, allowing faculty and students to engage in interdisciplinary research projects. Students will learn how volcanism and plate tectonics have shaped Japan’s natural history by hiking a live volcano and visiting some of Japan’s many geothermal hot springs. Students will also visit Fukushima Prefecture and learn about the meltdown of the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power plant in 2011 and how the lingering consequences of that disaster have affected the people living in the region. Students will also explore many facets of Japanese culture and history through visits to Japanese museums, castles, shrines, temples, and by watching a play at a Kabuki theater. Program information 2024 Trip Recap Video playlist Navigate: Barcelona to Paris - An Art, Science, and Engineering Journey Embark on a journey of discovery from the Mediterranean coast at Barcelona, Spain, across the Pyrenees Mountains to Toulouse, France; along the Garonne River to the Atlantic Ocean at Bordeaux; then finish in the city of lights, Paris. Along the journey, appreciate the masterworks of art through the centuries, the foundations of most fields of science that make our modern world function, and the marvel of aerospace engineering that has redefined ease of travel and space exploration in the last century. Program information Belize Marine Biology This hands-on field course will introduce students to various tropical marine ecosystems utilizing the coast of Belize as its study site. The course will focus on the ecology of these systems as well as examining environmental impacts and conservation efforts as they relate to the cultures and politics of Belizean society. This is a course, not a tour, so our main objective in designing the mechanics of this class is to get you to look closely, and to synthesize what you see! Explore funding opportunities, learn how to prepare a strong application, and get support throughout the application process. How We Support Graduate Students We can help you: Find funding opportunities that match your academic and career goals Plan an application strategy and timeline Strengthen proposals, personal statements, and other application materials Connect with faculty mentors and campus resources Prepare for nationally competitive fellowships and awards. Start exploring funding opportunities early and work closely with faculty mentors as you prepare your applications. When you are ready, search available options and use our resources to plan your next steps. Fellowships Available Across Disciplines External fellowships are available in many fields, not only STEM. Opportunities may support research, teaching, leadership, public service, international experiences, creative work, and professional development. Fellowships and Scholarships What Are Fellowships? Fellowships are competitive awards that can provide financial support for graduate study, research, teaching, and other academic or professional work. They also help you build experience, develop new skills, and grow as a scholar and professional. Why Apply for a Fellowship? Applying for a fellowship can be valuable even if you are not selected for funding. The application process can help you clarify your goals, strengthen your writing, and explain your academic and professional interests more effectively for future opportunities. Download our list of available Fellowships Our Office Offers Student Workshops Student workshops can help graduate students: Find relevant fellowship and scholarship opportunities Understand eligibility requirements and application deadlines Write a winning proposal Work with faculty mentors Prepare a complete application package Faculty Workshops Faculty workshops can help provide guidance on how to: Identifying students for competitive opportunities Mentoring students through the application process Write a strong letter of recommendation Consultation Services Meet with our office for individual support to: Identify appropriate funding Develop a timeline relative to the targeted calls Review applications You can find upcoming opportunities and other funding resource information in the Hootline. Featured Funding Opportunities Two specific opportunities that align with the workshops. National Science Foundation Graduate Research Fellowship Program (GRFP) The National Science Foundation Graduate Research Fellowship Program provides funding for three years of graduate study in research-based master's or doctoral degrees in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM), including STEM education. Who Should Apply: All STEM fields (including education - undergraduate seniors and first year MS). Award: The fellowship currently provides a three-year annual stipend of $37,000 along with a $16,000 cost of education allowance accepted by the institution as payment in lieu of all tuition and mandatory fees with no cost to the student. Eligibility Criteria: US citizen, national, or permanent resident Intend to enroll or be enrolled full-time in a research-based master's or doctoral degree program Never have previously accepted a graduate research fellowship Have declined any previously offered graduate research fellowship by the deadline (if applicable) Have completed less than one academic year in a graduate program Joint bachelor's-master's degree programs are considered graduate students and meet eligibility criteria. Deadlines vary by field of study; all deadlines fall in early November (2nd week). Learn More About the NSF GRFP Department of Energy Computational Science Graduate Fellowship (CSGF – Krell Institute) The Department of Energy Computational Science Graduate Fellowship (DOE CSGF)supports doctoral students pursuing degrees in high-performance computing fields to solve complex science and engineering problems. The program seeks energetic and committed Ph.D. students, DOE laboratory staff and scientists or alumni that are dedicated to advancing their research with the desire to have a nationwide impact. The fellowship includes two computational science tracks: Science and Engineering Mathematics and Computer Science Who Should Apply: Doctoral students pursuing research in scientific computing and engineering disciplines. Award Funding: A yearly stipend of $45,000, full tuition and required fees at any accredited U.S. university, and an annual $1,000 professional development allowance. Eligibility Criteria: Applications typically open in the fall and close in January. Review the DOE CSGF website for complete eligibility requirements, deadlines, and current award information. View Full CSGF Requirements and Award Information Deadlines: Applications Open – late October Application Closes – mid January Award Notifications – late April What Are Graduate Awards? Graduate awards recognize achievements in research, scholarship, teaching, leadership, service, and other academic or professional work. Awards may include: Dissertation or thesis awards Student paper awards Poster and presentation awards Travel grants Research competitions Other forms of scholarly recognition Fellowships generally provide support for future study, research, or professional development. Awards more often recognize work or accomplishments that have already been completed. External awards can help strengthen your CV or resume and increase the visibility of your work. Search the list below to explore graduate award opportunities by sponsoring organization. Submit Your Interest to Apply You do not need to be the perfect candidate to apply. Many successful fellowship recipients applied more than once, sought feedback, and strengthened their applications over time. Even if you are not selected, the process of preparing a competitive application can help you clarify your goals, refine your research or professional interests, strengthen your writing, and develop valuable skills for future funding opportunities. Graduate Student Success Centers Graduate students on both campuses have designated spaces that cater to their diverse needs and offer a serene environment for studying, group projects, brainstorming sessions, and workshops. A current Talon Card is required for entry to the Student Success Center on Kennesaw campus. Please charge your Talon card every seven days at any Hotspot location on campus. Kennesaw: Academic Learning Center, ALC3550 Open ALC building access: Mon.–Sun.: 7 a.m.–8 p.m. A Talon Card is required to enter the ALC building during these hours: Mon.–Thu.: 8–11 p.m. Fri.–Sun.: 8–10 p.m. Marietta: Norton Hall, second floor, in front of the elevators Mon.–Sun.: 7:30 a.m.–6 p.m. Talon card not required Graduate Catalog The Kennesaw State University Catalog contains important information and is the official source of the university’s academic programs, courses, and policies. The Catalog should be used as a guide, in conjunction with an academic advisor and DegreeWorks, in planning a course of study and in meeting requirements for graduation. Graduate Catalog Graduate Assistantships The Graduate College is pleased to offer Graduate Assistantships in the following categories: Graduate Teaching Assistant (GTA) Graduate Research Assistant (GRA) Graduate Assistant (GA) A Graduate Assistantship provides valuable benefits for students, including a stipend and significant tuition reduction. This opportunity allows students to gain practical experience in their field while helping offset the cost of their education. Assistantships often offer unique professional development opportunities, enhancing both academic and career growth. Hiring a Graduate Assistant (GA) offers faculty and staff at Kennesaw State valuable support for research, teaching, and professional projects. GAs bring specialized knowledge from their academic programs, allowing them to contribute meaningfully while gaining hands-on experience. By supervising a GA, faculty and staff members can focus on higher-level tasks, enhance research productivity, and foster the next generation of professionals. By offering students a GA and hiring additional GAs, we hope to continue to strengthen KSU's commitment to graduate education and research excellence! Learn More Graduate Assistantships Job Listings KSU Libraries and Writing Center Mastering your graduate research process is a crucial part of your academic success. As a graduate student, you have unique resources available to make your research exciting and simplified. The KSU Library System gives graduate students special borrowing privileges, one-on-one research consultations, in-depth research guides, and more on both the Kennesaw and Marietta campuses. The KSU Writing Center partners with the Graduate College to provide specialized writing coaches for graduate student writers. University Libraries Graduate Writing Program Scholarship and Financial Aid Information for Graduate Students In the Office of Scholarships and Financial Aid , we aim to connect incoming students with opportunities to enhance their education. No matter where you are in the scholarship process, we have resources available to walk you through each step of the way. The Boren Fellowship is a competitive award designed to fund graduate students’ study and/or research abroad for a duration of 3 to 12 months in various countries. Recipients of the Boren Fellowship are required to pursue a course of study or research project that includes a substantial component of language study. The objective of the award is to train Americans in languages that are not commonly spoken in the United States. Following the fellowship, Boren Fellows commit to spending a year working within a U.S. government agency, thereby offering an excellent start to their careers. To apply, please contact the KSU Office of National & International Scholarships & Fellowships (ONISF) as soon as possible at onisf@kennesaw.edu . Paul D. Coverdell Fellows Program offers financial support to returned Peace Corps volunteers who want to pursue graduate studies. For more information, contact Dr. Juliet Langman, Dean of the Gradaute College at gradcollege@kennesaw.edu . From overseeing our modern parking decks and vast lots to orchestrating a reliable fleet of Big Owl Bus shuttles, our department ensures you'll never miss a beat. Our goal: take care of the logistics so you can focus on making the most of your KSU experience. Below are links to information to guide you through the graduate assistantship process. Faculty : Please review the Graduate Student Hiring Guide . Assistantships Types Assistantships Tiers Assistantships Forms Assistantships Deadlines Contact Us Types of Assistantships Kennesaw State University has three main categories of graduate assistantships: Graduate Teaching Assistant (GTA), Graduate Research Assistant (GRA), and Graduate Professional Assistant (GPA). Below are descriptions of each. Comparison Chart of the Three Categories Decision Tree Showing the Three Categories Graduate Teaching Assistant (GTA) Graduate Teaching Assistant (GTA) refers to graduate assistantships with a primary job duty of instruction. KSU has two categories of GTAs - Teacher of Record and Teaching Assistant. Teacher of Record (TOR) are the primary instructors for an undergraduate course. They may teach a maximum of 6 credits each semester. Teacher of Record GTAs are responsible for instruction and management of their courses. Graduate student TORs will have a faculty mentor in the discipline. Teaching Assistant (TA) TAs assist faculty members with teaching. GTA Teaching Assistant responsibilities vary greatly and may include, but are not limited to: Teaching a small section of a course Holding office hours and meeting with students Assisting with the grading of homework, exams, and/ or written assignments Administering tests or exams Assisting a faculty instructor with large lecture classes by teaching students in laboratory or discussion sessions Graduate Research Assistant (GRA) Graduate Research Assistant (GRA) refers to graduate assistantships that work on campus in research-related positions. These research positions primarily exist in academic departments as well as some research centers and institutes. GRAs gain the experience of working alongside faculty members on cutting edge research. GRAs are generally funded through competitive faculty grants and contracts. GRA responsibilities vary greatly and may include, but are not limited to: Collecting, coding, and/or analyzing data Conducting literature reviews or library research Preparing materials for submission to funding agencies and foundations Writing reports Preparing materials for IRB review Research assistants work under the supervision of an individual faculty member or center director. Research assistants should not be engaged in work unrelated to their academic program or that does not further their educational experience and objectives. Graduate Professional Assistant (GPA) Graduate Professional Assistants (GPA) provide an opportunity for graduate students to be assigned work that is relevant to their graduate program and the professional and scholarly goals of the student. The graduate professional assistantship should provide the opportunity for the student to use knowledge of their academic field while enhancing skills relevant to the student's professional goals. The ideal graduate professional assistantship will provide the student with a broader and deeper understanding of work in their assigned site, under the supervision of a mentor. The following guidelines should be used when determining the work assignments and workload for assistantships: Assistantships best serve the student, the hiring unit, and the student’s academic department when they are used as an integral component of the graduate education experience. Assistantships should enhance the educational experience by exposing the student to the professional activities of their disciplines, involving them in university activities related to their academic and professional interests, and affording them the opportunity to work closely with faculty and professionals. Assistantships should provide high quality support for the academic mission of the University. Graduate Assistantship Tiers The Graduate College uses Tiers to better accommodate the correct allocation of stipends and waivers to the amount of work required of the student. There are three Tiers: Fall and Spring semesters (5 months each) Fall: Aug, Sep, Oct, Nov, Dec Spring: Jan, Feb, Mar, Apr, May Graduate Research Assistants (GRA) and Graduate Teaching Assistants (GTA) GRAs and GTAs are paid monthly. The total stipend for the semester will be determined by the date you are cleared to begin work by HR and could be pro-rated if you are not cleared by the contract start date. We support and challenge students to become lifelong learners, collaborative leaders, and civic-minded scholars. We serve students in all undergraduate majors, whether they are starting college, transferring, or already studying at KSU. Our programs foster curiosity, build knowledge, and develop skills for long-term success and impact. Honors at KSU features: Engaging honors curricula with experiential learning Mentoring and support in applying for prestigious external scholarships, fellowships, internships, and research opportunities Excellent faculty and small, seminar-style courses Specialized honors advising Co-curricular events to broaden connections and inspire intellectual growth Study abroad and study away opportunities Leadership opportunities Capstone experiences The KSU Journey Honors College supports excellence in undergraduate education at Kennesaw State University. To prospective honors students, please consider this your invitation to join us. We can’t wait to see what you will do with the opportunities we provide! Supported by purposeful interaction with peers, faculty, and staff, honors students create a customized curriculum from exclusive honors learning opportunities . As a distinctive feature of the honors core, students are taught how to leverage their knowledge, skills, and experiences into compelling narratives about themselves and their goals as we prepare them to apply for prestigious external scholarships and fellowships. The honors curriculum provides students with an incredibly rich undergraduate experience, prepares them to achieve personal success, and inspires them to make a positive impact on society. All Honors courses feature small class sizes and provide opportunities for faculty to involve students in collaborative, creative, experiential, or interdisciplinary work that may not be possible in larger classes. We especially welcome proposals for Honors Discovery courses , which allow faculty to focus on an area that is of special interest to them. Opportunities to Teach with Honors Faculty may participate in the Honors College in several ways: Teach an honors section of a general education course Supervise a student in your class on an Honors contract Teach a five-week Honors Discovery course (HON 2400) Apply to serve as an Honors Faculty Fellow or Honors Lecturer (applications open annually) These experiences enrich both faculty teaching portfolios and student learning journeys across disciplines. Additional Opportunities Additional faculty opportunities will be added below as they become available. Additional Information Course Proposal Information As a general guideline, proposals to teach an honors course in Summer or Fall semester should be returned by the first day of classes of the prior Spring term. Proposals to teach an honors course in Spring semester should be returned by the first day of class of the prior Fall semester. Decisions about course offerings will be based on focus of the proposal, program needs and enrollment projections, and instructor qualifications. Priority will be given to full-time faculty with a track record of teaching excellence. All honors faculty must have support of their department chairs. KSU Journey Honors College is a community of academically talented, highly motivated students challenged to excel through a specialized and innovative curriculum. Students engage in a wide range of learning experiences including Honors courses and interdisciplinary seminars that promote intellectual curiosity, discussion, and collaboration. We provide opportunities for undergraduate research, domestic and international travel, distinguished first-year cohort study programs, and community service. Do Honors students receive special benefits? Honors students receive a variety of benefits, including but not limited to: Scholarship opportunities Priority registration Specialized advising Access to Honors Lounges on the Kennesaw and Marietta campuses Small, seminar-style Honors courses Study abroad opportunities Development of peer and professional networks How can I learn more about KSU Journey Honors College? KSU Journey Honors College offers a variety of events for prospective students and parents. You can visit us during an Honors Spotlight Tour or KSU Open House . You are also welcome to contact our office directly to schedule an individual appointment. Please contact honors@kennesaw.edu or 470-578-2364. What is an Honors Designation? An Honors Designation is what is earned at Commencement if the student completes their Honors coursework. Honors Designations can be found here. An Honors Advisor will help you decide which designation is best for you. If you have been accepted to KSU Journey Honors College with more than 60 earned credit hours, you are placed automatically in the Honors in the Major track based on your anticipated time to degree. Students pursuing the Honors in the Major track who wish to switch to the Honors Scholar or Honors Research Scholar track may do so with the approval of an Honors Advisor. How do I know if I qualify for Honors? You can view eligibility requirements for different populations by visiting admissions. How do I apply and is there a cost? There is no cost to apply to the KSU Journey Honors College! You can apply on the Honors Admissions page . Newly Accepted Honors Students I have been accepted to KSU Journey Honors College. Now what? Congratulations on your acceptance! All newly accepted Honors students should follow the steps provided in the Honors Incoming Student Checklist . When do newly-accepted Honors students receive priority registration? Newly-accepted Honors students will register for the first time at their KSU Orientation. Students will be able to register for Honors courses once they have attended an Honors Welcome Session. Priority time tickets will be assigned to new honors students during their first full semester of enrollment in Honors at KSU. Are there any required courses that I must take as an Honors student? All newly-accepted Honors students must complete HON 1100, an Introduction to Honors within their first two semesters with KSU Journey Honors College. How do I apply for Honors Scholarships? You can apply for all KSU scholarships through KSU's scholarship application. By filling out this application, you are also considered for Honors scholarships. You can view a list of Honors scholarships below. KSU Open House provides an overview of Honors, while the Honors Spotlight Tour presents in-depth information about eligibility and opportunities. If you are a prospective student interested in the KSU Journey Honors College at Kennesaw State University, we encourage you to attend an Honors Spotlight Tour. During this event, you'll learn more about the benefits of being an honors student, receive honors scholarship information, and have an opportunity to ask any questions you may have. The Honors Spotlight Tour also includes a campus tour assisted by a current honors student. Register here For more information on campus tours please visit: Visit the Undergraduate Admissions website FAQs What if I need to reschedule my visit? If you need to reschedule, please reference your Honors Spotlight Tour confirmation email. If we already received a campus tour during a different event, may we opt out of the tour during the Honors Spotlight Tour? Yes. You are welcome to opt out of the campus tour during the Honors Spotlight Tour. Is the campus tour given during the Honors Spotlight Tour different from general campus tour? Yes. The campus tour given during the Honors Spotlight Tour is slightly different from the general KSU campus tour. While you will visit many of the same locations, your tour during the Honors Spotlight Tour will be accompanied by a current Honors student and you will receive the tour from an Honors perspective. What does The Honors Spotlight Tour consist of? The Honors Spotlight Tour consists of a campus tour from an Honors perspective followed by a 45-minute presentation about KSU Journey Honors College. During the presentation, you will receive information about special honors cohorts, honors scholarships, our flexible honors curriculum, honors housing, and more. I'm a high school sophomore. Is it too early to attend an Honors Spotlight Tour? It's never too early to attend an Honors Spotlight Tour. We encourage high school sophomores, juniors, seniors, and college transfer students to attend this event. Please contact honors@kennesaw.edu for more information.
