Little did the College of Architecture and Construction Management (CACM) alumnus know that he’d be designing entire city centers, guiding one of the most ambitious redevelopment efforts in metro Atlanta. Since earning his Bachelor of Architecture from the former Southern Polytechnic State University, Calvo has gone on to become an associate principal and Atlanta studio lead for the urban planning and design firm MKSK, overseeing projects that shape communities across the Southeast and Midwest. “Coming to Southern Polytechnic was a turning point in my life,” Calvo said. “It was my first experience living in the United States, and the sense of community on campus made that transition really meaningful.” Recently, Calvo took a lead role in the Downtown Smyrna Redevelopment Project, a public process to re-imagine a nine-acre site just south of the city’s downtown. The property, currently home to Smyrna First Baptist Church until their relocation in two years, will preserve a historic chapel for public use while opening the remainder of the land for mixed-use redevelopment. Rather than taking a passive approach, the City of Smyrna launched a yearlong planning and community engagement process. Calvo’s firm served as the lead consultant, working with residents, city officials, and stakeholders to craft a preferred redevelopment concept that reflects shared priorities and long-term goals. “People wanted it to feel like an extension of downtown,” he said. “They wanted high-quality public spaces, thoughtful architecture, the right mix of housing, businesses, and vibrancy.” The vision includes housing, retail and dining options, adaptive reuse of the historic chapel, and enhanced pedestrian and bicycle connectivity through the Jonquil Mile corridor. City leaders have emphasized the importance of creating a walkable environment that strengthens Smyrna’s identity while supporting responsible growth. The next phase will involve selecting a development partner to bring the community informed vision to life. Calvo credits his architecture education for laying the groundwork for his career in urban planning. “Luis represents the very best of our architecture alumni,” said CACM Dean Hazem Rashed-Ali. “His ability to apply design thinking at the scale of entire communities demonstrates the depth of education our students receive.” After graduating, Calvo worked as an architectural designer in South Florida before realizing his interests extended beyond individual structures. “I realized I was more interested in how cities were put together rather than buildings,” he said. He earned a master’s degree in urban planning from the University of Louisville in 2013 and later joined MKSK, where he has spent 13 years rising from entry-level planner to Associate Principal. Three years ago, he returned to Metro Atlanta to lead the firm’s local studio, bringing national experience back to the region where his career began. In his role, Calvo balances creative design work with client coordination, long-range planning, and public engagement. He often manages multiple projects simultaneously, helping cities navigate zoning challenges, funding realities, and infrastructure needs while keeping community priorities at the forefront. “We want people to understand that what they tell us at the beginning directly shapes the outcome at the end,” he said. Reflecting on his career journey, Calvo noted the broad applicability of his degree. “An architecture degree can take you to many different paths professionally,” Calvo said. “The creative problem-solving and communication skills are infinitely transferable.” – Story by Raynard Churchwell Photo provided Related Stories Alumna earns competitive scholarship to study in Japan Construction management gala celebrates 25 years of student support Kennesaw State architecture alumnus finds early career success Kennesaw State student explores the mental effects of workplace automation A leader in innovative teaching and learning, Kennesaw State University offers undergraduate, graduate, and doctoral degrees to its more than 51,000 students. Organized by Kennesaw State’s Department of Architecture , the 2026 Architectural Research Centers Consortium (ARCC) and the European Association for Architectural Education (EAAE) International Conference was held April 8-11 at the Loews Atlanta Hotel and KSU’s Marietta Campus, carrying a theme of “local solutions for global issues.” The two organizations have nearly 250-member academic institutions in North American and Europe. “The annual Architectural Research Centers Consortium conference brings together peer-reviewed research in architecture and the built environment, with an emphasis on methodological rigor and cross-institutional exchange,” said Giovanni Loreto, conference co-chair and KSU associate dean. “This year’s conference was organized around the theme ‘Local Solutions for Global Issues,’ focusing on how context-driven research—particularly in material systems, construction processes, and design methodologies—can generate scalable knowledge across different built environments.” The conference featured architectural educators, researchers, architects, engineers, and construction professionals representing 75 universities and 5 research and disciplinary organizations from across the globe and was co-chaired by Kennesaw State University faculty members Loreto and Jeffrey Collins, associate professor of architecture. “It was a great experience for Kennesaw State University’s Department of Architecture to host the ARCC-EAAE 2026 International Conference,” said Collins, associate chair and associate professor of architecture. “For KSU, it was an important opportunity to increase the national and international visibility of our program while contributing to conversations about how locally grounded research and design can address global challenges.” During the conference, Department of Architecture chair and professor Saif Haq received the 2025-2026 ARCC Mary Kihl Distinguished Service Award, which recognized his exceptional service to ARCC. As a board member and treasurer, Haq helped improve operational efficiency while advancing the organization’s mission, an experience that further refined his research agenda. “This award affirms my belief that research, design, and service are most powerful when they work together, and I am grateful to the ARCC Board of Directors,” Haq said. The conference was structured to connect research with unique places through Atlanta’s architectural landscape. The conference included 137 blind-peer reviewed paper presentations, 29 peer-reviewed posters, two plenary sessions, four workshops, and three keynote speeches from distinguished architectural scholars and practitioners from the U.S. and Europe. One of the tours went through the northeast section of the Atlanta Beltline from Ponce City Market to the finish at Krog Street. The second tour explored the forces of modernism and urban renewal that helped shape the development of Midtown around the Woodruff Arts Center, Colony Square, and Piedmont Park. College of Architecture and Construction Management Dean Hazem Rashed-Ali said hosting the ARCC-EAAE is proof positive of Kennesaw State's rising national prominence. “I was delighted to see conference attendees visit the Marietta Campus and to showcase the excellent infrastructure and facilities we have. I’m very grateful that Jeffrey and Giovanni were able to show our college in a wonderful light, and Saif’s commitment to ARCC has earned well-deserved recognition,” Rashed-Ali said. “Kennesaw State University is on the rise, and this conference is a testament to how far-reaching our impact is across the world.” Building on the success of the ARCC-EAAE Conference, next year, KSU will be co-hosting the 116 th National Meeting of the Association of Collegiate Schools of Architecture (ACSA) with Georgia Tech. It was there that she developed an early interest in architecture thanks to her mother, who once brought home a floor plan of her bedroom. “I remember coloring it and asking my mom what it was,” de Almeida said. “From that moment, I started drawing floor plans of my friends’ houses and imagining what my own space could look like.” Now an architecture student in KSU’s College of Architecture and Construction Management, de Almeida has since built a supportive community on campus. As an event director, she helps organize programming that brings architecture students together, creates opportunities for professional growth, and strengthens her leadership skills. She has also contributed to award-winning design work, helping lead a team that won an international architecture competition. While researching architecture programs in the U.S., de Almeida focused her search on schools in the South and discovered Kennesaw State. The University’s location in metro Atlanta and scholarship opportunities made the decision easy for her. She arrived in January 2022 and quickly realized that adjusting to life in a new country would take time. “It was cold, and I didn’t have a support system here yet,” she said. “But every day I experienced something new.” Determined to build connections, she applied for a job at the Horace W. Sturgis Library , where she has worked since May 2022. “That’s where I found my first community,” she said. Once she entered the architecture program, de Almeida said she quickly fell in love with the studio environment and collaborative culture among students and faculty. Studio courses, which form the core of the program, require students to spend long hours developing design concepts, collaborating with peers, and presenting their ideas to faculty for critique. Her efforts have been appreciated by the faculty and staff of CACM. “Gabriela embodies the creativity, leadership, and global perspective we strive to cultivate in our students,” CACM Dean Hazem Rashed-Ali said. “Her passion for architecture and commitment to supporting her peers demonstrate the kind of impact our students can have both within the college and in the profession.” De Almeida credits several faculty members with shaping her experience in the program, including Tim Frank, Arezou Shafaghat, Jereme Smith, Marietta Monaghan, and Peter Pittman. Outside the classroom, she serves as event director for the American Institute of Architecture Students (AIAS), organizing workshops, lectures, and professional development opportunities for fellow students. In the role, she works closely with student leaders and faculty advisers to plan events that connect students with industry professionals and provide opportunities to explore different career paths within architecture. “I’m really passionate about education,” she said. “Being involved in AIAS allows me to impact other students directly.” One of her proudest accomplishments has been helping expand the chapter’s Beaux Arts Ball, a traditional architecture celebration that brought together about 80 students, faculty, and professionals last fall. The event created a space for the architecture community to connect, celebrate the semester, and build relationships beyond the classroom. De Almeida has also gained experience through design competitions. She helped lead a team of KSU students in the TerraViva architecture competition with a project titled When Walls Roam , which focused on adaptive reuse and historic preservation. The proposal explored ways to transform historic structures into spaces that serve modern communities while preserving architectural character. The project also received the Community’s Choice Award in TerraViva’s Venetian Villa challenge, drawing support and recognition from viewers around the world. “I’m really interested in taking historic buildings and giving them new life,” she said. “Adaptive reuse allows us to respect history while designing for the future.” After graduating from KSU’s five-year architecture program, de Almeida hopes to become a licensed architect working on adaptive reuse projects and eventually return to academia as a professor. “Professors played such an important role in shaping my journey,” she said. “I want to have that same impact on future students.” For de Almeida, the decision to study at Kennesaw State has been transformative. “I truly believe coming to Kennesaw State was the right decision,” she said. “I couldn’t be happier with where I am today.” – Story by Raynard Churchwell Photos by Darnell Wilburn Related Stories Engineering student creates robotic hand designed to track patient health Engineering student uses NASA data to study distant star systems Engineering student combines technical and marketing skills through hands-on experiences Construction management gala celebrates 25 years of student support A leader in innovative teaching and learning, Kennesaw State University offers undergraduate, graduate, and doctoral degrees to its more than 51,000 students. From serving as a marketing student assistant in the dean’s office to completing an internship with Vantage Industries, the Lawrenceville native has gained firsthand experience in communication, project coordination, and operational problem-solving. Those experiences built on a foundation that began long before college, rooted in an early interest in engineering and a desire to blend technical and business-minded thinking. Konziase said that Kennesaw State stood out to her because of the opportunities available on the Marietta Campus. She would later decide to major in Industrial Engineering Technology , which proved to be a natural fit because it allowed Konziase to combine her technical interests with strengths she had already developed in business and marketing. “I knew I wanted to go into engineering, but I also knew that my strong suits were in business and marketing,” she said. “Industrial engineering combines a lot of those concepts.” That blend of interests has shaped the experiences Konziase has pursued outside the classroom. As a marketing student assistant in the SPCEET dean’s office, she has gained experience supporting communications and marketing efforts while developing skills that complement her engineering coursework. At the same time, her internship with Vantage Industries, an Atlanta-based performance textiles manufacturer, has allowed her to apply industrial engineering concepts in a hands-on professional environment. “Cynthia’s experience is a great example of how our students can take what they learn in the classroom and apply it across different areas,” SPCEET Interim Dean Christina Scherrer said. “By developing technical expertise alongside communication, business, and real-world problem-solving skills, she is preparing herself to contribute in a variety of professional environments.” Konziase discovered the Vantage Industries internship through KSU Director of Industry and STEM Partnerships Kent Lusk, who knew she was seeking hands-on experience. Lusk connected her with the company after learning it needed help addressing operational challenges. Her work has focused on improving operations within a section of the company’s warehouse, requiring her to take on responsibilities that change from day to day. Some days involve identifying goals for the space and coordinating with employees as machinery or pallets are moved. Other assignments require her to log products, organize information in spreadsheets, or communicate with outside companies. The experience has allowed Konziase to see how industrial and systems engineering extends beyond calculations and technical design. The field also requires communication, organization, project coordination, and an understanding of how people and processes interact. “There are many nuances to this warehouse space optimization project that require a lot of detail and attention, and things that I may not be able to experience everywhere,” Konziase said. “My manager at the time, Jason Fountain, was also a great help throughout the process and offered a lot of valuable advice.” As she continues her studies at Kennesaw State, Konziase said the experiences have helped her see how her different interests can work together in her future career. “I’ve learned that I don’t have to limit myself to just one area,” Konziase said. “Engineering, business, and marketing all require problem-solving and working with people, and I want to continue finding ways to bring those skills together.” – Story by Raynard Churchwell Photo provided Related Stories Engineering student creates robotic hand designed to track patient health Kennesaw State researchers receive NSF grant to advance soft robotics education Engineering student uses NASA data to study distant star systems Student cooks up success through engineering and content creation A leader in innovative teaching and learning, Kennesaw State University offers undergraduate, graduate, and doctoral degrees to its more than 51,000 students. The Southern Polytechnic College of Engineering and Engineering Technology student is building a 3D-printed robotic hand equipped with sensors designed to collect health information while interacting with a person. “The whole point of the robotic hand is to merge robotics and biomedical sensing into one thing,” said Garg, a graduate of FCS Innovation Academy in Alpharetta. “It moves as a normal human hand would, and I’m going to integrate fingertip sensors so that I can monitor vitals of patients.” Daksh Garg Garg uses fishing wire to mimic tendons that move the fingers. Bearings serve as joints, while silicone will create a skin-like exterior. Fingertip sensors are expected to measure heart rate, blood oxygen levels, and skin conductance, while an accelerometer will detect movement. The system works by bringing the sensors into direct contact with a person’s wrist. As the robotic hand closes around the wrist, sensors positioned in the fingers can detect a pulse and collect readings such as heart rate and blood oxygen levels. Garg then uses a Raspberry Pi computer to control the motors that move the fingers and coordinate the hand’s motion. The project began with an idea supported by an Office of Research seed grant, titled ‘Healing Hands,’ to develop robotic hands that could continuously support a user or patient during emergency care or serve in an assistive caregiving role. That idea evolved through Garg’s work in the First-Year Scholars Program with Assistant Professor of Robotics and Mechatronics Engineering Razvan Voicu, his faculty research advisor. “Daksh has shown a strong ability to bring together mechanical design, programming, and biomedical sensing in a way that addresses a real-world challenge,” Voicu said. “His project demonstrates how mechatronics can be used to develop practical technologies that could eventually support patients and healthcare professionals.” Affordability is another goal. Garg estimates commercially available robotic hands can cost about $3,000, while his 3D-printed design could cost $500 to $600. His prototype is mechanically complete, and he is now installing fingertip sensors and developing software that allows the hand to close around a person’s wrist. Ultimately, Garg hopes the robotic hand can reduce routine responsibilities for medical professionals while making patient monitoring easier in hospitals and assisted living environments. – Story by Raynard Churchwell Photo submitted Related Stories Kennesaw State researchers receive NSF grant to advance soft robotics education Engineering student uses NASA data to study distant star systems Engineering student combines technical and marketing skills through hands-on experiences Kennesaw State researcher earns prestigious NSF CAREER Award A leader in innovative teaching and learning, Kennesaw State University offers undergraduate, graduate, and doctoral degrees to its more than 51,000 students. Now, she is using data from a NASA satellite to help researchers distinguish distant planets from stars that can produce nearly identical signals. Tran, who is originally from Vietnam, is studying observations from NASA’s Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite, or TESS. The satellite monitors stars and looks for repeated dips in brightness that may occur when a planet passes in front of one. “When an object goes in front of the star, it blocks a little bit of the light and causes a dip in the brightness that we observe,” Tran said. “If that dip repeats over and over, there might be a planet orbiting that star.” The challenge is that binary star systems can produce similar signals. When two stars orbit one another and one passes in front of the other, the change in brightness can resemble the pattern created by a planet. Tran’s research focuses on determining which type of system researchers are observing. Making that distinction can save astronomers valuable telescope time while also providing useful information about binary stars. Researchers can study those systems to estimate characteristics such as the stars’ masses and sizes. “By understanding other stars, we will know more about the sun, and where it is in its lifetime or what we expect to happen when it evolves,” Tran said. Tran moved to the United States in 2020 and studied English and mathematics at Gwinnett Technical College before professors encouraged her to pursue electrical engineering. She transferred to Kennesaw State in 2024 and enrolled in the Southern Polytechnic College of Engineering and Engineering Technology. Although the project centers on astronomy, Tran said it connects closely to her electrical engineering studies. She analyzes light curves and graphs showing how a star’s brightness changes over time and looks for repeating patterns using skills similar to signal processing in her major. Research, however, was initially unfamiliar territory. “At first, I didn’t think that I was capable of doing research at all,” Tran said. “But now, after two semesters, I get the idea that research is a learning process. It’s not about solving the problem at first sight.” One of the project’s biggest lessons came after Tran and her research team spent months analyzing a star system that produced confusing results. Their model suggested characteristics that did not make sense together, prompting them to investigate further. They eventually discovered that the signal they were studying was coming from a different star than they initially believed. “The challenge of this research is that we don’t know the answer,” Tran said. “Even if there are published papers talking about it already, we still have to study it further.” Tran credits Associate Professor of Physics David Joffe with encouraging her to pursue research and helping her work through difficult questions. “Thi has shown tremendous curiosity, persistence and a willingness to work through difficult problems,” Joffe said. “She has grown tremendously as a researcher, and her ability to bring her engineering background into this project has made her an important part of our work.” Tran has submitted a manuscript based on the research to a journal and is awaiting review. She said the project has opened her eyes to opportunities she had not previously considered. “A year ago, I didn’t know anything about research or the opportunities KSU could bring,” Tran said. “Now I know research is a learning process, and I’m excited to see where it can take me.” – Story by Raynard Churchwell Photo provided Related Stories Engineering student creates robotic hand designed to track patient health Kennesaw State researchers receive NSF grant to advance soft robotics education Engineering student combines technical and marketing skills through hands-on experiences Student cooks up success through engineering and content creation A leader in innovative teaching and learning, Kennesaw State University offers undergraduate, graduate, and doctoral degrees to its more than 51,000 students. The Wellstar College of Health and Human Services graduate and lifelong soccer enthusiast played the sport until she was 14 and, along with her family, was a founding member of Atlanta United FC. Crews now works as a journalist for Soccer Down Here, a premier soccer news outlet in the Southeast, while also serving as a reporter for Atlanta’s 92.9 The Game. KSU alumna Maddie Crews at FIFA World Cup in Atlanta. “The beauty of soccer is that it's a universal language,” said Crews, who holds a degree in sport management . “There are so many parts of the world where people play soccer. For the World Cup, you get to experience different cultures, you get to experience different styles of play, and you just get to embrace the fan culture of soccer.” During the World Cup, Crews has proved to be a preeminent source for all things soccer by attending matches and press conferences, writing and creating videos, appearing on the radio, and hosting watch parties. “It's been a tiring couple of weeks,” Crews said. “But you know, it's what I love most about it, so I wouldn't trade anything else for it.” Crews is no stranger to big sporting events, having started her broadcasting career with the KSU Owl Network , working in every aspect of the game day experience, including the 2023 ASUN Men’s Basketball Championship game. Since then, she has covered everything from high school football to the U.S. Women’s National Team and now the World Cup. “Maddie came in with big dreams as a talented student,” said KSU Assistant Athletic Director for Communications and Broadcasting Nolan Alexander. “She seized opportunities, took coaching well, and began to hone her craft. The KSU Owl Network is proud of her success with the World Cup.” Crews’ experience with the KSU Owl Network encompassed all aspects of production, including operating cameras, working on graphics, updating the score bug, and eventually on-camera talent. Maddie Crews conducts interviews at FIFA World Cup in Atlanta. “The KSU Owl Network helped me tremendously,” Crews said. “Nolan always had us do small stand-ups on social, and I think that was a huge part of my success. It helped me build connections professionally. Before joining the KSU Owl Network, I didn't think broadcasting would be where I would end up, but broadcasters are storytellers, and I love storytelling.” Crews is part of the KSU Owl Network’s history of propelling students to careers in sports media. Students present broadcasts of KSU athletics in a professional environment with industry-standard equipment. “Our motto is ‘yOUR story’ — our story fits into your story,” Alexander said. “When you tell your story, you tell ours. As we’ve developed our program, we can enjoy these alumni success stories. We have alumni with the Braves, ESPN, and many professional organizations.” Soccer Down Here reached out to Crews and ultimately offered her a full-time position after seeing her covering KSU women’s soccer on television and social media. “There were a lot of people at KSU who helped further my career and put me on the right path to meet the right people to get me to where I am today,” Crews said. “The beauty of social media now is you can create your own content and put it out there because you never know who's going to see it.” As a mainstay in Atlanta sports media, Crews has seen the city embrace soccer over the last few years. The World Cup has proved no different with hundreds of thousands of fans attending the FIFA Fan Fest and the matches at Atlanta Stadium. Crews said one of her favorite moments of the World Cup so far has been watching fans from different cultures descend on Centennial Olympic Park to passionately cheer on their countries. “I saw a video from the fan fest, and I thought, ‘The scenes in Mexico City Stadium look so great,’” Crews said. “Then I realized, it wasn’t Mexico City; it was Atlanta. Then obviously you have the USA match against Paraguay, and to see how many Cape Verde fans that were here, it was a lot bigger than I thought.” As soccer continues to unite Atlantans and fans from different countries, Crews is ecstatic to have a hand in covering the sport she’s loved for so long. “It was always me and my dad going to games and that was something we bonded over,” Crews said. “The emotion hit me like a ton of bricks when I walked into Atlanta Stadium and saw everything all decked out. It made me emotional, and I got goosebumps.” Story by Kyle Dawson Photos provided Related Stories Kennesaw State names nursing simulation lab in honor of Katherine Scott Alumna earns competitive scholarship to study in Japan Kennesaw State student publishes study on alcohol's impact on Ugandan women Kennesaw State architecture alumnus finds early career success A leader in innovative teaching and learning, Kennesaw State University offers undergraduate, graduate, and doctoral degrees to its more than 51,000 students. Drilling is one of four Kennesaw State University students who spent part of their summer at an archaeological research center, studying human skeletal remains dating from the fifth to seventh centuries to uncover clues about how people lived, what they ate, and the injuries and illnesses they experienced. Led by Susan Kirkpatrick Smith, an associate professor of anthropology in KSU’s Norman J. Radow College of Humanities and Social Sciences , the students traveled to Greece for a hands-on study-abroad experience . Since 2007, Smith, a biological anthropologist and bioarchaeologist, has been bringing small groups of KSU students to the Institute for Aegean Prehistory Study Center for East Crete, a research facility dedicated to archaeology and archaeological science. There, they work alongside professional archaeologists, learning how to clean, reconstruct and analyze human skeletal remains excavated from sites across the island. This year, the students focused on remains from two adjoining graves — one containing 14 individuals, the other 20 — with almost no other archaeological context to explain who these people were or why they were buried there. “This is really all we know about the people," said Smith, a faculty fellow in the Keeping Sights Upward Journey Honors College . “We're trying to figure out if they all died at the same time, why they were all buried together, if they had any diseases and what life was like for them. So the students are really helping to contribute to telling the story of people in the past.” The students spent four weeks in the village, working in the lab, meeting conservation specialists, and visiting nearby archaeological sites for guided tours. They spent time cleaning soil from bones, reassembling broken pieces and determining the minimum number of people represented. Students also learned to photograph specimens and use X-rays to look for clues about disease, trauma, arthritis, and dental patterns that might reveal information about diet or how people used their teeth as tools. “They see how things go from, ‘Here’s the site,’ to studying it in the laboratory, to sharing that information with the community and the world,” Smith said. Drilling said the expereince built on their classroom learning and introduced them to areas of archaeology and anthropology they had never encountered. “I was exposed to so many niche subcategories of archaeology and anthropology, and it was very interesting to learn about each and every one of them,” Drilling said. “This experience taught me how to collaborate with people from other areas of archaeology to contribute to an overall goal.” Beyond analyzing bones, the students had the opportunity to meet with archaeologists who specialize in pottery, visited conservation laboratories where broken objects are reconstructed, and toured archaeological sites with the researchers who study them. Later, they saw pottery, tools, and jewelry from those sites displayed in a nearby museum. “Having the opportunity to travel to Crete with Dr. Smith and get hands-on experience, while also applying the methodologies I have spent the past few years studying, was the most rewarding and fulfilling experience of my academic career thus far,” said Morgan Fowler, a senior anthropology major. For Fowler, the human remains in front of him were never simply bones. Each one held part of a person’s story, and he felt a responsibility to help tell it. “We can honor the lives and stories of those whom we are studying and recognize that they were real people and more than the bones in front of us,” said Fowler, who is also president of the Student Anthropology Club at KSU. “Our work is meaningful because humans are meaningful.” Smith noted that students have limited opportunities to study human remains in the U.S. because of the country’s complex history surrounding the excavation of Native American and enslaved African American burial sites. She also noted that Greece has more excavated human remains than trained bioarchaeologists available to study them. Many remains are therefore protected and stored in museum warehouses until researchers can analyze them. “Greece is a really great place to do this research,” Smith said. “The students get both the research and the study abroad experience while helping the people of Greece uncover their history.” Smith said the findings from the study are being compiled for future publication. – Story by Christin Senior Photos provided Related Stories Student cooks up success through engineering and content creation Alumna earns competitive scholarship to study in Japan Kennesaw State rises in U.S. News rankings of top universities KSU associate professor honored with 2026 Georgia Civic Excellence Award A leader in innovative teaching and learning, Kennesaw State University offers undergraduate, graduate, and doctoral degrees to its more than 51,000 students. The Ingenico Fintech Hub officially opened on Sept. 28 in the Michael J. Coles College of Business , representing the latest milestone in Kennesaw State’s efforts to expand financial technology education and industry collaboration. The state-of-the-art space builds on the University’s partnership with Ingenico and further strengthens KSU's role in Georgia's fintech ecosystem. In the Ingenico Fintech Hub, students will apply concepts learned in the classroom, test technologies in real-world scenarios and collaborate with Ingenico professionals on the challenges shaping modern commerce. Students will work to develop solutions leveraging Ingenico’s industry-leading payments processing software and point-of-sale technologies. “At Kennesaw State, we believe meaningful industry partnerships enrich the educational experience and help ensure our programs remain responsive to workforce needs,” KSU President Kathy S. Schwaig said. “We are proud to deepen our relationship with Ingenico through the creation of the Ingenico Fintech Hub, which will provide students with hands-on opportunities to engage with real-world fintech innovation while strengthening the workforce talent pipeline.” The new Ingenico Hub further enhances opportunities for students pursuing careers in one of Georgia’s fastest-growing industries. KSU fintech graduates are likely to remain in metro Atlanta, which is also known as “Transaction Alley,” where firms process more than 70 percent of all U.S. credit and debit card transactions. The region’s concentration of fintech companies creates a unique environment for students to gain industry experience, build professional networks, and launch careers at the center of financial technology innovation. Kennesaw State’s proximity to Atlanta inspired the Coles College to launch the state’s first master’s degree in financial technologies in 2022 and the first fintech bachelor’s degree in early 2026. The Ingenico Fintech Hub represents the next step in expanding experiential learning opportunities for students in financial technology. “Atlanta has become one of the nation’s leading fintech centers, and partnerships like this are how the Coles College stays connected to that growth,” said Robin Cheramie, dean of the Coles College of Business. “The Ingenico Fintech Hub will give our students the kind of hands-on, industry-facing experience that turns classroom knowledge into career readiness. It solidifies our college’s role as a destination for fintech talent, and we’re grateful to Ingenico for helping us prepare our students to lead in a rapidly evolving digital economy.” KSU students took an active role in shaping the Ingenico Fintech Hub. A student team, including several participants who have since joined Ingenico, presented concepts for the hub to company leaders during last year’s Digital Payments Seminar, and many of their recommendations were incorporated into the final design. “We realized our students needed more than a classroom – they needed a place to build. I brought that vision to Ingenico, and it grew from there,” said Nick Suppiah, director of KSU’s Master of Science in Digital Financial Technologies. “We don’t know exactly what fintech innovations will spark from this lab setting, but that’s what makes it exciting. The sky is the limit, and I can’t wait to see what our students create.” Jaime Hawkins, president of Ingenico’s North American region, said the company is excited about the impact the hub will have on both students and the broader fintech industry. Through internships and other collaborative initiatives, Hawkins has seen firsthand the talent and creativity Kennesaw State students bring to the field. “Every interaction has reinforced that this is a place where people don't just learn about innovation, they actively pursue it,” Hawkins said. “What I love about KSU is that there is such a strong focus on connecting classroom learning to real-world experience. Approved by the Board of Regents of the University System of Georgia on May 12, 2026, the program will launch in Fall 2026 and will be available in-person on the Kennesaw Campus as well as online, providing flexibility for students pursuing careers at the intersection of finance, technology, and data analytics. Housed in the Michael J. Coles College of Business , the new degree builds on strong student interest in financial technologies, a field commonly known as fintech. Enrollment in fintech-related courses at KSU has more than quadrupled since 2021, and demand continues to grow. In addition to a popular minor in financial technologies, Kennesaw State in 2022 launched Georgia’s first Master of Science in Digital Financial Technologies . “The Bachelor of Science in Financial Technologies advances a strategic priority identified by the University System of Georgia that is directly aligned with workforce needs,” said Ivan Pulinkala, KSU’s provost and executive vice president for academic affairs. “Fintech continues to emerge as a high‑demand field statewide, and with enrollment in KSU fintech courses growing exponentially in recent years, this program provides a complete undergraduate pathway for students.” Financial technologies power systems such as digital payments, information security, blockchain, and financial data platforms. Georgia is uniquely positioned in the industry with Atlanta-based firms processing more than 70 percent of all credit and debit card transactions nationwide, earning the nickname “Transaction Alley.” Georgia is home to more than 250 fintech companies and more than 42,000 fintech-related jobs statewide. Students in the program will complete an interdisciplinary curriculum that integrates finance, information systems, analytics, cybersecurity, artificial intelligence, and business strategy. Graduates will be prepared for roles such as financial analysts, information security analysts, software developers, compliance officers, and digital payments specialists. Experiential learning is a core component of the program. Students will participate in work-based learning opportunities, capstone projects and client-focused coursework, collaborating with industry partners including the Ingenico, CDE, TOTVS, and Sapphirus Systems, among others. “Georgia’s fintech ecosystem is expanding at a remarkable pace, with hundreds of companies processing billions in transactions and creating thousands of new jobs,” said Robin Cheramie, dean of Kennesaw State's Michael J. Coles College of Business. “This new bachelor’s degree builds on the success of our master’s program in Digital Financial Technologies and strengthens our ability to meet the growing statewide demand for talent with the technical, analytical, and ethical expertise needed to fuel Transaction Alley and beyond. We are proud to prepare students not just for today’s workforce, but for careers that will continue to evolve across digital payments, AI, cybersecurity, and emerging financial technologies.” The new degree program aligns with the University System of Georgia’s strategic priorities by supporting student success, economic competitiveness and community impact. Many major-specific courses will utilize open educational resources to help reduce costs for students. So, for the Kennesaw State University biology major, spending the summer in India researching treatments for lung cancer not only built on his growing passion for research but also his goal of improving access to care in Guatemala. Through the Birla Carbon International Scholars Program , Roque Perez and eight other KSU students spent six weeks this summer in Goa, India, gaining real-world research experience in biology, chemistry, and physics projects alongside scientists at the Birla Institute of Technology and Science Pilani Goa Campus. “I was handling lung cancer cells in my hands,” Roque Perez said. “Just the fact that I had to treat them and also take care of these cells was an amazing opportunity.” In India, Roque Perez and three other KSU biology students tested a drug on lung cancer cells to learn which proteins it deactivated and how that process caused the cells to die. The researchers hope the drug will eventually lead to more effective chemotherapy treatments for patients. An Honors student, Roque Perez came to Georgia from Guatemala six years ago on a scholarship to play high school basketball and later enrolled at KSU on his path to becoming a physician. He never considered research until he joined KSU’s First-Year Scholars Program where he worked on a project developing a device for radiation therapy and cancer treatment. Since then, his passion for research has continued to grow, eventually leading him to pursue the opportunity to participate in the Birla Carbon International Scholars Program. “The experience in India was eye-opening to me because it confirmed my path for research,” he said. “I don’t just want to go to medical school. I still want to be involved in research and become a translational medicine scientist, being a bridge of research and new treatments for patients.” Biology major Samya Doggett researched a less expensive way to use spectroscopy sensors to detect toxins at extremely small molecular levels. She worked with a team that tested using gasket rubber as the sensor’s base instead of the more expensive ITO-coated glass and silicon wafers. Doggett said the experience not only taught her to work independently, but also how to adapt and improvise when familiar tools or chemicals were unavailable. “It really expanded my way of thinking,” Doggett said. “If you get too comfortable doing research the way you know how to do it at home, then you never know what it’s like to do research across the world in a completely different way.” The experience also introduced the students to the history and culture of Goa, India. For physics major Lucas Ruth, it was his first time traveling internationally. He participated in cultural lectures paired with visits to museums, a spice plantation, and a local village and enjoyed an array of local foods. “It was very eye-opening to see the different ways that so many people live,” said Ruth, who researched super-conductors, materials that can conduct electricity without resistance under certain conditions. Ruth said the experience also introduced him to working with specialized tools and lab equipment he had never used before. “This program gave our students much more than research experience,” said Bharat Baruah, director of international programs and chemistry professor at the College of Science and Mathematics, who accompanied the students on the trip. “They learned how to work as a team, communicate across cultures and see their work from a global perspective. These are skills that will serve them well in graduate school, their careers, and future international collaborations.” “It also strengthened KSU’s partnership with BITS Pilani Goa and Birla Carbon, opening the door to new research connections and even more opportunities for our students and faculty,” Baruah added. The Georgia Research Alliance membership recognizes Kennesaw State’s expanding research enterprise. GRA supports recruitment of world-class researchers, provides access to lab technologies and facilities, and helps move university innovations toward the market. A public-private partnership, GRA’s mission is to drive greater impact out of university research and entrepreneurship to benefit Georgia and the world. Since its founding in 1990, GRA has helped attract billions in research and development investment to Georgia, generated tens of thousands of jobs in labs and startups, and launched hundreds of startup companies. “Becoming a Georgia Research Alliance member reflects the tremendous momentum of our research endeavors and the impact that Kennesaw State is making across Georgia and beyond,” KSU President Kathy S. Schwaig said. “This milestone affirms our strategic investments in research and innovation and strengthens our ability to contribute to the state’s economic vitality while expanding opportunities for our students, faculty, and partners. We are thankful to the Georgia General Assembly and all the state leaders who support the growth of innovation in our state through GRA and through rapidly growing research universities such as Kennesaw State.” Kennesaw State is a Carnegie-designated R2 research institution and is on track to meet R1 benchmarks for a third straight fiscal year, surpassing $50 million in research expenditures and awarding more than 70 research doctorates each year. Another sign of KSU’s research growth was the recent opening of the Robin and Doug Shore Innovation Center , a 70,000-square-foot facility on the Marietta Campus where experts from varied fields collaborate on research in key areas such as energy, infrastructure, cybersecurity, food security, applied computing, digital healthcare, and interactive media. As research awards have climbed steadily, Kennesaw State faculty have in turn converted research breakthroughs into marketplace innovations. Faculty invention disclosures have increased by 300% over the past two years, signaling a surge in new ideas moving toward patents and products. The HatchBridge Incubator , serving as both a community resource and the commercialization arm of KSU Research, has supported more than 250 startups that have raised nearly $30 million in funding. “The dedication of our research community combined with the resources invested by the University signal to the world that Kennesaw State is a serious research destination,” said Karin Scarpinato, KSU’s executive vice president for research. “Joining the Georgia Research Alliance is both a recognition of how far Kennesaw State’s research enterprise has advanced and an opportunity to accelerate where we are headed.” Kennesaw State’s admission to the Georgia Research Alliance builds on an established track record, with KSU earning 14 competitive GRA Innovation and Entrepreneurship grants in recent years. The awards have helped faculty across disciplines advance promising discoveries toward commercialization, enabling startups, licenses, and partnerships that would not otherwise have been possible. One example is GRA’s support of GlucoCheck , a noninvasive device that monitors glucose levels, created by Associate Professor of Information Technology Maria Valero. “Kennesaw State University has demonstrated a strong commitment to building a robust research ecosystem and translating innovation into meaningful impact,” said Tim Denning , president and CEO of the Georgia Research Alliance. “We are excited to welcome KSU as a member institution and look forward to collaborating on initiatives that advance discovery, support entrepreneurs, and strengthen Georgia’s innovation economy.” Kennesaw State joins nine other public and private universities in Georgia as GRA member institutions: Augusta University, Clark Atlanta University, Emory University, Georgia Institute of Technology, Georgia Southern University, Georgia State University, Mercer University, Morehouse School of Medicine , and the University of Georgia. At just 23 years old, Rixom has achieved the rare distinction of becoming one of Georgia’s youngest licensed architects. “It means a lot to me in my career,” he said. “It’s very rare that people get their license this soon after graduation. I made it one of my goals when I graduated to get it done as fast as possible.” Architectural licensure is built around two major requirements: professional experience and examinations. In Georgia, candidates must document approximately 3,800 hours of experience across areas such as practice management, design, and working with contractors during construction. After this, they must pass six exams that evaluate their knowledge across those same areas. For Rixom, the two requirements came together almost simultaneously. He completed his required experience hours during the same week he sat for his final exam. “My reaction really came from when I completed my last test and I got the provisional pass,” he said. “There was a lot of anxiety because this could be the last one. But then it was straight relief after I got the official report.” Getting there meant giving up much of his free time. After graduating from KSU, Rixom spent roughly six months working through the exams. Most days, he arrived home from work around 6 p.m., ate dinner, and began studying around 7 p.m. He would often study until 10 p.m., repeating the routine after each workday. “I really had to lock myself down after the year started,” Rixom said. “I would sit down for about two to three hours every day after work and study, study, study.” His ability to become licensed so quickly was rooted in a decision he made years earlier at KSU. While studying in Kennesaw State’s College of Architecture and Construction Management , Rixom secured an internship during his third year. Because aspiring architects can begin accumulating required experience before graduation, those hours put him ahead in the licensure process by the time he entered the profession full time. “I think the thing I’m most proud of is being able to look ahead and have that forward outlook in life,” Rixom said. “Just by taking the tests doesn’t mean you’re licensed. You still have to have the experience.” One of the projects that helped open that door was “A Framed Story,” the sustainable reimagining of Marietta Square that Rixom designed with classmate Sean Spencer. The pair earned Silver in the International Design Awards , becoming the first KSU architecture students recognized by the global competition. Before the project earned international recognition, it caught the attention of a professional juror reviewing their work at KSU. Impressed by the students’ design direction and production skills, the juror later helped Rixom connect with the internship that began his professional experience. CACM Dean Hazem Rashed-Ali said Rixom’s rapid progress reflects the commitment he showed as a student. “Michael’s achievement at such an early stage in his career is a tremendous accomplishment and speaks to his discipline, talent and commitment to architecture,” Rashed-Ali said. “We are proud to see him reach this important milestone so soon after graduation.” Now working at Smallwood Architects, Rixom is putting his license to use while working on performing arts center projects. He said his next challenge is learning the project management and professional skills that come with taking on greater responsibility. “I feel like I just have an initial taste of the profession,” Rixom said. “Now I’m trying to dive deep into it.” – Story by Raynard Churchwell Photo provided Related Stories Alumna earns competitive scholarship to study in Japan Construction management gala celebrates 25 years of student support Kennesaw State student explores the mental effects of workplace automation Kennesaw State University Alumni Association announces 2026-2027 officers A leader in innovative teaching and learning, Kennesaw State University offers undergraduate, graduate, and doctoral degrees to its more than 51,000 students. Through the dual enrollment initiative, Fulton County students can earn college credit while in high school, gain early classroom experience, and have a streamlined admissions process into Kennesaw State’s Clarice C. and Leland H. Bagwell College of Education . Leaders from Fulton County Schools and Kennesaw State signed the agreement during a ceremony on Tuesday at KSU. “By partnering with Fulton County Schools, Kennesaw State University is creating a direct, supportive pathway from high school to a bachelor’s degree and into the teaching profession,” said Jacqueline Quiroga, KSU’s assistant vice president for Enrollment Services. “This collaboration reflects our commitment to prepare future educators while making college more accessible and affordable for students.” The structured academic pathway allows Fulton County high school students to take approved Kennesaw State courses through Georgia’s Career, Technical, and Agricultural (CTAE) program. Students can earn 30 or more college credits before high school graduation, saving time and significantly reducing the cost of earning a degree. Kennesaw State will provide dual enrollment courses aligned with its teacher preparation programs, along with academic advising and degree planning, to students pursuing the CTAE’s Teaching as a Profession career pathway. The partnership also enables participating Fulton County students to apply to KSU at no cost and receive priority orientation and registration. Together, Fulton County Schools and Kennesaw State will provide coordinated advising, shared resources, and ongoing support to help students succeed at every stage – from high school through college and into the workforce. “Through our partnership with Kennesaw State University, we are not only expanding dual enrollment opportunities but intentionally building a strong pipeline of future educators empowering Fulton students to pursue teaching, return to their community, and shape the next generation right here at home,” said Gonzalo La Cava, Fulton County Schools’ chief human resources officer. Fulton County Schools will play a key role in preparing and supporting students, promoting the program across its high schools, and connecting students with hands-on experiences in the classroom. Students will have access to job shadowing, field experiences, mentoring, student teaching opportunities within Fulton County Schools, and professional development support. The school district also plans to offer priority hiring consideration to program graduates who meet employment requirements, helping create a direct pipeline from high school to college to career. – Story by Paul Floeckher Photos by Matt Yung Related Stories Kennesaw State and Ingenico create hub for fintech innovation and learning Launch '26 celebrates new school year, sustained momentum Kennesaw State's economic impact tops $2.55 billion Kennesaw State adds more on-campus housing for students A leader in innovative teaching and learning, Kennesaw State University offers undergraduate, graduate, and doctoral degrees to its more than 51,000 students. Schwaig returned home following a busy day on campus, nestled into her couch, and switched on her television. Earlier that day, KSU had unveiled the 70,000-square-foot Robin and Doug Shore Innovation Center, and to her delight, an Atlanta news outlet led its evening report with talk of the new $60 million structure. She was drawn in by soundbites from administrators, researchers, and students touting the benefits of the new interdisciplinary building and its far-reaching impact. The report continued, highlighting KSU’s ascension as one of the fastest-growing institutions in the country, its surging student population, and the rise of Owls athletics teams bursting onto the national stage. A theme was emerging, one of momentum. That moment of serendipity served as a crescendo in the 18 months since Kennesaw State launched its strategic plan, Taking Flight. The plan, unveiled in August 2024, is an ambitious series of five goals that serve as critical guideposts in KSU’s trajectory toward national prominence. “At the end of the day, Taking Flight has been defined by clarity,” Schwaig said. “It provides a shared sense of direction and gives us something meaningful to come together around as a university community. We have raised expectations for Kennesaw State University, and I believe our faculty, staff, and students deserve our very best. We are committed to moving the institution forward at a level of true excellence.” Growth alone was never the end goal of Taking Flight. Instead, the plan has focused on advancing the institution sustainably, ensuring that growth in enrollment is matched by progress throughout the enterprise. “We’re not just focused on growing,” Schwaig said. “We’re also focused on making sure we’re supporting excellence and innovation, and looking at the outcomes that support them.” ESTABLISHING A CULTURE OF RESEARCH EXCELLENCE The expansion and enhancements of research opportunities and expenditures have steadily become one of the clearest indicators of Kennesaw State’s meteoric rise. Over the last two years, KSU’s research spending has nearly doubled, rising from $32 million to $60 million, while research awards have climbed 53% over the last five years. “That funding doesn't simply support capital investments, lab equipment, and research faculty salaries; it attracts top talent, opens doors to national partnerships, and signals to the world that KSU is a serious research destination,” said Karin Scarpinato, executive vice president for research. Kennesaw State faculty, in return, have been highly effective in converting research breakthroughs into marketplace innovations that drive economic impact. Faculty invention disclosures have increased by 300%, signaling a surge in new ideas moving toward patents and products. At the same time, KSU’s HatchBridge Incubator has supported more than 250 startups that have raised nearly $37.4 million in funding, turning university research into real-world businesses. “Every one of those companies represents an idea that is becoming a business, creating jobs, and generating value for our region,” Scarpinato said. Momentum across the research enterprise has a trickle-down effect benefitting KSU students, too. Through initiatives like the First-Year Scholars and the Summer Undergraduate Research programs, students have more opportunities than ever to engage in impactful research projects under the mentorship of leading faculty experts. Managed by the Office of Undergraduate Research, the programs pair students who are interested in research, with faculty, staff, or postdoctoral research mentors to engage in intensive research projects. Often, students convert those experiences into oral or poster presentations at one of the institution’s research showcases, such as the Symposium of Student Scholars. Externally, the University has continued to engage with prominent organizations to expand student research opportunities. This summer, KSU students have landed internships in numerous federal organizations, including Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Savannah River National Laboratory, and the National Laboratory of the Rockies. Kennesaw State is also strengthening its connections at the state and national levels, building on its already robust research foundation. In May, KSU became a member of the Georgia Research Alliance (GRA), a distinction that places the University among the state’s leading research institutions and positions KSU to further accelerate its role as a catalyst for innovation, economic growth, and discovery statewide. The research partnership builds on an established track record, with KSU earning 14 competitive GRA Innovation and Entrepreneurship grants in recent years. The awards have helped faculty across disciplines advance promising discoveries toward commercialization, enabling startups, licenses, and partnerships that would not otherwise have been possible. KSU's admission to GRA reflects years of deliberate investment in research infrastructure, an effort that places the University among the top research institutions in the country. KSU is on track to meet Carnegie Classification of Institutions of Higher Education R1 benchmarks for a third straight fiscal year, surpassing $50 million in research expenditures and awarding more than 70 research doctorates each year. KSU took an additional step toward national prominence by joining the Oak Ridge Associated Universities (ORAU) research consortium, reinforcing its commitment to advancing impactful and innovative research. “Together, these memberships accelerate everything else we are building,” Scarpinato said. “Our goal is not simply to grow our research numbers. Our goal is to position KSU as a university where groundbreaking ideas are born, where students challenge what’s possible, where entrepreneurs find a home, and where the people of Georgia and beyond see the direct benefits of what happens on our campuses.”Off-campus recognitions have begun to mount as well. In November, KSU’s Center for the Advancement of Military and Emergency Services received the Association of Public and Land-Grant Universities’ Public Impact Research Award, honoring its real-world influence on veterans, first responders, and emergency managers. “Being recognized on that stage puts KSU in remarkable company and reflects the quality of the work happening here every day,” Scarpinato said. BUILDING SUSTAINABLY As research productivity accelerates, KSU is simultaneously expanding its physical footprint, investing in facilities that enable collaboration and innovation or simply serving as a home away from home. Guided by its Facilities Master Plan, the University is strategically shaping these developments to support long-term growth and a cohesive campus experience. A major step was the opening of the Robin and Doug Shore Innovation Center. Situated along Technology Way near the entrance of the Marietta Campus, the center is designed to accelerate innovation and entrepreneurship, foster collaboration across disciplines, and translate research into real-world solutions that benefit communities beyond campus. It also serves as the home of the Robin and Doug Shore Entrepreneurship Center, a unit of the Michael J. Coles College of Business, and the Office of Research’s Center for Interactive Media. Across campus, near the Engineering Technology Center, another structure has transformed the landscape. Officially opened in June, the 12,000-square-foot Hornet Hub will serve as the newest collaboration space for KSU’s award-winning student competition teams, including the Night Owl Racing team, aerial robotics competition team, and hydraulic bike team, among others. And on the Kennesaw Campus, the University’s newest residence hall – The Summit II – will house 460 first-year students starting with the Fall 2026 semester. The nearly 97,000-square-foot residence hall sits on the south end of the Kennesaw Campus adjacent to The Summit I student housing, which opened in 2022. The addition of The Summit II will bring KSU’s total number of residential communities to 11, with a total capacity of more than 6,300 beds across the Kennesaw and Marietta campuses. Notably, construction on the newest residence hall wrapped both ahead of schedule and under budget, said Lesley Netter-Snowden, executive vice president and chief business officer. “Housing and Residence Life is an auxiliary department, meaning it does not receive state appropriations or tuition revenue, and it must generate its own revenue to cover expenses,” she said. “The project savings will allow the auxiliary departments to reallocate that funding to other capital projects supporting the strategic plan, specifically strengthening the student experience and enhancing our physical environment.” As the University maintains a strong commitment to fiscal responsibility, external funding continues to support key priorities across the institution. In 2025, KSU raised more than $47 million, including $14 million added to its endowment. In total, 541 endowments now benefit scholarships, student programs, research, and KSU Athletics. These efforts have driven significant momentum for The Campaign for KSU, the largest and most comprehensive fundraising initiative in the University’s history. Launched in 2023 with an initial goal of $200 million, the campaign has already surpassed expectations, raising more than $227 million to date. In April, KSU saw its most successful Giving Day, raising more than $400,000. Now in its third year, the event attracted a record 2,116 individual contributors, many of whom were alumni, demonstrating the continued momentum of KSU’s culture of generosity. EMPHASIZING THE STUDENT EXPERIENCE The student experience on campus has made great strides since the launch of the Taking Flight strategic plan. Provost and Executive Vice President of Academic Affairs Ivan Pulinkala points to the success of the FLIGHT program, spearheaded by Vice President of Student Affairs Eric Arneson, as proof-positive of KSU’s elevated student experience. Launched in 2022, FLIGHT is a class‑year connection program, designed to enrich the student experience through intentional, high‑impact engagement. Offering distinctive experiences at every stage of the collegiate journey, FLIGHT supports students’ social, personal, and academic growth from their first year through graduation. The program achieved a significant milestone in May as FLIGHT 26, named for the targeted graduation year, became the first cohort of the program to reach Commencement. This fall, KSU will welcome FLIGHT 30 to campus. “We’ve been laser-focused on helping students discover and engage with KSU traditions, particularly within their academic homes,” Arneson said. “We’re already seeing increased participation as a result. Several colleges have developed goals centered on connecting students beyond the classroom, and that work has sparked new programs, partnerships, and meaningful collaborations.” The student experience extends beyond new campus traditions. In addition to new residential offerings on campus, student demand for transportation options will be met this fall with a new fleet of buses and expanded Big Owl Bus service including new routes. And for the first time ever, the fleet will feature four hybrid buses, underscoring KSU’s commitment to sustainable practices. “These initiatives stand out not only for their outcomes, but for the way they exemplify the institution’s broader commitment to intentional, data-informed progress,” Netter-Snowden said. Building on its rapid growth and increasing national visibility, Kennesaw State has refined its admissions process. The University has joined other top-performing institutions in the University System of Georgia in requiring SAT or ACT scores and, by 2027 will implement new GPA standards, strengthening its position as a destination for high-performing students nationwide. At the same time, KSU is carving new degree pathways that meet industry and student demand. Currently, the University offers more than 220 degree and certificate programs and has announced three new degree programs since the launch of Taking Flight. In Fall 2025, KSU became just the second institution in Georgia to offer a Bachelor of Science in Aerospace Engineering, helping address the workforce demands of a rapidly growing industry. Soon thereafter, the Board of Regents of the University System of Georgia approved additional academic programs at KSU, including a Bachelor of Science in Artificial Intelligence, a Ph.D. in Biomedical Sciences, and a Bachelor of Science in Financial Technologies. “We are working to make sure that over time our growth isn’t just measured by student numbers,” Pulinkala said. “It’s measured by our academic distinction, the accolades our faculty, staff and students receive nationally, and the rankings we earn in the academic marketplace.” RAISING THE PROFILE EXTERNALLY To achieve prominence and raise Kennesaw State's external profile, several initiatives within taking Flight are centered on developing partnerships and sustaining the national profile set by the success of KSU's Athletics programs. Casey Tanner, vice president of external affairs, said strong recognition within KSU’s state and local communities serves as the gateway to national visibility. “It’s working,” she said. “To date, we have expanded the network of external advocates advancing KSU’s priorities while strengthening our presence at the federal level. These efforts have resulted in successful congressional appropriations funding requests, and a rising number of KSU students securing internships in Washington, D.C. What began as local momentum has scaled into national achievements, raising awareness of Kennesaw State across the country.” To support this momentum, Tanner said her unit is continuing to explore ways to advance the value of a KSU degree by engaging with business partners. “A key step in this effort is the planned opening of a Midtown Atlanta office dedicated to fostering industry partnerships,” she said. “By establishing a presence in one of the nation’s largest hubs for corporate headquarters, our aim is to strengthen relationships with employers and elevate KSU’s reputation in regional and national business communities.” The new Midtown Atlanta office is expected to open in Technology Square during the Fall 2026 semester. Nationally, the Kennesaw State brand has established visibility by way of numerous championship-caliber athletics programs. Since joining Conference USA (CUSA) in July 2024 and elevating to the highest echelon of college football, Owls men’s and women’s athletics teams have captured five CUSA championships, earning a men’s basketball March Madness appearance and the school’s first-ever football bowl game along the way. “Since the beginning, our primary goal has been increasing visibility and strengthening the KSU brand, and we’ve made meaningful progress,” said Milton Overton, director of athletics. “As visibility increases, engagement follows. Alumni give more, partners lean in, and momentum builds.” As Taking Flight continues to guide KSU’s moment, Pulinkala emphasized that the University’s goal champions are not guided by rigid assumptions about what Kennesaw State’s next chapter should be. Instead, they are allowing progress to take shape naturally, informed by shared purpose, collaboration, and momentum across campus. So how does a modern university grow from here? “In one word,” Pulinkala said, “intentionally.” Related Stories Engineering student creates robotic hand designed to track patient health Kennesaw State researchers receive NSF grant to advance soft robotics education Kennesaw State researcher earns prestigious NSF CAREER Award Kennesaw State researcher receives NIH Grant to study sleep apnea A leader in innovative teaching and learning, Kennesaw State University offers undergraduate, graduate, and doctoral degrees to its more than 51,000 students. Scott and Lance Burchett Kennesaw State University has honored longtime donor Katherine A. Scott by naming a nursing simulation lab in recognition of her $1 million gift establishing the Katherine A. Scott Nursing Scholarship Endowment. The Katherine Scott Simulation Lab was formally dedicated during a Sept. 9 celebration at the Wellstar School of Nursing . The space provides nursing students with opportunities to develop clinical skills through hands-on simulation and practice. “Katherine’s generosity reminds us that philanthropy is more than financial giving. It is about expressing confidence in the next generation and creating opportunities for hard-working students to thrive and launch meaningful careers,” said Ivan Pulinkala, provost and executive vice president for academic affairs. The endowment will provide enduring scholarship support for nursing students, helping reduce financial barriers as they prepare for careers in one of the nation’s most vital health care professions. More than 1,000 students are pursuing nursing education at Kennesaw State. “Kennesaw State University has a very unique and compelling student body,” said Lance Burchett, vice president for advancement and CEO of the KSU Foundation. “Approximately 40% of our students are Pell Grant-eligible, and another 40% are seeking to become the first in their family to earn a college degree. While 79% of our students qualify for financial aid, only 6% receive donor-funded scholarships. Those students are 80% more likely to graduate in four years. They tell us it’s because of the gravity of having someone believe in them — the realization that ‘someone is investing in me, and I don’t want to let them down.’” For Scott, the decision to support nursing students is rooted in a lifelong connection to health care. At 8 years old, she became seriously ill with undulant fever and experienced firsthand the impact of being cared for. Her early interest in medicine continued throughout childhood, when she played doctor with orange crates and carried a small black doctor’s bag. Although her parents did not encourage her to attend college, Scott ultimately became an X-ray technician and found a career she loved. Her experiences shaped a lasting belief in the importance of following one’s passion and making a difference in others’ lives. “I am giving, and these students are receiving the opportunity to learn, grow, and prepare for their careers,” Scott said. “What they receive here will carry over to the patients they care for. That is what giving and receiving means to me, and I hope these students remember their purpose, approach nursing with passion, and keep their focus on healing and caring for others.” Scott’s commitment to Kennesaw State extends beyond nursing. In 2017, she established the Katherine Scott Rehearsal Hall Endowment with a $500,000 gift supporting the Dr. Bobbie Bailey School of Music . The rehearsal hall inside the Dr. Bobbie Bailey and Family Performance Center bears her name and supports music education and performance opportunities. “These labs provide students with an invaluable opportunity to practice scenarios and techniques, develop advanced skills in teamwork and time management, and learn to balance the care of multiple patients and competing priorities in a safe, supportive environment,” said Laurie Tis, interim dean of the Wellstar College of Health and Human Services . The naming celebration also brought Scott together with nursing students who shared their experiences and aspirations as future health care professionals. “Your generosity is not simply providing us with a space to learn. You are helping us become the health care professionals we aspire to be,” said Violet Miller, a student in the Wellstar School of Nursing. Through the Katherine A. Scott Nursing Scholarship Endowment and the newly named simulation lab, Scott’s generosity will have a lasting impact, helping future nurses pursue their education, develop their skills, and carry that investment forward to the patients and communities they serve.
