Rising prominently over Technology Way near the main entrance of the Marietta Campus, the structure reflects the University’s ongoing commitment to accelerate research innovation and impact, and advancing society through bold, collaborative discovery. By connecting experts from varied fields, the building expands research capacity and speeds the path from discovery to real‑world solutions, all within a shared campus space. “Today marks a major milestone for Kennesaw State and for the future of research and innovation at KSU,” President Kathy S. Schwaig said. “The Robin and Doug Shore Innovation Center was designed to advance collaborative interdisciplinary research and teaching in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics, fields that are central to the challenges and opportunities of our time.” Among those gathered for a first look inside the $60 million structure were the building’s namesake—longtime KSU benefactors Robin and Doug Shore—and dignitaries from the Board of Regents of the University System of Georgia, state representatives, and community leaders. Following opening remarks, guests were invited to tour the facility, which houses four new labs, a makerspace, two classrooms, and 22 faculty research teams. The building also houses the Robin and Doug Shore Entrepreneurship Center , a unit of the Michael J. Coles College of Business , and the Office of Research’s Center for Interactive Media . In addition to the guided tours, the event served as an opportunity to honor the Shores, who since 1999 have made more than 80 individual contributions benefiting many Kennesaw State initiatives. They are among the largest combined donors in KSU history, with their impact ranging from arts and athletics to veterans and everything in between. “It is especially fitting that this building bears the names Robin and Doug Shore,” Schwaig added. “For years, Robin and Doug have played a pivotal role in expanding entrepreneurship education and innovation at Kennesaw State, while steadfastly supporting our students and their ideas. Their legacy of service and philanthropy at Kennesaw State touches nearly every corner of our university.” Campus collaborations with community impact The building is a shared research and teaching hub that places interdisciplinary labs side by side, supported by shared research spaces, modern computing tools, and flexible classrooms. It’s a space where faculty work within the reach of colleagues outside their home fields, where students move between projects and perspectives, and where external partners are invited into the space as collaborators rather than observers. President Kathy S. Schwaig and Robin and Doug Shore “Tomorrow’s most pressing challenges transcend any single discipline, and meeting them requires an environment where scholars from diverse fields can work side by side,” said Karin Scarpinato, executive vice president of research. “The Robin and Doug Shore Innovation Center embodies that philosophy. By fostering collaboration and expanding our research capacity, it positions KSU to translate discovery into meaningful impact for the communities we serve.” Among the examples of the collaborative efforts within the building is a water quality monitoring project that brings together faculty from four colleges to help communities detect contamination earlier. Led by Ahyoung Lee, assistant professor of computer science, the project focuses on developing systems that monitor water conditions in real time and provide earlier warnings when safety is at risk. “This is not just a schoolhouse project,” Lee said. “This is work with the community outside KSU.” The project is supported by external funding and partnerships with local governments and nonprofit organizations, allowing research to be tested in real environments rather than simulated ones. It exemplifies the KSU’s research model where, from the very beginning, projects are developed with application in mind. “In this building, the innovation lab is more hands-on,” Lee said. “It’s not just paper research. This is real-world impact.” Another example of this impact can be found in the work of Da Hu, assistant professor of civil and environmental engineering. His research uses advanced tools like ground‑penetrating radar and artificial intelligence to locate and map underground infrastructure, including gas and water pipelines. He said the Robin and Doug Shore Innovation Center will strengthen this work by bringing researchers from different fields closer together, making collaboration easier. “I believe this will speed up the research,” Hu said. “We will have space, and we can collaborate with other people, especially with input from computer science. That will help us move the work forward.” By placing related research efforts together, the new facility creates opportunities for shared problem-solving across disciplines that might not otherwise interact. Researchers focused on different challenges benefit from proximity, shared infrastructure, and a constant exchange of ideas. “Research is becoming more and more interdisciplinary,” said Mehmet Aktas, associate professor of data science and analytics. “To make that research active, it’s important to put people together in the same place.” An advantage for students For students, the building reshapes learning. Inside, education is not limited to lectures or isolated lab assignments. Scholars at every stage—from incoming freshmen to graduate students—work alongside faculty on active projects, collaborate with peers from diverse disciplines, and observe how problems are defined and solved in real time. “Putting all of us in one place is really advantageous, not only for KSU, but for the public good and definitely for our students,” said Amelia Estwick, assistant professor of information technology and director of the Cyber Nexus Lab. Students gain experience that mirrors how work happens beyond the university, where collaboration, communication, and adaptability are essential. They leave with a clearer understanding of how their knowledge connects to real-world challenges. “Over time, the impact of the Robin and Doug Shore Innovation Center will be measured not by the number of labs it contains, but by the culture it creates,” Scarpinato said. “It is a place where collaboration is expected, curiosity is visible, and discovery is tied to application.” – Story by Raynard Churchwell and Travis Highfield Photos by Darnell Wilburn Related Stories Engineering student creates robotic hand designed to track patient health Kennesaw State researchers receive NSF grant to advance soft robotics education Engineering student uses NASA data to study distant star systems Kennesaw State names nursing simulation lab in honor of Katherine Scott A leader in innovative teaching and learning, Kennesaw State University offers undergraduate, graduate, and doctoral degrees to its more than 51,000 students. The award will support her work advancing STEM education through a novel agentic artificial intelligence (AI) framework. The five-year award will support Dehbozorgi’s work developing an AI-powered decision support system to assist STEM educators make informed, evidence-based instructional decisions while keeping human expertise at the center of this process. In turn, the system will learn from educators’ experiences and feedback, contributing to a growing body of shared knowledge for the broader STEM education community. “I was incredibly excited and also deeply grateful to hear this news,” Dehbozorgi said. “I had a moment of joyful pause and reflection, thinking about the years of hard work, persistence and growth that brought me to this point.” College of Computing and Software Engineering Dean Darryl Ahner commended Dehbozorgi and said her work reflects the college’s growing research impact. “Dr. Dehbozorgi’s NSF CAREER Award is an outstanding achievement and a testament to the innovative research taking place within CCSE,” Ahner said. “Her work brings together artificial intelligence, education and the human element in a way that has the potential to make a meaningful impact on educators and students. We are incredibly proud of her accomplishment.” Dehbozorgi’s project will focus on developing a conversational AI assistant that educators can interact with to identify research-supported teaching practices and receive personalized recommendations based on their instructional goals and challenges they face in the classroom. For example, an instructor could tell the system that students are struggling with a particular concept or that classroom engagement is low. The AI assistant would consider the instructor’s goals and specific teaching environment before suggesting strategies that could be adapted for that classroom. Dehbozorgi said one challenge facing STEM educators is the amount of information available about new pedagogical approaches. Her project aims to make that knowledge easier to access and more tailored to individual educators’ needs while allowing instructors to determine which approaches work best for their students “The goal is not to replace their judgment or let the AI decide for them,” Dehbozorgi said. “It’s mainly to give them better support to make informed decisions.” The research will also examine issues surrounding trust, accuracy, transparency, and privacy while ensuring educators remain at the center of the decision-making process. “The broader question is not just if we can use AI in education, but how we can use it responsibly and effectively, while keeping humans in the loop so that it can really make a meaningful impact in education,” she said. Kennesaw State students will also play an important role in the project. Undergraduate, master’s, and doctoral students will have opportunities to contribute to the design, development and evaluation of the framework. Students will work in areas including artificial intelligence, software development, data analysis, user experience design, and research. Summer internship opportunities are also planned. The research could also help prepare students for a workforce increasingly shaped by artificial intelligence. Dehbozorgi said educators need to understand how to use AI, evaluate its output, recognize its limitations, and apply the technology responsibly. “Teaching is deeply human, and we are dealing with learners with different backgrounds, learning styles and paces,” Dehbozorgi said. “Combining the strengths of both human expertise and AI and using them in a meaningful way is really promising in the educational field.” Dehbozorgi credited CCSE and KSU’s Office of Research for supporting her work. She said the university’s focus on student success and applied research makes it a strong environment for the project. By the end of the five-year project, Dehbozorgi hopes the research will produce a trustworthy framework that can extend beyond Kennesaw State. – Story by Raynard Churchwell Photos by Darnell Wilburn Related Stories Engineering student creates robotic hand designed to track patient health Kennesaw State researchers receive NSF grant to advance soft robotics education Kennesaw State researcher receives NIH Grant to study sleep apnea Ph.D. student advances research regarding AI integration with devices with limited computing power A leader in innovative teaching and learning, Kennesaw State University offers undergraduate, graduate, and doctoral degrees to its more than 51,000 students. However, many engineering students still have little exposure to the technology. Kennesaw State University researchers are working to change that with the support of a recent National Science Foundation (NSF) grant. The $399,953 award is the first NSF grant received by KSU’s Mobility for Everyone (MOVE) Center and brings together three researchers from the Southern Polytechnic College of Engineering and Engineering Technology . MOVE Center Director and Professor of Mechanical Engineering Ayse Tekes will serve as principal investigator, alongside co-principal investigators Razvan Voicu, assistant professor of robotics and mechatronics engineering , and Lei Shi, assistant professor of mechanical engineering. The researchers will develop low-cost physical prototypes, digital twins, and artificial intelligence-enhanced learning tools designed to help undergraduate students understand soft robotics and other complex systems that are often introduced at the graduate level. Soft robotic systems use flexible or compliant materials that can bend and adapt to their surroundings. That flexibility creates possibilities for systems that work closely with people, including assistive technologies, wearable devices and biomedical applications. “This proposal will give us all the resources to implement and demonstrate these topics from freshman to senior engineering courses,” Tekes said. “We will be able to expose an emerging field to undergraduate engineering students at every level.” Razvan Voicu The project will combine several pieces into a single learning system. Students will help build portable, 3D-printed soft robotic prototypes and create digital versions of those systems. They will also develop learning activities that faculty can use for classroom demonstrations, assignments, and group projects. AI tools will then provide students with feedback as they work through the material. The team will pair physical prototypes with digital twins, or virtual models designed to mimic how the systems behave in the real world. Tekes will lead development using MATLAB Simscape, while Shi will work with open-source modeling tools. “We developed open-source software which can mimic the real behavior of the soft robots in the physical world,” Shi said. “In addition to teaching our own students, we can also leave a very good legacy to them for the future development of their own systems.” Artificial intelligence will serve as another component of the project. Voicu will lead work on AI tools that can monitor how students solve problems, assess their understanding and provide real-time feedback. “You can basically just pause and speak to an AI bot and say, ‘I don’t quite understand what’s happening here. Can you explain it?’” Voicu said. “Then you have a 24-hour-a-day tutor that can help you understand the topics.” Lei Shi Students will also help build the tools. The grant will directly support three graduate students and three undergraduate students, while additional students from the researchers’ labs and the MOVE Center will contribute to the project. Student teams will help design and 3D print prototypes, build digital twins, develop software and work with sensing and data acquisition systems. “Students own the research,” Tekes said. “We are advisors on this research. We give them the tasks, weekly tasks, and they’re the makers of this research.” Interest is already growing. Tekes said 44 mechanical engineering students ranging from sophomores to seniors registered for a semester-long training program focused on developing soft robotics virtual lab simulations in MATLAB Simscape. Ultimately, the researchers hope to share the educational tools developed at KSU with other universities. “It would be a long-lasting impact,” Voicu said. “Being able to see these tools used in other universities in different locations, those are the type of things that would be really impactful.” This work is supported by the National Science Foundation’s Division of Undergraduate Education under Award under Award No. 2613366 Established in 2025, the MOVE Center is dedicated to advancing interdisciplinary research and innovation in rehabilitation and assistive technologies by bringing together faculty expertise across engineering, health sciences, computing, and related fields. Its mission is to support the development of impactful solutions that can improve mobility, health, and quality of life for individuals and communities. – Story by Raynard Churchwell Related Stories Engineering student creates robotic hand designed to track patient health Engineering student uses NASA data to study distant star systems Engineering student combines technical and marketing skills through hands-on experiences Kennesaw State researcher earns prestigious NSF CAREER Award A leader in innovative teaching and learning, Kennesaw State University offers undergraduate, graduate, and doctoral degrees to its more than 51,000 students. The team, composed of students in the College of Architecture and Construction Management , outperformed 36 universities from across the country, adding to a strong legacy in the student competition. Prior to this year’s competition, Kennesaw State’s NAHB Competition Team was most recently crowned national champion in 2017. Hosted by the National Association of Home Builders , the competition challenges students to operate as development firms pitching to investors. Teams were given lakefront lots on Lake Martin in Alabama and asked to select a site, design a home, and create a proposal that could stand up to professional scrutiny. In the end, KSU bested students representing Clemson University, Auburn University, and the University of Oklahoma, among others. “It’s absolutely huge,” said team advisor and Senior Lecturer Jeff Setzer . “We beat some very well-funded schools. Our students did all the work, and they deserve all the praise for pulling together a superb competition packet.” KSU construction management students visited the property multiple times and collaborated with an architecture student. They then developed a detailed construction and financial plan that included scheduling, estimating, risk management, logistics, and overall financial strategy. They also produced a fly-through video to strengthen the pitch and help judges visualize the finished product. Six students presented to judges acting as investors. Rather than reading from slides, they spoke directly to the panel, defending their assumptions, financial projections, and construction timeline. For team leader Drew Williams , the goal was clear from the beginning. “From the moment I assembled this team, first place was the expectation,” Williams said. “Not hope. Expectation.” That mindset shaped the team’s preparation. Members met consistently throughout the fall semester, increasing to multiple meetings per week as deadlines approached. Many balanced internships, jobs and full course loads while dedicating evenings and weekends to refining their proposal and presentation. “At that level, everyone’s technically strong,” Williams said. “What separated us was that we approached it like a real development opportunity, not a classroom assignment. We built it as if it was already moving forward.” Preparation began in August and intensified through the fall semester. After submitting the proposal in December, the team spent weeks rehearsing, fine-tuning delivery, and preparing for detailed questions from judges. “The fact that they won first place is a testament to the amount of work and effort they put into it,” Setzer said. At the awards ceremony, anticipation built as third and second place were announced without KSU’s name being called. “Then they said, ‘First place,’” Williams said. “And the next words were, ‘Kennesaw State University.’ After the long nights and sacrifices, it was real.” CACM Dean Hazem Rashed-Ali said the achievement reflects the college’s emphasis on experiential learning and professional preparation. “Our students demonstrated technical excellence, leadership, and resilience,” Rashed-Ali said. “We are incredibly proud of the way they represented Kennesaw State nationally.” Beyond the trophy, the experience provided lasting career benefits. Several team members have secured full-time positions with major home builders and will begin their careers this summer. The competition required them to synthesize everything learned in the classroom and apply it to a realistic, high-stakes scenario. “They proved that Kennesaw State can compete with anyone in the country,” Setzer said. “I believe this competition will be a pivotal part of their development and lead them to great careers after they graduate.” – Story by Raynard Churchwell Photo provided Related Stories Construction management gala celebrates 25 years of student support Kennesaw State architecture alumnus finds early career success Kennesaw State student explores the mental effects of workplace automation Kennesaw State architecture chair honored with ARCC Mary Kihl Distinguished Service Award A leader in innovative teaching and learning, Kennesaw State University offers undergraduate, graduate, and doctoral degrees to its more than 51,000 students. In reality, they’re AI agents, better known as chatbots, helping to prepare future teachers to teach math more effectively. The agents were developed by a Kennesaw State University researcher who is using artificial intelligence to help prepare future teachers for one of the most challenging aspects of the classroom: responding to how students think about math. Funded by a three-year, $300,000 National Science Foundation grant, Associate Professor of Instructional Technology Dabae Lee developed an AI-powered agent system that simulates student interactions. The aim is to give pre-service teachers practice in “responsive teaching,” which is the ability to elicit and interpret students’ thinking and to extend their mathematical ideas by questioning. “The major benefit is helping pre-service teachers develop their responsive teaching skills,” said Lee, who helps educate future teachers in the Clarice C. and Leland H. Bagwell College of Education . “In turn, that will help their future students develop mathematical reasoning and positive attitudes toward mathematics, which has been an area that students in the U.S. have always struggled with.” Lee explained that the idea of the simulating agents came from Swiss psychologist Jean Piaget’s socio-cognitive conflict theory, which says students build a higher level of understanding by explaining and negotiating their perspectives with others who have different perspectives. For example, students who have different wrong answers to the same question can reach the correct answer by discussing their reasonings with one another. Responsive teaching allows teachers to elicit students’ own ways of thinking, sometimes with misconceptions, and to have productive conversations with them to help them resolve their misconceptions without taking over their thinking. Student-teachers sometimes have limited opportunities to practice responding to students’ reasoning in real time, Lee noted. Traditional methods, such as peer role-playing, do not always reflect authentic classroom interactions. “What has been done is that either the instructor, a trained adult or peer student-teachers will play the role of children,” Lee said. “It’s not ideal because adults may not respond the same as children would.” The AI agents help to address that challenge by allowing student-teachers to interact with virtual students who respond uniquely to their explanations and questions in real-time. Lee designed the system with three virtual students — Gabriel, Noah and Jiwoo – each with different personalities and varying mathematical skills. “They are all different in terms of their personalities and their ways of thinking,” Lee said. “Gabrielle is a playful student who is strong in math, while Noah shares the same playful personality but struggles with the subject. Jiwoo is articulate but has specific misconceptions about certain math concepts.” The system recently completed its second implementation in the fall with collaborators in the teacher education program at the University of Missouri and is currently being refined for another round of testing planned for next fall. Lee said the feedback from student-teachers who have used the system has been favorable as many say the interactions feel more authentic than traditional practice exercises. “The students really appreciated the ability of practicing responsive teaching with the virtual students,” Lee said. Lee’s work has been published in the Computers & Education journal, Journal of Computer Assisted Learning, and Journal of Mathematics Teacher Education . The project, which initially used IBM Watsonx technology also captured the attention of IBM and was featured on IBM’s Smart Talks podcast, including a featured interview with renowned author and journalist Malcolm Gladwell. Lee said the goal is to eventually share the technology more widely with teacher education programs. “Our plan after the third round of testing is to make the agents and instructional modules accessible to other educators,” Lee said. – Story by Christin Senior Photos by Matt Yung Related Stories Kennesaw State professor earns national award for contribution to education KSU student helps bring a fresh approach to music education using colors Bagwell College of Education hosts 2026 Georgia Elementary Science Olympiad 'Triple Owl' turns passion for teaching into doctoral success A leader in innovative teaching and learning, Kennesaw State University offers undergraduate, graduate, and doctoral degrees to its more than 51,000 students. That conversation prompted Uchendu, an Honors student in the Keeping Sights Upward Journey Honors College , to apply for multiple scholarships and by the time she boarded a plane to Tokyo earlier this summer, scholarships had covered nearly all her costs. Uchendu is one of a record number of KSU students awarded the Benjamin A. Gilman International Scholarship this year. The Gilman Scholarship is a prestigious award funded by the US State Department that provides recipients up to $5,000 to support study or internships abroad; only about 20%-25% of applicants are selected for the award. During the March 2026 application cycle, 56 KSU students applied, and 10 received the award. Across the full academic year, 73 KSU students applied, and 11 students earned scholarships to study abroad. The milestone reflects a growing partnership between KSU's Office of Prestigious Undergraduate Awards (OPUA) and Education Abroad , which expanded workshops and one-on-one mentoring to help students prepare competitive applications. “We made some really important steps forward," said Jamie Elliott, associate dean for academic affairs in the KSU Journey Honors College. “The first was to be very intentional about working with our partners in Education Abroad to provide workshops, both informational workshops and mentoring workshops for students.” Aaliyah Uchendu Those efforts helped students see the Gilman Scholarship as an attainable opportunity while strengthening their applications, Elliott said. For Uchendu, the experience became much more than a trip abroad. Visiting a Japanese university with her education abroad cohort gave her a behind-the-scenes look at emerging technologies. She was especially fascinated by a project that used nerve sensors to transmit hand movements from one person to another and by researchers working on early self-driving car technology. “I got to see the behind-the-scenes look at the development process behind technologies people often take for granted,” she said. “It's nice to have that perspective because we just see the final stages and we don't really know how they produced it.” Honors political science student Sidney Agee, another Gilman Scholar, also had a transformative experience studying abroad in Peru. Montavian Walker Though she once envisioned a career in law, Agee said her experience in Peru shifted her perspective. Visiting communities in the Andes and seeing the limited access to resources and education ignited a desire to make education more accessible. "I thought I wanted to go to law school and work in Congress," she said. "But it wasn't until I studied abroad that I realized a passion I didn't even know I had. I realized that if I'm going to do something political, then I want to make education accessible." During her two weeks in Peru, Agee also visited Machu Picchu, one of the New Seven Wonders of the World; the Sacred Valley of the Incas, and Universidad Nacional Mayor de San Marcos in Lima, recognized as the oldest university in the Americas. Now a Global Ambassador with the Office of Global Education, Agee is preparing a Fulbright Scholarship application with support from OPUA. Honors nursing student Montavian Walker, who studied in the Dominican Republic, said the scholarship allowed him to experience healthcare beyond the United States. "I wanted to study abroad because I knew it would expose me to a completely different healthcare system and culture," Walker said. "The Gilman Scholarship took away a major financial barrier and allowed me to focus on learning instead of worrying about how I was going to afford this experience." Over the summer, they both helped track legislation and conduct policy research for U.S. congressional offices on Capitol Hill. The two Kennesaw State University students, who received the university’s D.C. Owls Scholarship , spent their summer interning in Washington, and both credit a semester at the Georgia State Capitol with helping them succeed. Barronton, a junior political science major in the Norman J. Radow College of Humanities and Social Sciences , spent last spring in the Georgia Legislative Internship Program (GLIP) assisting with the Senate Judiciary and Transportation committees. Barronton said the experience gave her a taste of constituent casework and the legislative process she didn’t fully appreciate until she used it to land her next opportunity: a congressional internship in Washington. “I honestly know I would not be where I am today without GLIP,” Barronton said. “I gained hands-on experience working with two very busy committees, and I think that constituent services experience helped set me apart when I was applying for opportunities in D.C.” She applied for internships in Washington without much expectation of hearing back. In late April, she received an interview request, and by the first week of May she had been formally accepted to serve an office in the U.S. House of Representatives. Chilukuri, a sophomore finance major in the Michael J. Coles College of Business , began his government internship experience as a freshman at the Georgia State Capitol, where he tracked legislation and conducted research. He credits the pace of his statehouse experience with making the transition to the nation’s capital easier. No two days on Capitol Hill looked alike for either student. Barronton attended meetings with advocacy groups and constituents who flew in from Georgia, drafted memos, and supported staff whenever needed. Meetings, she said, became her favorite part of the internship. “Every time I sat in on a meeting, I walked away learning about an issue I had no prior knowledge of,” Barronton said. “Something I really enjoyed is being exposed to a lot of different policy areas, specifically international affairs and humanitarian crises outside of the committees my member serves on.” Saideep Chilukuri Chilukuri split his time between common intern duties of constituent correspondence and giving tours, as well as tracking legislation related to his areas of interest: artificial intelligence (AI), pharmaceuticals, and financial services. He spent much of the summer working on what he called his most meaningful project: helping the office’s legislative team research an AI regulation bill. Outside the office, both students made the most of a summer in Washington that coincided with the nation’s 250 th anniversary. Chilukuri leaned into the networking culture of the Hill, making a habit of at least one coffee chat a day with staffers, lobbyists, and lawyers. Barronton took advantage of similar opportunities, adding that she and her friends made their way through the city’s museums and monuments and discovered a new coffee shop nearly every week. “One of the biggest lessons I learned was that policy work is about people,” Chilukuri said. “Whether I was meeting staffers, lobbyists, or attorneys, every conversation taught me something new and showed me how important relationships are in this field.” Now home and preparing for the fall semester, both are weighing what’s next: Barronton considering whether to return to Capitol Hill or apply what she’s learned elsewhere, and Chilukuri is eyeing law school. The students’ advice to peers considering a Washington internship is simple: do it. “Do it scared,” Barronton said. “You don’t have to have everything figured out. And don’t compare yourself to other people; you’re just as qualified as anyone else in the room.” “These internships taught me that growth comes from putting yourself in unfamiliar situations,” Chilukuri said. “Every day, I spoke with people whose careers I hope to emulate someday, and it gave me the confidence to realize that those opportunities are within reach if you’re willing to learn and work hard.” The D.C. Owls Scholarship helps fund living expenses for Kennesaw State students who secure internships with the federal government in Washington. The division is tasked with improving strategic and institutional planning and execution, creating a culture of leadership, and promoting a welcoming campus climate, all aligning with our ongoing efforts for continuous growth and improvement. Considering these goals, Dr. Sonia Toson has been appointed as the Vice President to lead this new division and initiative. Her leadership will play a pivotal role in supporting our pursuit of excellence in all that we do. Three Pillars of Growth to Strategize Dr. Toson will oversee three interconnected areas in this new division at KSU: Organizational Effectiveness This encompasses strategic planning, continuous improvement, and change management functions, led by Julie Page, Executive Director of Strategic Initiatives. Inclusive Excellence This unit will ensure a welcoming community through education, assessments, and compliance support. Student-facing initiatives will transition to the Office of the Provost to contribute to student success. At Orientation, you will learn about how to be a student at KSU. This includes learning about available campus resources, meeting current student leaders, and meeting with an academic advisor to map out your academic journey. When is New Student Orientation? See what dates are offered for New Student Orientation by visiting our Orientation Dates webpage. New Student Orientation Dates When will I register for classes as a new student? New freshmen will register for classes at New Student Orientation. All other student types, including new transfer students, can see their registration information on the Registration tab of Owl Express (select "Prepare for Registration"). Is New Student Orientation mandatory? New Student Orientation is mandatory for all new freshman undergraduate students. This includes: New Freshman Transfer Freshman (students admitted with less than 30 transferrable credit hours) If you have any questions about your student type, please email ksuadmit@kennesaw.edu When can I register for an orientation session? Students are able to register for orientation 24-48 hours after they are officially accepted to the university. If you have questions about your admission status, please contact ksuadmit@kennesaw.edu How much does it cost to attend New Student Orientation? For both virtual and in-person orientation sessions, the student fee is $80.00. NOTE: Student orientation fees are non-refundable and non-transferable. The Supporter Orientation fee is $20.00 for in-person sessions and free for virtual sessions. If I previously attended orientation but have changed my admissions term, do I have to sign up for orientation again? Students who signed up and attended an orientation within two semesters (e.g. changed term to Spring 2027 but attended orientation for Summer 2026) of their new admissions term may be exempt from having to re-attend a New Student Orientation session. To apply for an exemption, please email ksuorientation@kennesaw.edu . What does the student orientation fee cover? The student orientation fee covers a meal at one of our dining halls, your Mobile Talon Card, giveaways and important materials, staffing and space for us to host the Orientation session both virtually and in-person. How do I know my session is confirmed? Student orientation sessions are officially confirmed when payment is made, and you receive an official confirmation email sent to your KSU email address. If you have questions about if you are confirmed for your session, please email KSUorientation@kennesaw.edu What is your refund policy? The Orientation fee for students, parents, and guests is non-refundable and non-transferable. I can’t register for a session. What do I do? If you are having trouble seeing session dates or registering for a session, please contact us at ksuorientation@kennesaw.edu . Include the issue you’re experiencing, your first and last name, and your KSU ID number when contacting us for a faster resolution time. What should I do before my New Student Orientation session? You will receive more information sent to your KSU email about everything you need to do before attending orientation. You can also check your official orientation task list. See Official Task List Can I meet my academic advisor before orientation? Yes, we highly recommend that you meet with your academic advisor before your orientation experience to feel comfortable with what courses to take. For general advising questions please email askadvising@kennesaw.edu FIND YOUR ACADEMIC ADVISOR In-Person Orientation Where do we park for New Student Orientation? You will receive an email outlining where to park for your session. What should I bring to my New Student Orientation session? We highly recommend you bring a government-issued ID (like a driver’s license or passport), mobile phone, comfortable walking shoes, and rain gear. Where do I go for check-in when I arrive on campus? We will have staff and signs directing you to check-in for your session. Is there a lot of walking during New Student Orientation? Yes, you will walk across campus, so wear comfortable shoes. Please indicate any mobility concerns and accommodation requests when you sign up for your orientation session. If you need a specific accommodation, please email sds@kennsaw.edu Should I arrive to campus early for my New Student Orientation session? We highly recommend you arrive at least 5-10 minutes before your check-in time, so you are able to attend the required sections of your orientation. I am late for my session. What do I do? Late check-in will be held at the check-in location until 11 a.m. If you are going to be later than 11 a.m., please go back to the sign-up system and choose a new date. If you have questions about this, please email ksuorientation@kennesaw.edu How long is the in-person Orientation session? Students and supporters can expect to participate in required programming from 8:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. Optional programming will be held until 4 p.m. I require special accommodations for my in-person Orientation session. What should I do? Individuals who seek additional assistance should reach out to Student Disability Services at sds@kennesaw.edu prior to their orientation date, as well as fill out the appropriate sections of their orientation sign-up portal. Our office will be in contact with you before your orientation session. Virtual Orientation How do I access my virtual orientation session? You will receive an email to your KSU student email with the link to your orientation session at least 24 hours before the date of your Orientation session. If you do not see an email from us, please reach out to ksuorientation@kennesaw.edu What is a “virtual” New Student Orientation? Students can choose to attend a virtual session to meet the orientation attendance requirement. Virtual sessions are facilitated live on Zoom. These sessions offer similar information for new students which includes meeting with your academic advisor, learning about campus services such as housing, dining, and parking, and meeting with your Orientation Leader. How long is the virtual New Student Orientation session? The live portion of the Virtual New Student Orientation experience is roughly 2 hours. This is to allow you to get as much information as possible to prepare you to join the KSU community. Following the live portion, you will register for classes and review post-orientation modules on your own. Your academic advisors will be available starting 1 hour after the live portion of your session ends. How do I access my virtual New Student Orientation session? You will receive an email with the link to your orientation session at least 24 hours before the date of your Orientation session. I require special accommodations for my in-person Orientation session. What should I do? Individuals who seek additional assistance should reach out to Student Disability Services at sds@kennesaw.edu prior to their virtual orientation date, as well as fill out the appropriate sections of their orientation sign-up portal. Our office will be in contact with you before your virtual orientation session. Supporter Orientation Are parents or guests required to attend Supporter Orientation? No, supporters are not required to attend orientation with their students. Are parents or guests with their students during In-Person Supporter Orientation? While supporters are with their students for most of the day, students will break out with Orientation Leaders to meet with their Academic Advising teams and register for classes. Students will meet back up with their supporters/guests during lunch or afternoon programming. A detailed schedule will be sent within 48 hours of the session. What is the cost to attend Supporter Orientation? $20.00 (Note: Orientation fees are non-refundable). The Supporter fee covers the program fees, materials, and lunch in the dining hall with your student. How many guests can attend orientation? Due to space limitations, students are only able to sign up one guest for orientation. Additional guests may be added at check-in on the day of your session, if space allows. We recommend getting to the session when check-in begins (8:30 a.m.) to make sure you have the best opportunity to add a guest. The $20.00 Supporter Orientation fee must be submitted for each supporter/guest to attend orientation programming. What if my student checks in to orientation before I arrive? If your student has already checked in for orientation, please contact them to have them meet you at the check-in station. All supporters must check with their students for orientation programming. I am signed up for virtual supporter orientation, what do I do? Supporters will receive a separate Zoom link for their orientation session. Parents or supporters should not use the zoom link sent to their students to access the virtual session. What is the policy for bringing children to Supporter Orientation? Children aged 6 years and younger can attend supporter orientation free of charge. Supporters will have to pay an additional $20.00 for any child above 6 years of age. Dual Enrollment Orientation Am I required to attend Dual Enrollment Orientation? Yes, all fully accepted Dual Enrollment students must attend orientation. Accepted Dual Enrollment Student Info I’m trying to sign up for Dual Enrollment Orientation, but it is showing an incorrect term. What do I do? If you have been accepted as a freshman student in addition to Dual Enrollment, your record will need to be updated to allow you to sign up for Dual Enrollment Orientation. Please reach out to ksuorientation@kennesaw.edu with any questions. I have already attended Dual Enrollment Orientation; do I need to also attend Freshman Orientation? Yes, all new Freshman admits are required to attend Freshman Orientation. Is there anything I need to do before my orientation session? Yes, please use the Tasklist feature in your reservation to prepare for your session. Please make sure to complete all required tasks before your orientation session. View Your Registration What is the difference between virtual and in-person orientation? While both options provide the same content, in-person orientation takes place on campus while virtual orientation takes place via Zoom. In-person orientation allows students to come to campus to register for classes, eat at the dining hall and take a campus tour to get a full experience of campus life. What time does orientation start? For in-person orientation, check in begins at 8:30 a.m. Required programming is from 9:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. with optional programming until 4 p.m. Virtual orientation is from 3 p.m. to 5 p.m. International Student Orientation Who is required to attend International Student Orientation? All undergraduate and graduate International Students are required to attend International Student Orientation. What is International Student Orientation? At International Orientation you will learn about the programs, resources, and campus services that will guide you in your transition as a new Owl. You will: Meet with the International Student and Scholar Services Team to learn about important visa information. Connect with university faculty, staff, and other KSU students, including current international students. Take a campus tour, visit the campus bookstore, learn about your Mobile Talon Card, and more! How much is International Student Orientation? $80.00. This covers the program fees, materials you will receive, and lunch in the dining hall. What should I bring to International Orientation? A government issued ID (driver’s license, passport, or Talon Card) is required to check into International Student Orientation. We also recommend you bring comfortable walking shoes and rain gear. When do I register for classes as an International Student? We recommend students register for classes before their orientation session. For assistance with course registration please contact your Academic Advisor. Find My Academic Advisor Can I bring a supporter to International Student Orientation? No, due to capacity limitations, students are not able to bring guests with them to International Student Orientation. Still have Questions? All new first-year undergraduate students are required to attend a New Student Orientation session. During your session, you will: Connect with university faculty, staff, and other KSU students Attend a group academic advising session with other students who share your major Register for your first semester of classes Receive more information about student services, including your Mobile Talon Card and parking options Explore KSU departments and organizations New Student Orientation Sign-Up Session Modality Option We offer both virtual and in-person orientation options for freshman students. Both options will provide students the opportunity to register for their classes, meet with academic advisors, meet new students, and receive information for a successful transition to campus. Session dates are offered on a first-come, first-served basis. Your session is not confirmed until the orientation fee has been paid during the sign-up process. Student Orientation Schedule Detailed schedules will be provided to students via email within 48 hours of their New Student Orientation session. Required programming for in-person sessions will be held from 9:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m., and optional programming will be held from 12:30 p.m. to 4:00 p.m. Required programming for virtual sessions will be held from 10 a.m. to 12 p.m, and optional programming will be held from 1 p.m. to 4 p.m. orientation dates Supporter Orientation Students can sign up one guest to attend Supporter Orientation when they sign up for their New Student Orientation session. Supporter Orientation sessions are held in tandem with student sessions. Guest attendance is encouraged but not required. NOTE: Due to space capacity limitations, students are only allowed to sign up one guest during the sign-up process. Additional guests may be added at check-in on the day of the event if space allows. Please contact us for questions about this policy. Supporter Task List Students can also sign up their supporters for an orientation task list which features a variety of tasks for supporters to complete before and after orientation to ensure their student has everything they need to start their journey at KSU! Once a student signs up their supporter, the supporter will receive an email with instructions on how to sign into the task list. Supporters can complete the following items to prepare for their Orientation session: Join the Owl Family Hub! The Owl Family Hub is your number one source of information from Parent and Family Programs! In the hub, parents and family members will have access to important campus news and deadlines, insight to your student’s progress, financial details, and receive personalized newsletters on your preferred schedule. Create an account for free today! Join the Owl Family Hub Complete the Support FLIGHT Modules. Supporter FLIGHT Modules is Parent and Family Programs' first year virtual learning program designed specifically for parents and supporters of our students. Each pathway provides the tools, resources, and insights you need to support your students as they navigate college life, from launching their first year to preparing for graduation. Access the Supporter Flight Modules Prepare for Orientation. Check out our website for more information on how to prepare for your student's upcoming orientation session and frequently asked questions about orientation. Learn more on our orientation webpage Pre-Orientation Checklist Please complete the following items prior to your New Student Orientation session: Check your personal and KSU email daily. KSU highly suggests that you schedule a Pre-Orientation Advising session. We recommend meeting with your academic advisor within two weeks of your scheduled New Student Orientation date. For more information visit academic advising . No appointments are available on your orientation day. Holds can be viewed by logging into Owl Express, selecting "Registration," and then selecting "Prepare for Registration." If you require accommodations, ASL interpreting, or real-time captioning to participate in Orientation, please contact Student Disability Services at sds@kennesaw.edu at least five business days before your Orientation date. Submit your photo and a photo of your government photo ID for your Mobile Talon Card . The Talon One administration fee is included in the New Student Orientation fee. Attend the New Student Orientation session on your scheduled date. An email reminder will be sent to you within 72 hours of your scheduled session. We are excited for you to join Owl Nation! If you have any questions, please email us at ksuorientation@kennesaw.edu or call us at 470-KSU-INFO (470-578-4636). Campus Maps Kennesaw State University includes two main campuses in Cobb County about 20-30 minutes north of Atlanta, GA. No matter where you choose to visit us, we hope you’ll love Kennesaw State University as much as we do. Owl Family Hub Your number one source of information from Parent and Family Programs is our online parent and family portal, the KSU Parent and Family Experience! You'll receive newsletters filled with great information that is tailored to your student's experience. Join the portal today! Owl Family Hub Frequently Asked Questions How does academic advising work? Academic advisors at Kennesaw State University play a transformative role in the student experience through personalized and holistic strategies that promote each student's success. Through a collaborative relationship, we empower all students to take ownership of their education. We provide students with information about program requirements, coursework, campus resources, university policies and procedures, and career options. Embracing cross-campus collaboration, we work alongside faculty to help students become civically engaged, lifelong learners. We are fully committed to fostering a campus environment that respects and values the uniqueness and diversity of the students we serve. When are breaks and other important dates? The dates of the Academic Calendar are maintained by the Office of the Registrar and published each semester. How are students notified in case of an emergency? Kennesaw State University has developed a robust, multi-layered approach to emergency notification. This system is designed to reach the Kennesaw State University students, faculty, and staff in a variety of ways with immediate emergency messaging. Kennesaw State University utilizes outdoor warning sirens, email notifications, text notifications, voice phone call notifications, a desktop override system, the Kennesaw State University webpage, and social media pages to provide emergency messages to our students, faculty, staff, visitors, and other community stakeholders. The goal of this system is to provide multiple points of communication to ensure that the entire Kennesaw State University community is provided with timely and pertinent emergency messaging. What medical services are available on campus? Our KSU Student Health primary care clinics offer a variety of services: Illness diagnosis and care for colds, flu, sore throat, infections and more. Chronic disease management including asthma, diabetes, and hypertension. Routine exams, such as physicals, women’s and men's health, STD testing and treatment. Immunizations: routine and travel immunizations. Learn more about KSU's immunization requirements. The psychiatry clinical team is located in Kennesaw Hall (Kennesaw Campus) and the Joe Mack Wilson Student Center (Marietta Campus). To make an appointment, please visit the Counseling and Psychological Services website . Does my student need a permit to park at KSU? Yes, all students, faculty and staff must have a permit to park in any KSU parking area, including off-site shuttle lots. KSU allows one vehicle per permit to be on campus at a time. If two vehicles are on campus at the same time, both vehicles will be considered in violation, and both will receive a citation. Visitors and anyone who does not have a parking permit must utilize a Visitor parking area and pay at the pay-per-plate station in that lot. President's Award of Distinction The President’s Award of Distinction is the highest accolade conferred upon an undergraduate student by Kennesaw State University. This distinguished honor celebrates the extraordinary accomplishments of one exceptional graduating Owl each semester. Bestowed during Fall and Spring Commencement ceremonies, the award illuminates those who have soared above and beyond in their academic or research pursuits, leadership roles, and/or community service. This award is the pinnacle of recognition at the university, honoring an individual who exemplifies Kennesaw State’s core values of respect, integrity, collaboration, inclusivity, and accountability, and who serves as an inspiration to their peers, their community, and the entirety of Owl Nation. Overview Criteria & Requirements Honorees Overview Eligibility: Applicants must be graduating in six or fewer years (started at KSU in Fall 2020 or later) and be eligible, per the Office of the Registrar, to participate in the Fall 2026 commencement ceremony. Recognition: The award is formally presented as a special presentation at one designated commencement ceremony. The honoree is invited to sit as part of the platform party, receives their degree first in the undergraduate procession, is featured in online, print, and campus news materials, and enjoys VIP ceremony accommodations, including reserved seating for family and guests, during the ceremony. Submission Instructions: This is a self-nomination. Students applicants should organize all application components (essay, letters, and resume) into a single PDF document and submit via the official submission form. The PDF file name should include the applicant's last name. Deadline: Submissions must be received no later than 7:59 p.m. on Mon. Oct. 5, 2026 . Late or incomplete submissions will not be considered. Criteria & Requirements Award Evaluation Criteria Examples of an applicant’s achievements, can include, but are not limited to: Academic GPA (no minimum requirement) Scholarly research Entrepreneurial or intrapreneurial activities Excellence in the extracurricular activities Leadership Service and contributions to campus or community Activities that exemplify KSU Values: respect, integrity, collaboration, inclusivity, and accountability Other unique details about the student's journey at KSU Application Requirements & Deadline This is a self-nomination . Student applicants should complete the following: Personal statement or essay (1,500 words max): should include specific examples that illustrate how the applicant fulfills the award evaluation criteria and why the applicant is an outstanding candidate for the award. Minimum of three letters of recommendation: must include one letter each from (1) a member of the KSU faculty or staff, (2) a non-family contact, and (3) a peer or fellow KSU student. Note: letters should specifically address how an applicant meets the requirements for the award. Applicants are encouraged to provide a summary of the award to the recommendation letter writer. KSU college deans and members of the KSU Cabinet cannot serve as recommendation writers. Current professional resume: should not exceed 2 pages. Submission Instructions: Students applicants should organize all application components (essay, letters, and resume) into a single PDF document and submit via the official submission form. The PDF file name should include the applicant's last name. Deadline: Submissions must be received no later than 7:59 p.m. on Mon. Oct. 5, 2026 . Late or incomplete submissions will not be considered. Finalists: All applicants will be notified directly of the status of their application. Any applicant who is named a finalist is required to complete a background check. For additional questions or concerns, please contact presidentaward@kennesaw.edu . The Fall 2026 application cycle is closed. Finalists will be notified in November. Schwaig Office of the President Home About President Schwaig President's Cabinet Community Advisory Board Presidential Participation Request Contact Us President Kathy S. Schwaig Kathy "Kat" Schwaig is the sixth president of Kennesaw State University, one of Georgia's largest public universities and an emerging top public research institution in the United States, serving more than 50,000 students. Schwaig initially served as interim president in 2021 before being named president in 2022. Under her leadership, KSU has launched "Taking Flight," a new strategic plan aimed at achieving national prominence and institutional excellence. During Schwaig’s tenure, KSU has embarked on a comprehensive student success initiative, established more than 50 new undergraduate and graduate degrees and minors, professional programs, and credentials for in-demand fields, launched FLIGHT — a class-year, student success engagement program for first-year students focused on community, progress, and retention, realized an 81% increase in external research awards, and nearly tripled research expenditures. The university has also made significant investments in academic, research, and technology infrastructure and facilities, including more than 20 capital projects that have enhanced the learning, living, and working environments on both campuses. Schwaig also oversaw KSU’s move to Conference USA and relaunched HatchBridge, a community-focused business incubator. Schwaig’s presidency began during the private phase of The Campaign for KSU, the university’s first-ever comprehensive campaign. During her tenure, KSU secured the largest gift in the university’s history and successfully increased average annual fundraising by more than 300%. When the campaign went public in 2023, KSU boldly raised the campaign’s goals from $125 million to $200 million, including a $30 million campaign goal for KSU Athletics, a first for the university. Schwaig has served in several senior administration roles in her more than two decades of service to Kennesaw State. She served as provost and senior vice president for academic affairs from 2019 to 2021. As provost, she led the development of the R2 Roadmap to enhance undergraduate and graduate education and research and facilitated KSU’s transition to a formal research (R2) institution. Schwaig also led an extensive faculty hiring initiative, launched the Double Owl program, expanded the KSU Journey Honors College, and established the Provost Leadership Fellows and the Women’s Leadership Academy. Prior to serving as provost, Schwaig was the dean of the Michael J. Coles College of Business, where she was named the Dinos Eminent Scholar Chair of Entrepreneurial Management. Schwaig oversaw the creation of the College’s first doctoral program, increased educational opportunities for entrepreneurs, and achieved the top ranking in Georgia for the College’s MBA programs. Schwaig is a professor of information systems with research focusing on the strategic and ethical implications of computer technology. She is published in key academic journals in her field, including the Journal of Management Information Systems and Information Systems Research. Schwaig received the Oscar Burnett Award for Distinguished Achievement in Business from the Morris Brown College Foundation, the Cobb Executive Women’s Glass Ceiling Award, and Atlanta Magazine’s Women Making a Mark Award. A dedicated community partner and volunteer, she is the immediate past chair of Select Cobb and serves on the Executive Committee for the Board of Directors of the Cobb Chamber of Commerce and the Board of Directors for the Metro Atlanta Chamber of Commerce. She previously served on boards for the Cobb Community Foundation, Mount Paran Christian School, Children’s Healthcare of Atlanta - Cobb County, Junior Achievement of Georgia, Engage Scholarship Consortium, and the Alliance for Children Everywhere. A native of central Texas, Schwaig holds a BBA in Accounting and an MBA in Information Systems from Baylor University, a Master of Liberal Arts from Johns Hopkins University, a Master of Biblical and Theological Studies from Dallas Theological Seminary, and a Ph.D. in Information Systems from the University of South Carolina. Schwaig is the proud mom of her high school daughter, Emma Grace. This Notice describes the type of information KSU collects from visitors to this Site, what we do with that information, and how visitors can update and control the use of information collected by this Site. Type of Information Collected and Why Links to Other Websites Security and Accuracy of Confidential Information Sharing of Information European Union General Data Protection Regulation (EU GDPR) Privacy Notice Georgia Open Records Act Data Retention Type of Information Collected and Why Kennesaw State University (KSU) is committed to ensuring the privacy of your information. KSU collects two kinds of information on this site: Information that is voluntarily supplied by visiting the site and enrolling in programs and Information that is automatically collected as you navigate the site. Information voluntarily supplied by visitors seeking to access various features and information includes, among other things, name, address, and phone number. Any personal information that you choose to provide through the Site will be protected in accordance with the provisions of this Notice. If you refuse to provide personal data that is required by KSU in connection with one of KSU’s lawful bases to collect such personal data, such refusal may make it impossible for KSU to provide education, employment, or other requested services. Information automatically collected includes the user’s IP address, date and time of the website access along with the web pages(s) visited. In addition, KSU may also collect any information that it receives from your web browser, including browser type and version, and operating system. This information helps us understand aggregate uses of our site, track usage trends and improve our services. Additionally, university web sites use cookies to collect certain information. Cookies are small pieces of data that are sent by our Website to your Web browser. They are stored on your computer and are used to improve your web experience and improve the availability of web content. We may also use cookies to pre-fill forms so that you do not need to re-enter data. Accepting a cookie does not give us access to your computer or any personal information about you. Links to Other Websites Links within the university website may direct you to other websites not affiliated with KSU. KSU is not responsible for the privacy practices, policies, actions, web content, services, or products of non-KSU sites to which we link. These links are not intended to, nor do they constitute, an endorsement by KSU of the linked materials. We encourage you to read the privacy statements of other sites for assurance that their practices safeguard your privacy. Security and Accuracy of Confidential Information KSU does its best to reasonably ensure that the personal information obtained from you is accurate. Visitors may review the information saved or submitted via the Site at any time up to the point when it is purged. If there is an error in your personal information, we will correct the information upon your request, which may be submitted through Service Now . We have put in place reasonable physical, technical, and administrative safeguards designed to prevent unauthorized access to the online information we collect and use. While we strive to protect visitor’s personal information by encryption and other means, we cannot guarantee or warrant the security of the information you transmit to us, and if you choose to use the Site, you do so at your own risk. If you post any data within a public forum on any KSU website, that data is now public. Sharing of Information KSU is committed to maintaining the privacy of your personal information. Any information submitted via the website will only be used for the purposes stated on the submission page. KSU does not actively share personal information gathered from the Site, except: as required by law (including but not limited to the Georgia Open Records Act); as necessary to protect KSU interests; as necessary to further research efforts pursuant to approvals from the appropriate data stewards and the Institutional Review Board; and/or with contracted service providers acting on behalf of the university who have agreed to protect the confidentiality of the data. KSU also complies with the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (“FERPA”), which generally prohibits (with some exceptions) the release of education records without student permission. Please visit KSU’s FERPA website for more information. European Union General Data Protection Regulation (EU GDPR) Privacy Notice Lawful Basis for Collecting and Processing of Personal Data Kennesaw State University is an institution of higher education involved in education, research, and community engagement. For KSU to educate its students both in class and on-line, engage in world-class research, and provide community services, it is essential, necessary, and KSU has lawful bases to collect, process, use, and maintain data of its students, employees, applicants, research subjects, and others involved in its educational, research, and community programs. The lawful bases include, without limitation, admission, registration, delivery of classroom, on-line, and study abroad education, grades, communications, employment, applied research, development, program analysis for improvements, and records retention. Examples of data that KSU may need to collect in connection with the lawful bases are: name, email address, IP address, physical address or other location identifier, photos, as well as some sensitive personal data obtained with prior consent. For more information regarding the EU GDPR, please review Kennesaw State’s EU General Data Protection Regulation Compliance Policy . All personal data and sensitive personal data collected or processed by KSU under the scope of the KSU EU General Data Protection Regulation Compliance Policy must comply with the security controls and systems and process requirements and standards of KSU policies. The majority of KSU’s collection and processing of personal data will fall under the following categories: Processing is necessary for the purposes of the legitimate interests pursued by KSU or third parties in providing education, employment, research and development, and community programs. Processing is necessary for the performance of a contract to which the data subject is party or in order to take steps at the request of the data subject prior to entering into a contract. This lawful basis pertains primarily but not exclusively to research contracts. Processing is necessary for compliance with a legal obligation to which KSU is subject. The data subject has given consent to the processing of his or her personal data for one or more specific purposes. This lawful basis pertains primarily, but not exclusively, to the protection of research subjects. There will be some instances where the collection and processing of personal data will be pursuant to other lawful bases. Where KSU Obtains Personal Data and Special Categories of Sensitive Personal Data KSU receives personal data and special categories of sensitive personal data from multiple sources. Most often, this data comes directly from the data subject or under the direction of the data subject who has provided it to a third party (for example, application for admission to KSU through use of the Common App). Individual Rights of the Data Subject under the EU GDPR Individual data subjects covered by KSU’s EU General Data Protection Regulation Compliance Policy will be afforded the following rights: information about the controller collecting the data the data protection officer contact information the purposes and legal basis/legitimate interests of the data collection/processing recipients of the personal data if KSU intends to transfer personal data to another country or international organization the period the personal data will be stored the existence of the right to access, rectify incorrect data or erase personal data, restrict or object to processing, and the right to data portability the existence of the right to withdraw consent at any time the right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority (established in the EU) why the personal data are required, and possible consequences of the failure to provide the data the existence of automated decision-making, including profiling if the collected data are going to be further processed for a purpose other than that for which it was collected Note: Exercising of these rights is a guarantee to be afforded a process and not the guarantee of an outcome. Any data subject who wishes to exercise any of the above-mentioned rights under the EU GDPR may do so by submitting a Service Request with the Office of Cybersecurity. Website Data Collected and Why; Cookies Please see the “ Type of Information Collected and Why ” section above for details regarding information collected from KSU websites and cookies. Security of Personal Data subject to the EU GDPR All personal data collected or processed by KSU under the scope of the KSU EU General Data Protection Regulation Compliance Policy must comply with organizational security controls, standards, processes and policies. If you have questions about this Notice or believe that your personal information has been released without your consent or if you wish to correct information held by KSU, please contact us at via Service Now . KSU will not share your information with third parties except as necessary to meet one of KSU’s lawful purposes. Georgia Open Records Act As an entity of the government of the State of Georgia, KSU is subject to the provisions of the Georgia Open Records Act (ORA). Except for those records that are exempt from disclosure under the ORA, the ORA provides that all citizens are entitled to view the records of state agencies on request and to make copies for a fee. For more information on KSU’s ORA compliance, please visit the Open Records Requests page on the Division of Legal Affairs website . KSU is dedicated to providing a safe and healthy environment for those who participate, volunteer and work in University sponsored programs, or programs operated by third parties held on University facilities. In conjunction with BOR Policy - Programs Serving Minors Kennesaw State University established KSU Programs Serving Minors Policy on May 1, 2017. This policy governs all KSU programs involving minors to ensure compliance with federal and state laws and the BOR/USG policies. Key areas of focus under this policy are registration, education and compliance. KSU staff, faculty and sponsoring departments of programs that involve minors should review the Program Serving Minors website, training and resources to become familiar with the policies, procedures and requirements needed to comply with both BOR and KSU policies. BOR Policy - Programs Serving Minors The Board of Regents (BOR) of the University System of Georgia (USG) - Programs Serving Minors policy applies to outside organizations and groups that may use institutional facilities for programs serving non-student minors. The effective date for this policy is Monday, May 1, 2017. KSU Policies Relating to Minors on Campus The Policy at KSU website provides links to KSU and related policies that govern all activities on KSU campuses. Listed below are links to key ones that govern activities involving minors on KSU campuses. KSU Programs Serving Minors Policy The purpose of the KSU Programs Serving Minors Policy is to provide guidance to the campus community and ensure compliance with federal and state laws and the BOR/USG policies and procedures. This policy was presented to KSU governance bodies for feedback in November/December, 2016. On December 13, 2016 the KSU President approved this policy to post on the Policy at KSU website and to submit to the BOR as required by January 1, 2017. The effective date for this policy is Monday, May 1, 2017. KSU Employee Handbook 5.4.5 Children in the Workplace The KSU Employee Handbook 5.4.5 Children in the Workplace governs employees and their children on KSU campuses and states: "The University cannot accommodate children of employees and students on campus during normal operating hours. Children are welcome to make brief visits and to attend scheduled events." KSU Institutional Review Board (IRB) The KSU Institutional Review Board (IRB) regulates all research activities involving human subjects on the campus of Kennesaw State University, including research activities involving minors. KSU requires prior review and approval from the IRB for all research involving human participants. KSU University Handbook Policy 5.2.13 Visits by Children KSU University Handbook Policy 5.2.13 Visits by Children governs visits by children on KSU campuses and states: "The university cannot accommodate children of the faculty, staff, and students on campus during normal operating hours; i.e., 8:00 a.m. - 10:30 p.m., Monday through Thursday, and 8:00 a.m. - 5:00 p.m., Friday. Children are welcome to attend scheduled events and to make brief visits when accompanied by a parent or other adult." text: Skip to main navigation Skip to main content Skip to footer Apply Visit Give Calendar A-Z Index Campus Resources Current Students Faculty & Staff Parents & Families Alumni & Friends Community & Business campus.kennesaw.edu Campus Resources Current Students Faculty & Staff Parents & Families Alumni & Friends Community & Business campus.kennesaw.edu About KSU About KSU University News KSU Community Strategic Plan University Initiatives Alumni Careers Conferences University Leadership Office of the President Administration KSU Foundation Academics Programs & Information Degrees & Programs Academic Affairs Global Education KSU Online Double Owl Pathways Academic Calendar University Libraries Course Catalog Academic Advising Colleges Coles College of Business Geer College of the Arts College of Architecture & Construction Management Bagwell College of Education College of Computing & Software Engineering Norman J.
